**Sūrat Yūsuf**

(Makkan, except verses 1, 2, 3 and 7, which are Madinan. It has one hundred and eleven verses. [It was revealed after Sūrat Hūd].)

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Those﴾ refers to the verses of the sūrah. ﴿And the Clear Book﴾ is the sūrah, meaning: those verses that were revealed to you in this sūrah, the verses of the sūrah, whose matter is manifest in proving the inimitability of the Arabs and in rebuking them. Or, they are the verses that make clear to whoever reflects upon them that they are from God and not from human beings. Or, they are the clear verses whose meanings are not obscure to the Arabs, because they were revealed in their language. Or, what is meant is that I have made clear in them what the Jews asked about: the story of Joseph. It is related that the scholars of the Jews said to the leaders of the polytheists, "Ask Muḥammad why the family of Jacob moved from Syria to Egypt." And concerning the story of Joseph: ﴿We have sent it down﴾, meaning, We have sent down this Book, which contains the story of Joseph, ﴿as an Arabic Qur'an﴾, and some of the Qur'an is called a Qur'an, because the word "Qur'an" is a generic noun that applies to all of it and to part of it. ﴿So that you may understand﴾, meaning, that you may comprehend it, grasp its meanings, and that it not be confusing to you.

﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, "Why are its verses not explained in detail?"﴾

The word *al-qaṣaṣ* (the narratives) has two usages. It may be a verbal noun (*maṣdar*, the infinitive) meaning "the act of narrating", as you say: *qaṣṣa al-ḥadīth yaqussuhu qaṣaṣan*, just as you say: *shalla yashullu shallan*, meaning "he drove him away". It may also be the pattern *fa'al* used in the sense of *maf'ūl* (the passive participle, "that which is narrated"), like *al-naqḍ* (the shaking out) and *al-ḥasab* (the reckoning, i.e., "that which is counted"). Similar to it are *al-naba'* (the news) and *al-khabar* (the report), which mean "that which is reported" and "that which is told". It is also permissible that it be the naming of the object by the verbal noun, like *al-khalq* (the creation, meaning "the created") and *al-ṣayd* (the game, meaning "the hunted").

If the verbal noun is intended, then its meaning is: We narrate to you the best narration. ﴿By Our revealing to you this Qur'an﴾, meaning, by Our revelation to you of this sūrah, with *aḥsan* (the best) put in the accusative (*naṣb*) as a verbal noun because it is in a construct relationship (*iḍāfa*) with it, and the object of narration is omitted, because His saying ﴿by Our revealing to you this Qur'an﴾ suffices in its place. It is also permissible that ﴿this Qur'an﴾ be in the accusative governed by *naqussu* (We narrate), as if it were said: "We narrate to you this Qur'an, the best narration, by Our revelation to you." The meaning of "the best narration" is that it is narrated in the most wondrous method and the most marvelous style. Do you not see that this account is narrated in the books of the earlier peoples and in the books of history, yet you do not find its narration in any of those books close to its narration in the Qur'an?

If by *al-qaṣaṣ* the narrated thing is intended, then its meaning is: We narrate to you the best of what is narrated of accounts. It is the best only because of what it contains of lessons, subtleties, wisdoms and wonders that are not in others [[The phrase "laysat fi ghayrihā" is perhaps "laysat fi ghayrihi", as in the wording of al-Nasafī. (ʿ)]]. And it is apparent that it is the best of what is narrated within its genre, as one says of a man: "He is the most knowledgeable of people and the most excellent", meaning in his field.

If you say: From what is the derivation of *al-qaṣaṣ*? I say: It is from *qaṣṣa atharahu*, meaning "he followed his trace", because the one who narrates a account follows what he has memorized of it bit by bit, just as one says: *talā al-Qur'ān*, meaning "he recited the Qur'an", because he follows what he has memorized of it verse after verse.

﴿And indeed you were﴾: the *in* is the lightened (*mukhaffafa*) form of the heavy *inna*. The *lām* is what distinguishes it from the negative *in*. The pronoun in ﴿before it﴾ refers back to His saying "what We revealed". The meaning is: Indeed the matter and the account, before Our revelation to you, you were among those *ghāfilīn* (the heedless) of it, meaning, among those ignorant of it. You had no knowledge of it at all, and no part of it had ever reached your hearing.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 4:

﴿When Joseph said﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the best of stories﴾, and it is a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal, where the substitute is a part of or contained within what it replaces), because the time includes the stories and what is narrated. So when its time is narrated, the stories are narrated. Or it is governed by an implied verb, "remember" (udhkur). Yusuf (Joseph) is a Hebrew name. It was said to be Arabic, but this is not correct, because if it were Arabic it would not take tanwin (the nunation that is dropped here), since it would have no reason for diptote treatment other than definiteness.

If you ask: what do you say about one who reads "Yusuf" with a kasra on the sin, or with a fatha on it? Can it be said on his reading that it is Arabic, because it fits the pattern of the imperfect active or passive from asafa, so that the diptote treatment would be due to definiteness and the verbal pattern? I answer: No, because the well-known reading is established by the testimony that the word is non-Arabic, so it cannot be Arabic at one time and non-Arabic at another. Similar to Yusuf is Yunus (Jonah): these three dialects have been transmitted for it, yet one does not say it is Arabic, because in two of them it has the pattern of the imperfect of anasa and aunasa.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "When it is said: Who is the noble one? Say: The noble one, son of the noble, son of the noble, son of the noble: Yusuf son of Yaqub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim." [[Reported by al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and al-Hakim, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "Indeed the noble one, son of the noble," and so on. In al-Bukhari, from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "The noble, son of the noble," and so on. It is also in the agreed-upon collection (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from Abu Hurayrah, but with the wording: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked: Which of the people is most noble? He said: The most noble of them before Allah is the most righteous of them. They said: O Messenger of Allah, we are not asking you about this. He said: Then the most noble of people is Yusuf, the Prophet of Allah, son of a Prophet of Allah, son of a Prophet of Allah, son of the Friend of Allah."]]

﴿O my father﴾: it is read with the three vowel-harakat (on the final consonant). If you ask: what is this ta'? I answer: it is the feminine tā' (tā' al-ta'nith), which took the place of the ya' of possessive pronoun (ya' al-idafah, "my"). The proof that it is a feminine tā' is that it changes into hā' when pausing.

If you ask: how is it permissible to attach the feminine tā' to a masculine noun? I answer: just as it is permissible in your saying: "hamamah dhakar" (a male pigeon), "shah dhakar" (a male sheep), "rajul rabi'ah" (a man of medium build), and "ghulam yufa'ah" (a youth).

If you ask: why was the feminine tā' allowed to replace the ya' of possession? I answer: because the feminine and the possessive correspond in that each is an addition attached to the noun at its end.

If you ask: what is this kasrah? I answer: it is the kasrah that was before the ya' in your saying "ya abi," which has slid over to the tā', because the feminine tā' requires that what precedes it be fatha-vowelled.

If you ask: why did the kasrah not drop out in favour of the fatha required by the tā', leaving the tā' sukun? I answer: that was not permitted for it, because it is a noun, and nouns by their nature take movement, since they are basic in i'rab (grammatical inflection). The ya' may be made sukun, though its original state is to be vowelled, for lightness, because it is a soft letter (harf layyin). But the tā' is a sound consonant, like the kaf of the pronoun, so it must be vowelled.

If you ask: the combination of the tā' with this kasrah resembles the combination of the replacement (al-iwad) with what it replaces (al-mu'awwad minhu), because it has the status of the ya': when you say "ya ghulam," just as "ya abati" is not permitted, so "ya abat" is not permitted. I answer: the ya' and the kasrah before it are two things, and the tā' is a replacement for one of the two, namely the ya', while the kasrah is not affected, so there is no combining of the replacement with what it replaces, unless the tā' and the ya' are combined and nothing else. Do you not see their saying "ya abata," where the alif is a substitute for the tā', how it is permitted to combine it with the tā', and this is not considered a combining of the replacement with what it replaces? So the kasrah is further removed from that.

If you ask: the kasrah in "ya ghulam" indicates the possessive, because it is the companion and adjoining of the ya'. If it indicates the same in "ya abat," then the replacing tā' is superfluous, its presence being like its absence.

I answer: rather, its status with the tā' is like its status with the ya' when you say "ya abi."

If you ask: what is the reasoning of the one who reads with fatha on the tā' and with damma? I answer: as for the one who reads with fatha, he deleted the alif from "ya abata" and retained the fatha before it, just as the one who deletes the ya' in "ya ghulam" did. It may also be said that he vowelled it with the vowel of the bā' that replaced it in your saying "ya abi."

As for the one who reads with damma, he considered it a noun ending in a feminine tā', and treated it like feminine nouns ending in tā', saying "ya abat," just as you say "ya tabah" [[his saying "ya tabah," with a kasrah on the tā' and a shaddah on the bā': the severe calamity. In another copy: "ya ibnah," as noted in the margin of the original (ʿ)]] without regard to its being a replacement for the ya' of possession.

It is read: "innī ra'aytu" with the ya' vowelled. And "aḥad ʿashar" with the ʿayn sukun, for lightness, because of the succession of moving letters in what is in fact one word. Likewise up to "tis'ata ʿashar," except "ithnā ʿashar," so that two sukun letters do not meet.

﴿I saw﴾ here is from ru'ya (dream), not from ru'yah (sight), because what he mentioned is known to be a dream. For if the sun and the moon had gathered with the stars prostrating to Yusuf in a waking state, it would have been a great sign for Yaqub (peace be upon him), and it would not have been hidden from him and from the people.

If you ask: what are the names of those stars? I answer: Jabir narrated that a Jew came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, tell me about the stars that Yusuf saw." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was silent. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) came down and informed him of that. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to the Jew, "If I tell you, will you accept (Islam)?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Jiryan, al-Tariq, al-Dhayyal, Qabis, ʿAmudan, al-Faliq, al-Musbih, al-Dharuh, al-Farigh, Wathab, and Dhu al-Kaftayn."

[[The narration: "Yusuf saw them, the sun and the moon came down from the sky and prostrated to him." Reported by al-Hakim through Asbat, from al-Suddi, from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Sabit, from Jabir, who said: "A Jew came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Muhammad, do you know the stars that Yusuf saw, and they prostrated to him? ..." and he was silent. The hadith... It does not mention the sun and the moon among them, and he said: Yusuf saw them encircling the shoulders of the sky, prostrating to him, and he added: he related it to his father, and he said to him: "This is a matter that has been scattered, and Allah will gather it after." Narrated by Abu Ya'la, al-Bazzar, al-Bayhaqi, Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, al-Tabarani, and Abu Hatim, in the narration of al-Hakim, from Zuhayr through al-Suddi, similarly. Al-Uqayli mentioned it from his narration and said: it is not established. Al-Bazzar said: we know no route for it other than this. Al-Hakim is not strong, and likewise al-Bayhaqi said that al-Hakim alone transmitted it, and he overlooked the route of al-Hakim's teacher. Ibn al-Jawzi mentioned it among the fabricated (mawdu'at) reports and faulted it on account of al-Hakim. The route of al-Hakim is refuted by the ruling. Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Ilal related from Abu Zur'ah that he said: it is a munkar hadith.]]

The Jew said: "Yes, by Allah, these are their names."

It was said: the sun and the moon are his parents, and the stars are his brothers. It was also said: his father and his maternal aunt, and the stars are his brothers.

From Wahb: Yusuf saw, when he was seven years old, that eleven long staves were fixed in the ground in the shape of a circle, and a small staff leapt over them until it uprooted them and overcame them. He described that to his father, who said: "Beware of mentioning this to your brothers." Then, when he was twelve years old, he saw the sun, the moon and the stars prostrating to him. He related it to his father, who said to him: "Do not relate it to them, lest they plot against you."

It was said: between Yusuf's dream and his brothers' coming to him there were forty years. It was also said: eighty.

If you ask: why was the sun and the moon postponed? I answer: they were postponed so that they could be conjoined to the stars by way of specification, to show their excellence and their singular distinction in merit over other celestial bodies, just as Jibril and Mikail were postponed from the angels, and then conjoined to them for that reason.

It is also permissible that the waw be in the sense of "with," meaning: I saw the stars along with the sun and the moon.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the repetition of "saw"? [[Mahmud said: "If you ask what is the meaning of the repetition of 'saw'... etc." Ahmad said: Better than that is that the speech was lengthened between the verb and the circumstance, so the mention of the verb was repeated to match the circumstance, which is the intended matter, since the verse concerns prostration, and Allah knows best.]] I answer: it is not a repetition. It is rather a new sentence, given as an answer to an implied question. As if Yaqub (peace be upon him), when Yusuf said ﴿Indeed, I saw eleven stars﴾, had said: "How did you see them?" asking about the manner of his seeing. So he said ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾.

If you ask: why were they treated as rational beings in ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾? I answer: because he described them with what is specific to rational beings, namely prostration, he applied to them the rulings of rational beings, as if they were rational. This is common and widespread in their speech: that a thing is associated with another thing in some respect, so it is given one of the rulings of that thing, to show the effect of the association and proximity.

Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) recognised from the vision that Yusuf would be brought by God to a station of wisdom, would be chosen by Him for prophethood, and would be favoured with the honour of both abodes, just as He had done with his forefathers. So he feared for him the envy and malice of the brothers.

Ru'ya (vision) means the same as ru'ya-h (sight), except that it is specific to what is seen in sleep rather than in waking. The two are distinguished by the feminine endings, as it is said: al-qurba (nearness) and al-qurba (the relative nearness), i.e., the form with the ta' marbuta and the form with the alif maqsura, as in "al-qurba" and "al-qurba." It is also read ru'yak, with the hamza changed to a waw. al-Kisa'i heard ruyyak and riyyak, with idgham (assimilation) and with the ra' vowelled with damma and with kasra; but these are weak, because the waw is in the position of a hamza, so its idgham is not strong, just as idgham was not strong in their saying "ittazara" from al-izar (waist-wrapper) and "ittajara" from al-ajr (wage). Fa-yakīdū (so that they plot against you) is in the accusative, with "an" (that) implied; the meaning is: if you relate it to them, they will plot against you. If you ask: why was it not said "fa-yakīdūka" (so they will scheme against you), as was said "fa-kīdūnī" (so scheme against me)? I say: the verb was made to imply a verb that takes the preposition lam, so that it conveys the sense of the act of plotting together with the sense of the implied verb; this makes it more emphatic and more forceful in intimidation, like "fa-yaḥtālū laka" (so that they devise a stratagem against you). Do you not see how it is emphasised by the verbal noun: "Indeed, Satan is to man an open enemy" (innahu lakum ʿaduwwun mubīn), manifest in enmity, for what he did to Adam and Eve, and by his saying "Certainly I shall sit in wait for them on Your straight path" (la-aqʿudanna lahum ṣirāṭaka al-mustaqīm)? So it entails plotting, deceit and every evil, to ensnare whoever carries it out, and one is not safe from his leading them to the like. "Wa-kadhālika" (and thus): the like of this choosing—"yajtabīka rabbuka" (your Lord will choose you): that is, just as He chose you for this great vision, which indicates nobility, might and greatness of rank, so likewise your Lord will choose you for great matters.

His saying "wa-yuʿallimuka" (and He will teach you) is a fresh statement, not included in the force of the comparison, as if it were said: "He teaches you and completes His favour upon you." Al-ijtibāʾ means al-iṣṭifāʾ (choosing), a reflexive form from jibaytu al-shayʾ, when you gather a thing for yourself, and jibaytu al-māʾ fī al-ḥawḍ, I collected the water in the basin. Al-aḥādīth (the narrations): the vision, because a vision is either a discourse of the self, or of an angel, or of a devil.

Its ta'wil means its interpretation and explanation, and Yusuf (peace be upon him) was the most skilled of people in interpreting visions and the most accurate in expounding them. It is also permissible that by the ta'wil of narrations is meant the meanings of God's books and the ways of the prophets, and what is obscure and confused for people of their aims and purposes; he explains them to them, clarifies them, and guides them to the stored-up wisdom within them. They are called narrations because he speaks of them on behalf of God and His messengers, saying: "God said" and "the Messenger said such and such." Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: "Then in what narration after this will they believe?" (Q. 45:6) and "God has sent down the best narration" (Q. 39:23)? It is a collective noun for ḥadīth and not the plural of uḥdūthah.

The meaning of completing the favour upon them is that He joined the favour of this world to the favour of the Hereafter, by making them prophets and kings in this world, and by transferring them from it to the highest ranks in Paradise. It is said: He completed it upon Ibrahim by friendship (khullah), by deliverance from the Fire, and from the sacrifice of the son. And upon Ishaq by his deliverance from being slaughtered, and by ransoming him with a great sacrifice, and by bringing Yaʿqub and the tribes (al-asbāt) from his loins. It is also said:

Yaʿqub knew that Yusuf would become a prophet, and his brothers prophets, by inference from the light of the stars; therefore he said "and upon the family of Yaʿqub" (wa-ʿalā āli Yaʿqūb). It is also said: when the vision reached Yusuf's brothers, they envied him and said: "Has he not been content that his brothers should prostrate to him, until his parents prostrated to him too?" It is also said: Yaʿqub favoured him with extra love and tenderness because of his youth, and because of the signs he saw in him. His brothers were envious of him, and when he saw the vision he doubled his love for him, so that he would hug him to his breast every hour and could not bear to be apart from him, so their envy intensified. It is also said: when he related his vision to Yaʿqub, he said: "This is a scattered matter, which God will gather for you after a long time." Āl Yaʿqub means his family, and they are his offspring and others. The origin of āl is ahl (family), as shown by its diminutive uhayl, except that it is used only of those who have distinction. One says: āl al-nabī (the family of the Prophet), and āl al-malik (the family of the king). One does not say āl al-ḥāʾik (the family of the weaver) or āl al-ḥajjām (the family of the cupper), but ahluhumā. By "the two fathers" he meant the grandfather and the great-grandfather, since they are in the status of a father in origin; that is why they say "son of so-and-so," even when there are many generations between him and so-and-so. "Ibrahim and Ishaq" is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to "your two fathers." "Inna rabbaka ʿalīm" (indeed your Lord is All-Knowing): He knows who deserves to be chosen; "ḥakīm" (All-Wise): He does not complete His favour except upon the one who merits it.

Yaʿqub (peace be upon him) recognised from the vision that Yusuf would be brought by God to a station of wisdom, would be chosen by Him for prophethood, and would be favoured with the honour of both abodes, just as He had done with his forefathers. So he feared for him the envy and malice of the brothers.

Ru'ya (vision) means the same as ru'ya-h (sight), except that it is specific to what is seen in sleep rather than in waking. The two are distinguished by the feminine endings, as it is said: al-qurba (nearness) and al-qurba (the relative nearness), i.e., the form with the ta' marbuta and the form with the alif maqsura, as in "al-qurba" and "al-qurba." It is also read ru'yak, with the hamza changed to a waw. al-Kisa'i heard ruyyak and riyyak, with idgham (assimilation) and with the ra' vowelled with damma and with kasra; but these are weak, because the waw is in the position of a hamza, so its idgham is not strong, just as idgham was not strong in their saying "ittazara" from al-izar (waist-wrapper) and "ittajara" from al-ajr (wage). Fa-yakīdū (so that they plot against you) is in the accusative, with "an" (that) implied; the meaning is: if you relate it to them, they will plot against you. If you ask: why was it not said "fa-yakīdūka" (so they will scheme against you), as was said "fa-kīdūnī" (so scheme against me)? I say: the verb was made to imply a verb that takes the preposition lam, so that it conveys the sense of the act of plotting together with the sense of the implied verb; this makes it more emphatic and more forceful in intimidation, like "fa-yaḥtālū laka" (so that they devise a stratagem against you). Do you not see how it is emphasised by the verbal noun: "Indeed, Satan is to man an open enemy" (innahu lakum ʿaduwwun mubīn), manifest in enmity, for what he did to Adam and Eve, and by his saying "Certainly I shall sit in wait for them on Your straight path" (la-aqʿudanna lahum ṣirāṭaka al-mustaqīm)? So it entails plotting, deceit and every evil, to ensnare whoever carries it out, and one is not safe from his leading them to the like. "Wa-kadhālika" (and thus): the like of this choosing—"yajtabīka rabbuka" (your Lord will choose you): that is, just as He chose you for this great vision, which indicates nobility, might and greatness of rank, so likewise your Lord will choose you for great matters.

His saying "wa-yuʿallimuka" (and He will teach you) is a fresh statement, not included in the force of the comparison, as if it were said: "He teaches you and completes His favour upon you." Al-ijtibāʾ means al-iṣṭifāʾ (choosing), a reflexive form from jibaytu al-shayʾ, when you gather a thing for yourself, and jibaytu al-māʾ fī al-ḥawḍ, I collected the water in the basin. Al-aḥādīth (the narrations): the vision, because a vision is either a discourse of the self, or of an angel, or of a devil.

In Yusuf and his brothers there are signs (ayat) of evidence and proofs of God's power and wisdom in everything, for those who ask, for whoever inquires about their story and comes to know it. It has also been said: the signs are evidence of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) for the Jews who asked him about it, and he informed them of its truth without having heard it from anyone and without having read a book.

It is recited as "ayah" (a sign), and in some copies of the Qur'an it reads "ibrah" (a lesson). It has also been said: God related to the Prophet (peace be upon him) the account of Yusuf and the envy of his brothers toward him only because he saw the hostility of his own people toward him, so that he might take them as an example (yatasa bihi).

It has been said of their names:

Yahudha (Judah), Rubil (Reuben), Shim'un (Simeon), Lawi (Levi), Rabalun (Zebulun), Yashjur (Issachar), Dinah (Dan? no: Dinah is named here as a name in this list), Dan, Naftali (Naphtali), Jad (Gad), and Ashir (Asher).

The first seven were from Liya, daughter of Yaqub's maternal aunt, and the last four were from two concubines, Zilfa and Bilha. When Liya died, he married her sister Rahil (Rachel), and she bore him Binyamin (Benjamin) and Yusuf.

**Layūsufu**: the *lām* is *lām al-ibtidāʾ* (the emphatic *lām* that marks the beginning of a sentence). It carries emphasis and confirms the content of the sentence. They meant that the increase in their father's love for them is a established fact.

[[Mahmud said: "The *lām* is for emphasis (*lām al-tawkīd*); it was introduced to indicate that the increase in their father's love for them is an established fact... etc." Ahmad said:

This supports the reading of Ibn Marwan, *hāʾulāʾi banātī hunna aṭhharu lakum* ("These are my daughters, they are purer for you"), with *hunna* in the accusative. Sibawayh said of it: "Ibn Marwan was bold in his solecism," meaning he was firmly established in it. Since it is supported by the reading of Amir al-Mu'minin, may God honour his face, we must seek a sound interpretation for it, and this is not far off, God willing. We say: if they had said, "Yūsuf and his brother are more beloved to our father than us, and we are *we*," following the pattern of:

*Anā Abū al-Najm wa-shiʿrī shiʿrī*
("I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is poetry")

and like *anā anā* ("I am I") and *anta anta* ("you are you"), there would have been no objection to its eloquence. You know that the meaning of *anā anā* is: I am the one described by the well-known attributes, which need not be mentioned. In that case, there is no difficulty in omitting the predicate, since it is equal to the subject and not longer than it in wording, and it avoids repeating the same word, while the context points to what is omitted. If that is so, then the statement of those who said *Layūsufu wa-akhūhu aḥabbu ilā abīnā minnā wa-naḥnu* means: "and we are *we*," but they dispensed with the predicate for the reason we have mentioned. Their saying *naḥnu* is a complete utterance by implication with what was mentioned, so there is no oddity in a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) coming after it. The same applies to His words *hāʾulāʾi banātī hunna aṭhharu lakum*: *hunna* is in the position of a complete utterance. The meaning is: "These are my daughters, who are known for their apparent praiseworthy qualities." The original sentence was *hunna hunna*, so the circumstantial clause came after the completion. And God knows best.]] There is no doubt about it.

**Wa-akhūhu** refers to Benjamin. They said "his brother" although they were all his brothers, because their mother was one.

It is said that **aḥabb** is used for the two of them, because *afʿal* (the comparative/superlative form) is not differentiated between singular and plural, nor between masculine and feminine when *min* accompanies it. But it must be differentiated when it has the definite article *al-*. When it is in a construct phrase (*idāfa*), both options are permitted.

The *wāw* in **wa-naḥnu ʿuṣbatun** is the *wāw* of circumstance (*wāw al-ḥāl*). The meaning is: he prefers the two of them in love over us, although they are two small children who have no capability and no benefit, while we are a group of ten men, capable and able to attend to his needs. So we deserve the greater love more than they do, because of our superiority in number and usefulness.

**Inna abānā la-fī ḍalālin mubīn**: that is, "our father is clearly going astray from the path of right judgment in this matter."

**Al-ʿuṣbah** and **al-ʿiṣābah** mean a group of ten or more. It is said up to forty. They were so named because they are a group by whom affairs are supported and who suffice in calamities.

It is narrated by al-Nazzal ibn Sabrah from ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, that he read *wa-naḥnu ʿuṣbatan* with the accusative. It is also said that the meaning is "and we gather as a group (*ʿuṣbah*)." Ibn al-Anbari said: this is like the way the Arabs say, *innamā al-ʿāmirī ʿammatuhu*, meaning: he takes care of his paternal aunt.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 9:

"Kill Yusuf" is part of what He related after His saying, "when they said." It is as if they all agreed on this, except for the one who said, "Do not kill Yusuf." It is also said that the one who ordered the killing was Shim'un, and it is said that he was Dan, while the rest were content. They made him (Yusuf) "a land" (ardan), "a land" that is unknown, indefinite, and far from inhabited areas. This is the meaning of its being indefinite and stripped of description. Because it is vague in this respect, it was put in the accusative as indefinite adverbial nouns of place: "yakhlu lakum wajhu abikum" ("your father's face will be free for you"), meaning that he will turn toward you with a single turning, not turning away from you toward others. The intended meaning is the purity of his love for them, free from anyone who shares it with them and competes with them for it. So mentioning the "face" serves to depict the sense of his turning toward them, because when a man turns toward something he turns his face to it. It is also permissible for "face" to refer to the essence (dhat), as in His saying, "and there remains the face of your Lord" (Qur'an 55:27). It is also said that "yakhlu lakum" means he will be free for you from preoccupation with Yusuf, "min ba'dihi" meaning "after him," that is, after Yusuf, i.e., after you have dealt with him by killing or banishing him. Or the pronoun may refer to the verbal noun of "uqtulu" or "utrahu" (the act of killing or casting away). "Qawman salihin" means "repentant people," turning back to God for what you have done to him.

Or he may set right what is between you and your father by an excuse you prepare. Or your worldly affairs may be set in order and arranged after him, with your father's face being clear for you. "Takunu" is either jussive, coordinated with "yakhlu lakum," or accusative by the implied "an" with the "wa" meaning "with," as in His saying, "and conceal not the truth" (Qur'an 2:42).

Speaker among them: he was Judah, and he was the best of them in opinion concerning him. And he is the one who said, "I will not leave the land" (cf. 12:80).

He said to them: "Killing is a great thing. Cast him into the depths of the well" (ghayabat al-jubb), which is its bottom, and that which is hidden from the eye of the one who looks, and darker at its base. Al-Munakhkhal said:

"And if one day my grave conceals me in its depths (ghayabati), then travel in my manner (sayri) among the clan and the family."
[[Of al-Munakhkhal. Al-ghayabah is what is hidden from the viewer at the bottom of a well or the like. He means: if my tomb conceals me, a metaphor for my death, then travel in my manner, i.e., mourn me and spread the mention of my qualities, as is the custom of the Arabs when a chief of theirs dies. It is also possible that he is enjoining his relatives to good, and that they should travel in a manner like his, doing as he did toward his neighbors and kin.]]

He meant the depth of his pit in which he is buried. It was read as ghayabat (plural), ghayabat (with shaddah). Al-Jahdari read ghaybah. Al-jubb is a well that has not been lined with stones, because the earth is cut (tujabb) into a pit only, nothing more.

"Some of the travelers (sayyarah) will pick him up" (yaltaqituhu): some of the caravan, some people traveling along the road. It was also read taltaqituhu with the feminine ta', according to the sense, since "some of the caravan" is a caravan (sayyarah), as in the verse:

"As the spear's breast was reddened with blood (kama shariqat sadr al-qanah min al-dam)" [[The explanation of this witness was given earlier in the first volume, page 395, so refer to it if you wish. Its editor.]]. And from the same usage: "some of his fingers were lost (dhahabat ba'd asabi'ihi)."

"If you are doing (in kuntum fa'ilin)": if you are going to do what achieves your aim; this is the opinion.

Why do you not trust us with Joseph, when we are sincere toward him? (Qur'an 12:11)

Recited with both nuns made clear (tuzhir al-nunayn), and with idgham (assimilation) both with ishmam (a slight rounding of the lips) and without ishmam. Also: timan, with a kasra on the ta' together with idgham. The meaning: "Why do you not fear for him from us, when we want good for him, love him, and are compassionate toward him? And nothing has been found in our conduct toward him that indicates opposition to sincere counsel and affection." [[His words "that indicates opposition to sincere counsel and affection" — al-mahabba (love). It is said wamaqahu, yamquhu, with kasra in both, meaning he loved him, so he is wāmiq (one who loves), as in al-Sihah.]] They meant by this that, since they had resolved upon a plot against Joseph, they wanted to draw Jacob away from his opinion and to bring him to a state in which he would be under their guardianship. This is evidence that he (Jacob) perceived from them something that made him not trust them with Joseph.

Yartaʿ (وَيَرْتَعْ): "let him enjoy himself," i.e., we will expand in eating fruits and other things. The origin of al-rutʿa is abundance and ease. It is recited as nartaʿ (نرتع), from irtaʿā, yartaʿā. Also recited as yartaʿ and yalʿab (يلعب) with the ya', and as yartaʿ from arta'a mashiyatahu (to pasture his livestock). Al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Sayyaba recited:

yartaʿ with a kasra on the ʿayn, and yalʿab with a raf' (ḍamma), as a mubtadaʾ (inceptive subject).

If you ask: how did Jacob, peace be upon him, permit them to play? I say: their play was racing and archery, so that they would train themselves in what is needed for fighting the enemy, not for amusement, as evidenced by His words, ﴿Indeed, we went off racing one another﴾ (12:17). They called it "play" only because it resembled it in form.

The lam here is the lam of emphasis (lam al-ibtida', the "lam of beginning"), as in the verse ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them﴾. Its entry into the verb is one of the two causes of the present tense that Sibawayh mentioned. He gave two reasons for his grief: first, that their taking him away and his separation from him would grieve him, because he could not bear to be parted from him even for an hour; and second, his fear for him from the wolf's attack when they were heedless of him. [[Mahmud said: "He offered them two reasons: his grief at being separated from him, and his fear for him from the wolf when they were heedless of him..." etc. Ahmad said: The more preoccupying of the two matters for his heart was the fear of the wolf for him, because that is the likely cause of his destruction. As for his grief at separation for the short time that he would graze, play and return to him safe soon after, that is a minor matter. It was as though they were occupied only with reassuring him and calming him about the thing that most troubled him. And God knows best.]] Or his concern for them in their pasturing and playing was small, and his care did not trust in their guarding him. It has also been said: he saw in a dream that the wolf had attacked Joseph, so he was wary of it, and therefore he said that, and so he gave them the reason. In their proverbs: "Calamity is entrusted to speech." The word ﴿الذِّئْبُ﴾ (al-dhi'b, "the wolf") was recited with a hamza, in accordance with the original form, and also with the hamza lightened. It has been said that its derivation is from "tadhaabat al-rih" (تذاءبت الريح), meaning when the wind came from every direction.

The oath is omitted; its implied form is: "By God, if the wolf eats him," and the lam is a preparatory lam (lam al-muwatta'a) for the oath. The words "Innā idhan la-khāsirūn" ("Indeed then we would be losers") are the answer to the oath, standing in for the answer to the conditional clause. The waw in "wa-naḥnu ʿuṣba" is the waw of the circumstantial clause (wāw al-ḥāl).

They swore to him: if what he feared of the wolf snatching his brother from among them should happen, and their condition was that they were ten men, by whose likeness affairs are carried out and calamities are averted, then they would indeed be people who are losers, meaning those who perish through weakness, incapacity and impotence.

Or: they deserve to perish, because there is no benefit or use in their lives. Or: they deserve to be cursed with loss and ruin, and to have it said: "May God make them lose and destroy them, since the wolf ate one of them while they were present."

It was also said: if we cannot protect one of us, then our livestock have perished, and we have lost them. If you ask: he gave them two excuses, so why did they answer one and not the other? I say: it was the one that angered them and made them taste the "amrayn" (bitter calamities) that they answered, so they lent him deaf ears and paid it no heed.

[[The words "wa-yudhīqahum al-amrayn": al-amrayn (with the plural nūn ending) means the calamities; so noted in the margin. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-amrān are poverty and old age. Also there: al-amr is the intestines in which the dung gathers. The poet said:

So do not destroy the matter and what follows it, nor destroy the one with thin, lean bones.

Abū Zayd said: "I met from him the amrayn" (with the plural nūn), meaning the calamities. End of the marginal note (ʿ).]]

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 15:

"That they should make him" is the object of "ajma'u" (they resolved), from your saying: "ajma'a al-amr wa-azma'ahu" (he firmed up the matter and resolved upon it), ﴿So resolve upon your plan﴾.

It is also read: "fi ghayabat al-jubb" (in the depths of the well). It is said that it is a well in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It is said: in the land of the Jordan. It is said: between Egypt and Midian. It is said: three farsakhs from Ya'qub's dwelling. The answer to "lamma" (when) is omitted, and its meaning is: they did to him what they did of harm. It is related that when they brought him out to the desert they showed him enmity and began to humiliate him and beat him, and whenever he sought help from one of them, he got nothing but contempt and beating, until they nearly killed him. He began to cry out: "O father, if only you knew what your son is suffering at the hands of the sons of the slave-women!" Then Yahudha said: "Did you not give me a covenant that you would not kill him?" When they wanted to throw him into the well, he clung to their garments, and they pulled them off his hand. He then clung to the wall of the well, so they tied his hands and stripped off his shirt. He said: "O brothers, return my shirt to me so I may cover myself with it." They had only stripped it off so that they could smear it with blood and deceive their father with it. They said to him: "Call upon the sun, the moon and the eleven stars, and they will keep you company," and they lowered him into the well. When he reached halfway down, they dropped him so that he would die. There was water in the well, and he fell into it. Then he took refuge on a rock and stood on it, weeping. They called out to him, and he thought it was mercy that had come to them, so he answered them. They then wanted to crush him to death, but Yahudha prevented them, and Yahudha used to bring him food. It is narrated that when Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was cast into the fire and stripped of his clothes, Jibril came to him with a shirt of silk from Paradise and dressed him in it. Ibrahim passed it to Ishaq, and Ishaq to Ya'qub, who put it in an amulet that he hung around Yusuf's neck. Then Jibril came, took it out, and dressed him in it.

"And We revealed to him": it is said that he was given revelation in his childhood, as revelation was given to Yahya and Isa. It is said that he was of age at that time. It is related from al-Hasan that he was seventeen years old.

"You will surely inform them of this affair of theirs": the revelation was given to him only to comfort him in the darkness and loneliness, and to give him good news of what his affair would come to. Its meaning: you will certainly be delivered from what you are in, and you will surely tell your brothers what they did to you, "while they do not perceive" that you are Yusuf, because of your high rank and the greatness of your authority, and because your state is far from their imaginings, and because of the long time that changes appearances and forms. For when they entered upon him seeking provisions, he recognized them while they did not recognize him. He called for the drinking-cup, placed it on his hand, then struck it, and it rang. He said: "This cup tells me that you had a brother from your father called Yusuf, whom he favoured over you, and that you took him away and threw him into the depths of the well, and told your father: 'The wolf ate him,' and sold him for a paltry price."

It is permissible for "while they do not perceive" to be connected to "And We revealed," meaning: We comforted him with revelation and removed the loneliness from his heart, while they did not perceive that, and they thought he was distressed and lonely with no one to keep him company. It is also read "linunabbi'annahum" with the nun, as a threat to them. And the phrase "while they do not perceive" is connected only to "We revealed."

And on the authority of al-Hasan: ʿashiyyan (in the diminutive form of ʿashiyy). It is said: "I met him ʿashiyyan and ʿashiyyanan," and ʿashiyyan and ʿashiyyanan, and aṣīlan and aṣīlānan. [[The author's words, "It is said: I met him ʿashiyyan and ʿashiyyanan," if its final nūn is dropped it becomes ʿashiyyan, as in the reading of al-Hasan. (ʿAyn)]] Ibn Jinnī transmitted it as ʿashan, with a damma on the ʿayn and the alif maqṣūra. He said: ʿashawan from weeping. It is also reported that a woman brought a case before Shurayh and wept. Al-Shaʿbī said to him: "O Abū Umayya, do you not see that she is weeping?" He replied: "The brothers of Joseph came weeping, and they were liars. No one should judge except by what he has been commanded to judge by, the praiseworthy Sunnah."

It is also reported that when he heard their voices [[Maḥmūd said: "It is reported that when he heard their voices he said: 'My sons, has anything happened to your flock?' They said, 'No...' etc." Aḥmad said: What strengthens the suspicion of their guilt is that they claimed the specific matter, the harm to which Jacob, peace be upon him, feared first, namely that the wolf would eat him. So he suspected that they had seized upon the excuse from his statement to them, ﴿and I fear that the wolf will eat him﴾. Often false excuses produce anxiety in the one who offers them to the one to whom they are offered, so much so that some of the commanders of the believers would coach a thief to deny the theft.]] he was alarmed and said: "What is wrong with you, my sons? Has anything happened to your flock?" They said: "No." He said:

﴿So what is wrong with you, and where is Joseph?﴾ They said: ﴿O our father, we went off racing one another (nastabiq)﴾, meaning we were competing with one another. The iftiʿāl and tafāʿul forms share a meaning, as in intiḍāl and tanāḍul (shooting at one another with arrows), and irtimāʾ and tarāmī (throwing at one another), and other such pairs. The meaning is: we were racing in running or competing in shooting.

It is stated in the tafsir: ﴿nantaḍil﴾ (we shoot at one another), ﴿and you would not believe us (bi-muʾminin lanā)﴾, meaning you would not accept us as trustworthy, ﴿even if we were truthful (wa-law kunnā ṣādiqīn)﴾, meaning even if we were, in your presence, among those known for truthfulness and trustworthiness, because of your intense love for Joseph. How much more so, since you think ill of us and do not trust our word?
