I need to translate this passage faithfully. Here it is:

"With false blood." Or it is described by the verbal noun (maṣdar) for emphasis, as if it were the very falsehood itself and its essence, just as one says of a liar: "He is falsehood itself, and forgery in his very self." Similar to it is the line of poetry:

"They are generous with it, and you are stingy with it."

It is also read as kadhiban (accusative), as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: they came with it as liars; and it may be a causative object (mafʿūl lahu).

ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, read: kadibin, with an unpointed dāl, meaning "turbid" (kadir). It was also said: "fresh." Ibn Jinnī said: its origin is from al-kadab, which is al-fawf, the whiteness that appears on the nails of youths. It is as if it were blood that had left its mark on the shirt. It is narrated that they slaughtered a young goat and smeared his shirt with its blood, and it slipped their minds to tear it. It is also narrated that when Yaʿqūb heard the news of Yūsuf, he cried out at the top of his voice and said: "Where is the shirt?" He took it, placed it over his face and wept until his face was dyed with the blood of the shirt, and he said: "By Allah, I have never seen a wrongdoing more outrageous than this today: a wolf ate my son, yet did not tear his shirt!"

It was also said that there were three signs in Yūsuf's shirt: it was a proof for Yaʿqūb of their lie; he placed it over his face and he regained his sight; and it was a proof of Yūsuf's innocence when it was torn from behind.

If you ask: what is the grammatical position of ʿalā qamīsihi? I say: it is in the accusative as an adverbial of place (ẓarf), as if it were said: "And they came upon his shirt with blood," just as you say: "He came upon his camel with loads."

If you ask: may it be a preceding circumstantial clause (ḥāl)? I say: no, because the circumstantial of a genitive-governed noun cannot precede it.

sawwalat: made easy, from al-sawl, which is relaxation; that is: your selves made easy for you a grave matter that you committed against Yūsuf, and made it trivial in your eyes. He inferred their act against him from what he knew of their envy and from the soundness of the shirt. Or it was revealed to him that they had intended him harm.

fa-ṣabrun jamīlun: it is either a predicate or a subject, since it is described: i.e., "my affair is beautiful patience," or "beautiful patience is most fitting." In the reading of Ubayy: fa-ṣabran jamīlan.

Beautiful patience (al-ṣabr al-jamīl) is mentioned in a raised (marfūʿ) hadith: "It is the patience in which there is no complaint made to the creation." [Al-Ṭabarī narrated it through Ḥayyān ibn Abī Ḥathla, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about His saying "fa-ṣabrun jamīl," and he said: "Patience in which there is no complaint. Whoever complains has not been patient." This is a mursal report.] Do you not see His saying: "I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah"?

It was also said: "I will not make you live with a gloomy face; rather I will be to you as I was." It was also said: Yaʿqūb's eyebrows fell over his eyes, so he would lift them with a bandage. He was asked: "What is this?" He said: "The length of time and the abundance of sorrows." So Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "O Yaʿqūb, do you complain about Me?" He said: "O Lord, it was a fault; forgive it for me."

"And Allah is the One whose help is sought" — i.e., I seek His help in bearing what you describe concerning the destruction of Yūsuf, and in patience over the calamity regarding him.

And there came a caravan (sayyarah), a company traveling from the direction of Madyan toward Egypt, and that was three days after Yusuf had been thrown into the well. They lost their way and so they descended near it. The well was in a barren wasteland far from habitation, frequented only by shepherds. It is also said that its water was brackish; then, when Yusuf was cast into it, it became sweet. So they sent a man named Malik ibn Dhu'r al-Khuza'i (a man of the Khuza'ah tribe), to seek water for them. The warid (the one who comes to the water to draw it for the people) let down his bucket, and he exclaimed: "Good news (ya bushra)!" as if he were saying: "Come, for this is one of your times." It is also read as "ya bushraya," with the pronoun suffix attached to himself. In the reading of al-Hasan and others it is read "ya bushra" with a yā' in place of the alif; the yā' is placed in the position of the kasrah before the yā' of possession, and this is a well-known dialect of the Arabs. I have heard the people of the highlands (ahl al-sarawat) say in their supplication: "Ya sayyidi wa mawlaya" (O my master and my lord). It is reported from Nafi': "Ya bushraya" with a sukun, but this is not the correct form, because it involves two consecutive sukuns contrary to the rule, unless it is intended as a pause (waqf).

It is also said: when he let down his bucket, that is, sent it into the well, Yusuf grasped the rope; and when he drew it out, behold, there was a boy of the utmost beauty. So he said: "Ya bushra, this is a boy!" It is also said that he took him away, and when he drew near his companions he called out with this news to give them glad tidings of him.

﴿And they concealed him﴾: the pronoun refers to the warid and his companions, who concealed him from the caravan. It is also said they concealed his matter and their finding him in the well, and told them: "The people of the water handed him to us so that we may sell him for them in Egypt." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the pronoun refers to Yusuf's brothers, and that they told the caravan: "This is a slave of ours who ran away; buy him from us." And Yusuf remained silent, fearing that they would kill him.

﴿As merchandise﴾ (bida'ah) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: they concealed him as a trade good. Bida'ah is that part of wealth set aside for trade, that is, cut off from the rest.

﴿And Allah was Knowing of what they did﴾: nothing of their secrets was hidden from Him, and this is a warning to them, since they had made trade of what was not theirs. Or: "And Allah was Knowing of what the brothers of Yusuf did to their father and their brother of evil conduct."

And they sold him for a paltry price, meager and deficient compared with the true value, or debased coins of short weight, dirhams and not dinars, counted out (ma'dudah), that is, few. [[Mahmud said: "The phrase 'counted' (al-ma'dudah) is a metaphor for 'few'..." Ahmad said: Among the expressions of fewness by means of counting is the well-known supplication against the disbelievers: "O God, count them one by one, scatter them in dispersion, and leave not one of them alive." Although the object of the supplication, their being counted, is apparent, this is not what is meant, since God has counted all things in number and encompassed them in knowledge. So there must be an intended meaning beyond that, namely the necessary implication of counting, which is fewness. Since every little thing is countable and every great amount is uncountable, he prayed against them for fewness and expressed it by its necessary implication, which is counting. And God knows best.]] They were counted out and not weighed, because they did not weigh anything that reached an ounce (awqiyyah), which is forty, but counted what was less than that. It was said that "counted" means few, because the large amount is too much to count. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that it was twenty dirhams. It is related from al-Suddi that it was twenty-two. And they were among those who were indifferent to him (wa kanu fihi min al-zahidin), meaning those who turn away from what is in their hand and so sell it for a meager price [[The phrase "fa-yabi'uhu bi-ma tafif min al-thaman" means: for a small price. In al-Sihah: al-tafif means little. (Ai)]], because they had picked him up, and one who finds a thing is careless about it and does not mind what he sells it for, and because he fears that a claimant may appear and snatch it from his hand, so he sells it to the first bargainer for the least price. It is also possible that the meaning of "they sold him" (wa sharawhu) is "they bought him," meaning the caravan of his brothers, and "they were among those who were indifferent to him" because they believed he was a runaway slave and feared that they would risk their wealth on him. It is narrated that his brothers followed them, saying to them: "Make sure of him, lest he run away." As for His saying "fihi" (in him), it is not a complement of "al-zahidin" (those who are indifferent), because a complement may not precede the thing it complements. Do you not see that you would not say "wa kanu zaydan min al-darribin"? Rather, it is an explanation, as if it were said: "In what did they show indifference?" and he said: "They showed indifference in him."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 21:

﴿The one who bought him﴾. It is said he was Qitfir, or Itfir, and he was the ʿAziz who was over the treasuries of Egypt. The king at that time was al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, a man of the Amalaqa. He had believed in Yusuf and died during Yusuf's lifetime. He was succeeded by Qabus ibn Mus'ab, whom Yusuf invited to Islam, but he refused. The ʿAziz bought him when he was seventeen years old and stayed in his house for thirteen years. Al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid made him his vizier when he was thirty years old, and Allah gave him knowledge and wisdom when he was thirty-three. He died at the age of one hundred and twenty.

It is also said that the king in his time was the Pharaoh of Musa, who lived four hundred years, based on the statement of Allah: ﴿And Yusuf had already come to you before with clear proofs﴾ (40:34). It is also said that the Pharaoh of Musa was one of the descendants of the Pharaoh of Yusuf.

It is said that the ʿAziz bought him for twenty dinars and two pairs of sandals and two white garments. It is also said that they brought him into the market to display him, and the bidding for his price rose until his price reached its weight in musk, silver, and silk, and Qitfir bought him for that amount.

﴿Make his stay honorable﴾: make his residence and his lodging with us honorable, meaning good and pleasing. This is based on the statement of Allah: ﴿Indeed, He is my Lord; He has made my stay good﴾ (12:23). What is meant is that she should take care of him with kindness and look after him with good management, so that his soul is content in our company and settled in our care. One says to a man, "How is the father of your stay and the mother of your stay?" to someone who has come to stay with him, whether a man or a woman, meaning: "Is your soul content with your staying with him, and is the right of your being his guest observed?"

The lām in ﴿to his wife﴾ is connected to "said," not to "bought him." ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾: perhaps, when he is trained, has mastered affairs, and understands their courses, we will rely on him in some of what we are undertaking, and he will benefit us through his sufficiency and trustworthiness. Or we may adopt him and make him in the place of a son, since Qitfir was sterile and could not have children. He had perceived in him right guidance, and so he said that.

It is said: the most perceptive of people are three: the ʿAziz, when he perceived in Yusuf and said to his wife, ﴿Make his stay honorable; perhaps he will benefit us﴾; the woman who came to Musa and said to her father, ﴿O father, hire him﴾ (28:26); and Abu Bakr, when he appointed ʿUmar as successor, may Allah be pleased with them both.

It is narrated that [the ʿAziz] asked him about himself, and he informed him of his lineage, so he recognized him.

﴿And thus﴾: the demonstrative refers to what has preceded, namely his rescue and the softening of the ʿAziz's heart toward him. The kaf is in the accusative case, its implied sense being: "Like that rescue and softening, ﴿We established him﴾," meaning: just as We rescued him and caused the ʿAziz to be kind to him, so We established him in the land of Egypt and made him a king who disposes of its affairs by his command and prohibition.

﴿And that We may teach him the interpretation of events﴾: that rescue and establishment happened because Our purpose is nothing but what has a praiseworthy outcome, namely knowledge and action.

﴿And Allah is dominant over His affair﴾: over His own affair, He is not prevented from what He wills, nor is what He wants and decrees disputed. Or [it means] over the affair of Yusuf, which He manages and does not leave to another. His brothers intended against him what they intended, but nothing happened except what Allah willed and arranged.

﴿But most of mankind do not know﴾ that the whole affair is in the hand of Allah.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 22:

It has been said regarding al-Ashudd (the prime of manhood): eighteen, twenty, thirty-three, and forty. And it has been said: its utmost limit is sixty-two. Hukman (judgment/wisdom): hikmah (wisdom), which is knowledge together with acting upon it and abstaining from what one is ignorant of in it. And it has been said: hukman means a judgment among people, and fiqh (jurisprudence). ﴿And thus We reward the good-doers.﴾ This is an indication that he was a good-doer in his deeds, God-fearing in the early vigor of his affair, and that God gave him judgment and knowledge as a reward for his goodness. And from al-Hasan: whoever worships his Lord well in his youth, God will give him wisdom in his maturity.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf, on Surah 12, verse 23:

Al-murawada (تعالى المراودة): it is a mufa'ala form, from rada yarudu, meaning "to come and go," as if the meaning is: she sought to deceive him concerning himself, i.e., she did what one who deceives his companion does concerning a thing he does not want to let out of his hand, scheming to overcome him with it and take it from him. It is an expression for her insistence on having intercourse with him. "And she closed the doors" — it was said that there were seven of them.

It is read "hayta" (هَيْتَ) with a fatha on the ha and with a kasra, with the ta fatha, and its construction is like the construction of ayna (أين), and 'ayt (عيط). "Hayta" is like jayr, and "hayta" is like haythu (حيث). And "hayyatha" (هثت) means "made oneself ready" (تهيأت). It is said: haa yahay'u, like jaa yajee'u, meaning he prepared himself. "Hayyi'at lak" (هيئت لك) — and the lam is part of the verb's complement. As for its use in calling out (الأصوات), it is for clarification [[His saying "as for its use in calling out, it is for clarification": in al-Sihah: hayta bihi and hawta bihi, meaning he cried out to him and called him. Also in it is their saying "hayta laka," meaning "come on, for you," and in it: "halumma ya rajul" — with a fatha on the mim — meaning "come here." (Ṭ)]], as if it is said: "For you I say this," just as you say "halumma laka" (come, for you). Ma'adha Allah (مَعاذَ اللَّهِ): I seek refuge in Allah, a seeking of refuge. Innahu (إِنَّهُ): indeed, the matter and the account. Rabbi (رَبِّي): my lord, my master and owner, meaning Qitfir. Ahsana mathwaya (أَحْسَنَ مَثْوايَ): when he said to you, "Honour his lodging." So what is the recompense for this that I should betray him in his household with bad betrayal and be treacherous to him concerning them? Innahu la yuflihu al-zalimun (إِنَّهُ لا يُفْلِحُ الظَّالِمُونَ): those who repay good with evil. It was also said: he meant the fornicators, because they wrong themselves.

It was also said: he meant Allah the Exalted, because He is the Causer of causes.

He resolved upon the matter when he intended it and determined on it. The poet said:

*"I intended but did not do it, and I nearly did, would that I had left on Uthman women weeping over him."*

[[This is said by Umayr ibn Dabi' al-Burjumi. He entered upon Uthman while he was being killed, trampled on his belly, broke his rib, and said: "I resolved to kill Uthman and did not kill him; I nearly did it, and would that I had killed him." He alluded to this with his words "I left on Uthman women weeping over him," and this is an instance of *tanazu'* (the grammatical construction of two verbs contending for one noun). The original was: "I left on Uthman his women weeping," and so he made "his women" the subject. The first object of "left" is omitted because it is known from the context, and because it is an accusative complement (*fadlah*), which is not left implicit in this construction. The meaning is: "Would that I had killed him, so that I had made his women weep over him."

This man entered upon al-Hajjaj and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I am an old and weak man, and my name came out for this expedition, so accept my son as a substitute for me." He accepted it from him and the man went out. Utba ibn Sa'id said: "O Amir, this is the one who did such-and-such to Uthman." He said: "Bring him back to me." Then he said to him:

"O old man, why did you not send a substitute to Uthman, the Commander of the Faithful, on the day of the house? In your killing there is a benefit. O my guards, strike off his neck!"

The Amir addressed him with the dual form of address, in the dialect of the guards to whom this speaker is attributed. It is also said that the story concerns Dabi' himself, and that Uthman had imprisoned him for his satire against the Banu Nahshal; when Uthman was killed, he escaped and did that.]]

From the same usage is your saying: "I will not do that, neither by intent (*kayd*) nor by resolve (*hamm*)," meaning: "I would not nearly do it by intent, nor resolve to do it." Sibawayh reported this. From the same root is *al-hammam*, the one who, when he resolves on a matter, carries it out and does not shrink from it.

His saying ﴿And she certainly resolved upon him﴾ means: she certainly resolved to have intercourse with him. ﴿And he resolved upon her﴾ means: he resolved to have intercourse with her. ﴿Had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾: its answer is omitted. Its estimated form is: "Had he not seen the proof of his Lord, he would have had intercourse with her." It is omitted because his saying "and he resolved upon her" indicates it, as when you say: "I resolved to kill him, had I not feared God," meaning: "had I not feared God." 

If you say: How could it be possible for a prophet of God to have an intention toward sin and aim at it? I say: The meaning is that his soul inclined toward the intercourse and was drawn to it out of youthful desire and its ardour [[His saying "its ardour" (*qarmuh*) means its intensity of desire, as reported in al-Sihah]], an inclination resembling the resolve toward it and the aim at it, as the form of that situation requires, a situation that nearly takes away reason and resolution. But he breaks this by considering the proof of God, which is binding on the responsible, namely the obligation to avoid what is forbidden. Had that intense inclination, which is called a resolve because of its intensity, not existed, its bearer would not have been praised by God for abstaining, because the greatness of patience in trial is in proportion to the greatness and severity of the trial. And had his resolve been like her resolve, a resolve of determination, God would not have praised him as being among His sincere servants.

It is also permissible that by his saying ﴿and he resolved upon her﴾ he means that he came close to resolving on her, as a man says: "I killed him had I not feared God," meaning that he approached killing and nearly did it. It is as if he began to do it.

If you say: Is his saying ﴿and he resolved upon her﴾ within the scope of the oath in his saying ﴿and she certainly resolved upon him﴾, or is it outside it? I say: Both are permissible. It is proper for the reader, if he regards it as outside the scope of the oath and as an independent sentence, to pause at ﴿and she certainly resolved upon him﴾ and begin with ﴿and he resolved upon her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord﴾. This also indicates the difference between the two resolves.

If you say: Why did you make the answer of *law-la* (had it not been) omitted, indicated by "he resolved upon her," and why not make it the answer, placed first? I say: Because *law-la* does not have its answer placed before it, since it is in the sense of a conditional, and the conditional takes precedence at the beginning of the sentence; together with what is in its domain, the two clauses are like a single word, and it is not permissible to place part of a word before another part. As for omitting part of it when evidence indicates it, that is permissible.

If you say: Why did you make *law-la* dependent on "he resolved upon her" alone, and not dependent on the clause "she certainly resolved upon him" and "he resolved upon her" together? Because resolve is not connected to bodies but to meanings, so it is necessary to estimate intercourse, and intercourse is only between two together. So it is as if it were said: "They both certainly resolved upon intercourse, had not a preventer prevented one of them?" I say: What you said is good, but God, glory be to Him, has brought the two resolves in detail when He said ﴿And she certainly resolved upon him, and he resolved upon her﴾, so to neglect it would be to nullify it. Therefore the estimate must be: "She certainly resolved upon his intercourse, and he resolved upon her intercourse," with the meaning that the two intercourses are her reaching what is her share of satisfying her desire from him, and his reaching what is his share of satisfying his desire from her, had he not seen the proof of his Lord; so he abandoned reaching his share of desire. Therefore *law-la* is rightly connected to "he resolved upon her" alone.

Yusuf's resolve has been explained as his loosening the belt and sitting in the position of one who has intercourse, and as his loosening the drawstring of his trousers and sitting between her four limbs while she lay on her back. The proof has been explained as his hearing a voice: "Beware of her and her!" He paid no attention to it. He heard it a second time and did not act on it. He heard a third time: "Turn away from her!" It did not take effect on him until Ya'qub appeared to him biting on his finger-joint. It is said: he struck his chest with his hand, and his desire came out through his fingertips. It is said: every son of Ya'qub had twelve sons except Yusuf, who had only eleven sons, because of what was reduced from his desire when he resolved. It is said: he was called: "O Yusuf, do not be like the bird that had feathers; when it committed fornication, it sat without feathers."

It is said: a palm appeared between them, without forearm or wrist, and on it was written ﴿And indeed there are over you guardians, noble recorders﴾; he did not turn away. Then he saw written on it ﴿And do not approach fornication, indeed it is an abomination and an evil way﴾, and he did not desist. Then he saw written on it ﴿And fear a Day on which you will be returned to God﴾, and it did not take effect on him. Then God said to Jibril, peace be upon him:

"Reach My servant before he commits the sin!" So Jibril descended saying: "O Yusuf, will you do the deed of the foolish while you are written in the register of the prophets?"

It is said: he saw the image of the Aziz. It is said: the woman went to an idol that was there and covered it, and said: "I am ashamed before it that it should see us." Yusuf said: "You are ashamed before one who does not hear or see, and I am not ashamed before the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing, the Knower of what is in the breasts."

This and the like is what the people of *hashw* (superfluous, literalist traditionalism) and *jabr* (compulsion, fatalism) report, [[His saying "what the people of hashw and jabr report, whose religion is slandering God Most High" means the Sunnis, and by "the people of justice" he means the Mu'tazila. To *bahata* a person is to attribute to him an ugly thing he did not do. Were it not that this circulates among the early generations, they would not have reported it. (ʿ)]] whose religion is slandering God Most High and His prophets. The people of justice and monotheism, thank God, have no part in their statements and narrations. If we had found in Yusuf, peace be upon him, the slightest slip, we would have censured him and mentioned his repentance and asking forgiveness, as we censure Adam for his slip, and David, Noah, Job, and Dhu al-Nun, and mention their repentance and seeking forgiveness. How could that be, when He praised him and called him "sincere" (*mukhlas*)? It is therefore known with certainty that he stood firm in that slippery position, and that he struggled against his soul with the struggle of men of strength and resolve, looking at the proof of prohibition and the ugliness of the act, until he deserved God's praise in what He sent down in the books of the former peoples, then in the Qur'an, which is a proof over all His books and a confirmation of them. He did not confine himself to recounting his story and devoting a whole surah to it, in order to give him a tongue of truth among later generations, as He gave it to his grandfather Abraham, peace be upon him, and so that the righteous might follow him until the end of time in chastity, purity of garment, and steadfastness at the places of stumbling. God shamed those who report what leads to saying that God sent down the surah which is "the best of stories" in "the clear Arabic Qur'an" so that a prophet among God's prophets might be followed in sitting between the limbs of an adulteress, and in loosening his drawstring to fall upon her, and in his Lord forbidding him three times and three cries being shouted at him from Him with the striking verses of the Qur'an, with a great rebuke and a severe threat, and with a comparison to the bird that lost its feathers when it mated with other than its female, while it crouched in its place, not moving, not stopping, not waking, until God reached him through Jibril and through compulsion. If the most shameless of fornicators, the most sinful, the most one-eyed, and the ugliest in face, had met with even the least of what the prophet of God is said to have met with, no vein would remain to pulse in him nor any limb to move. How vile is a school of thought, and how manifest is its error!

﴿Thus﴾: the *kaf* (like) is in the accusative position (*mahall*), meaning: "We established him in the likeness of that establishment." Or it is in the nominative, meaning: "The matter is like that," ﴿so that We might turn away from him evil﴾, from betrayal of the master, ﴿and immorality﴾, from fornication. ﴿Indeed he was of Our servants, the sincere ones﴾, who made their religion sincere for God; and with *fath* (the vowel of the *lam* is open), it means "those whom God purified for His obedience by protecting them."

It is also permissible that by "evil" he means the preliminaries of immorality, such as kissing, looking with desire, and the like. His saying ﴿of Our servants﴾ means "some of Our servants," that is, he is sincere from among the sincere ones. Or he is of their lineage, for he is among the descendants of Abraham, of whom He said: ﴿Indeed We purified them with a pure purity﴾.

And they raced each other to the door. Here the preposition is omitted and the verb is made to take a direct object, as in His words, "And Moses chose his people" (7:155), where "chose" is construed as implying a sense of "rushed". [He] "Yusuf fled, rushing towards the door in order to get out, and she hurried after him to stop him from going out." If you ask: why is "the door" singular, when He has used the plural in "and they locked the doors"? I say: he meant the outer door, the one which is the exit from the house and the escape from shame. For Ka'b related that when Yusuf fled, the bolt's catch began to fall away and drop until he went out through the doors. "And she tore his shirt from the back": she pulled him from behind and it was torn, that is, it was split as he fled from her towards the door and she followed him, trying to stop him. "And they met her lord at the door": they came upon her husband, who was Qitfir. The woman says to her husband, "My lord," [which is why He did not say "your lord" (sayyidahuma)] as Yusuf's dominion was not valid, so he was not truly her lord.

It is said that the reason He did not say "sayyidahuma" (their lord) is that Yusuf's ownership was not valid, so he was not truly her lord. It is said: [a poet said]:

"They found him coming, wishing to enter."

It is also said that he was sitting with a cousin of the woman. When her husband saw her in that suspicious state, and she was enraged at Yusuf because he had not complied with her, she devised a stratagem which combined two aims: clearing herself in her husband's eyes of suspicion and anger toward Yusuf, and frightening him, in the hope that he would comply out of fear of her and her scheming, and out of reluctance once she despaired of his compliance willingly. Do you not see her words: "And if he does not do what I order him, he will surely be imprisoned," where "ma" is negative, meaning: his punishment is nothing but prison. It may also be interrogative, meaning: what is his punishment but prison, as you say: "Who is in the house but Zayd?" If you ask: why did she not state Yusuf's name in her words, when he intended evil toward her? [Mahmud said: "If you say: why did she say what she said without explicitly mentioning Yusuf..." Ahmad said: By this vagueness she displayed modesty and decorum, so as not to tell her husband, "This man intended evil toward me." For this reason also she spoke of "evil" in general terms, to conceal what she had harboured of wrongdoing, out of exaggeration in scheming and plotting, and to remove suspicion from herself by avoiding anything that suggested wantonness and brazenness. The reverse of her aim, though it matched her purpose with modest vagueness, is the statement of the daughter of Shu'ayb praising Musa, peace be upon him, as Allah related: "One of them said, 'O my father, hire him; indeed the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy.'" She did not say "he is strong and trustworthy," out of modesty, reserve and shyness. But the disposition of shame prompted her to this courtesy, whereas the wife of the ruler was prompted to it by artifice and deliberate effort for that corrupt purpose of scheming. And Allah knows best.] I say:

She intended generality: whoever intends evil toward your family deserves to be imprisoned or tortured, for that is more effective for her aim of frightening Yusuf. It is said: "painful punishment" means flogging with whips. When she incited against him and exposed him to prison and torment, it became obligatory for him to defend himself, so he said: "It was she who sought to seduce me," and had it not been for that, he would have kept silent about her. "And a witness from her family testified." It is said he was a cousin of hers. Allah only placed the testimony on the tongue of one from her family so that it would be more binding as proof against her, more firm in establishing Yusuf's innocence, and more effective in removing suspicion from him. It is said: he was the one who had been sitting with her husband by the door. It is said he was a wise man to whom the king would return and consult. It is possible that one of her relatives was in the house and saw her without her noticing, and Allah angered her on Yusuf's behalf by the testimony and by standing for the truth. It is said: he was her maternal cousin, a child in the cradle. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ: "Four spoke while they were infants: the son of Pharaoh's hairdresser, the witness of Yusuf, the companion of Jurayj, and Jesus." [Related by al-Hakim, Ibn Hibban, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bazzar and Abu Ya'la; al-Tabari and al-Bayhaqi in the sixteenth section of al-Shu'ab all narrated it through Hammad ibn Salamah, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, raised to the Prophet: "When I was taken on the night journey, a fragrant scent passed me..." — the hadith, in which is the story of the hairdresser, and at its end the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Four spoke in the cradle while they were infants: this one, the witness of Yusuf, the companion of Jurayj, and Jesus son of Mary." Also in al-Hakim, from the narration of Muslim ibn Ibrahim, from Jurayj ibn Hazim, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayrah, raised: "None spoke in the cradle except four while they were infants: Jesus, the witness of Yusuf, the companion of Jurayj, and the son of Pharaoh's hairdresser," and he mentioned it with the wording of three, and he mentioned the third as the son of the woman who was thrown into the fire, for she feared for her child, and he spoke. In the two Sahihs from another route from Abu Hurayrah, raised: "None spoke in the cradle except three: Jesus son of Mary, the companion of Jurayj, and an infant who was nursing, when a man rode past on a mount..." — the hadith. Al-Tibi limited himself to this, and was not correct, and on this reckoning they become five. Al-Tha'labi related from al-Dahhak that they were six, adding Yahya ibn Zakariyya.] If you ask: why did He call his words "testimony" when they are not in the form of testimony? [Mahmud said: "If you say: why did He call his words testimony when they are not in the wording of testimony..." Ahmad said: whatever is assumed of that in his following her, the same may be assumed of her following him, for she could have torn his shirt from the front by supposing that he pulled her until they faced each other, and she pushed him away from herself. This same possibility holds if she was the one who followed: she pulled him until they faced one another, then pulled his shirt toward herself from the front. Indeed, this is more evident here, because what usually causes a shirt to be torn is pulling, not pushing.] I say: when it fulfilled the function of testimony, in that Yusuf's words were established by it and her words were nullified, it was called testimony. If you ask: how is the conditional clause permissible to be reported after the act of testifying? I say: because it is a statement among statements, or with the intention of saying, as if it were said: "And a witness testified and said, 'If his shirt is torn from the front...'" If you ask: if the tearing of the shirt from behind shows that she is lying and that she is the one who followed him and pulled his garment toward herself until it tore, how does its tearing from the front show that she is truthful and that he was following her? I say: from two aspects. The first: if he was following her and she was pushing him away from herself, then his shirt would be torn from the front by her pushing. The second: he rushed after her to catch her and stumbled over the front of his shirt, so it tore. [His words continue: "The second: that he hurried after her to overtake her, and stumbled over the front of his shirt, and so it was torn." Ahmad said: this same possibility holds if she was the one following while he was fleeing from her, and his shirt was torn as he hurried to escape. And so Zamakhshari's discussion in this section is not that. The truth, and God is the granter of success, is that if the witness mentioned was a child in the cradle, as some hadith reports, then the verse concerns merely his speech before its time; even if he had said, "Yusuf spoke truly and she lied," that would have sufficed as proof of his truthfulness, just as the mere report of Jesus in the cradle was proof of Mary's truthfulness. Then there is no connection between the sign set up and what was based on it, for the foundation of the proof is the setting up of the sign, not its connection. If the witness was one of her relatives who was in the house and saw her without her noticing, then Allah angered her on Yusuf's behalf by the testimony and by establishing the truth, as Zamakhshari mentioned. In this case it was his duty to state plainly what he had seen, so that he would confirm Yusuf and refute her; but he wished not to be the one who exposed her, and he trusted that the tearing of the shirt was from behind, so he set it as a sign of his truthfulness and her lying. Then he mentioned the other case, the tearing from the front, knowing that it had not been torn from the front, so that he might clear himself of suspicion in the testimony and of intending disgrace, and be fair to both of them, mentioning a sign of her truthfulness whose absence is known, just as he mentioned a sign of his truthfulness whose presence is known. For this reason he placed the sign of her truthfulness before the sign of his truthfulness in mention, to remove suspicion, and because of his confidence that the second sign was the actual event, so its later mention did no harm. This very subtlety, and Allah knows best, is what the believer of Pharaoh's family observed in his words: "If he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; and if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you," where he put the case of lying before the case of truth, to remove the suspicion he feared might fall upon him regarding Musa, peace be upon him, and out of confidence that the second case, his truthfulness, was the actual one. Its later mention does no harm, for this purpose. For this reason he said "some of what he promises you," and did not say "all that he promises you," implicitly indicating that he was with them against him and was eager to deprive him of his right. This manner of delaying the mention, as with Yusuf's delay in uncovering his brother's bag, is similar, for had he begun with it they would have realized that he was the one who ordered the cup placed in it, and Allah knows best. So this witness intended only the latter sign.

The connection in it is established. As for the first sign, it is not the intended one; it was mentioned only as a preliminary, as previously stated. So no clear and certain connection was sought for it; it is rather like a supposition and assumption, and Allah knows best. It is as if he said: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she is truthful." But he knew that the said sign did not occur, so he made her truthfulness depend on an impossibility, namely the existence of its tearing from the front in that state. This explanation is the correct and essential truth. As for if the wise witness, to whom the king would return and consult, as is reported in some exegeses, is meant, then the connection must be sought on both sides, since that is the responsibility of the wise man. The closest way to see the connection is that the tearing of the shirt from behind is evidence of his turning away from her, and its tearing from the front is evidence of his turning toward her with his face, and Allah knows best.]. It was read "min qubul" and "min dubur" with a damma, according to the doctrine of the ends of phrases, meaning: from the front of the shirt and from its back. As for the indefinite form, its meaning is from a direction called "front" and from a direction called "back." It is related from Ibn Abi Ishaq that he read "min qubul" and "min dubur" with a fatha, as though he made them proper names for the two directions, so they were not declined, owing to definiteness and femininity. And both were read with a sukun on the 'ayn. If you ask: how is it permissible to combine "in" which is for the future with "kana" (was)? I say: because the meaning is that it be known that his shirt was torn, and it is like your saying: "If you do good to me, then you have already done good to me before," to someone who reproaches you with his favour, meaning: if you reproach me, I will reproach you.

"So when he saw" — meaning Qitfir — "and knew Yusuf's innocence and her lying, he said: 'Indeed it is' — that is, your words — 'of your guile, which is what you say, the punishment of one who intends evil against your family, or the matter, namely her desire for Yusuf, is of your guile.' [Mahmud said: 'The pronoun refers to her words, "What is the punishment of one who intends evil against your family..."' Ahmad said: There is room for reflection in what this scholar said, for the verse in which the guile of Satan is mentioned is the speech of God, Exalted, not reported speech. But in this verse the guile of women is the speech of the Mighty, yet God reported it from him, so the reporting of it may be taken as affirmation of it, and it may be that the intention is not to approve it. Also, the guile of Satan is mentioned in the verse as opposed to the guile of God, so it is weak in comparison to it. Do you not see the beginning of the verse: 'Those who believe fight in the cause of God, and those who disbelieve fight in the cause of the Taghut. So fight against the friends of Satan; indeed the guile of Satan is ever weak.' Furthermore, the guile practised by women and others derives from Satan through his whispering and enticement, and the evidences of the Law stand on this, so it is not conceivable then that their guile is greater than his, and Allah knows best.] Or the matter, namely her desire for Yusuf, is of your guile. The address is to her and to her female servants. He magnified the guile of women because, although it exists in men, women are subtler in guile and more penetrating in stratagem. They have in this refinement and gentleness, and by it they overcome men. From this is His words: 'And from the evil of the blowers in knots' (113:4), and the adversities among them have what they do not have from other things. It is related from some scholars: 'I fear women more than I fear Satan, for God, Exalted, says: "Indeed the guile of Satan is ever weak," and He said to women: "Indeed your guile is great."'

"Yusuf" — the call particle is omitted from it, because he is a near addressee, present to the discussion, and in this there is nearness to him and gentleness toward his station. "Turn away from this matter and keep it secret, do not speak of it. And ask forgiveness, you, for your sin; indeed you were of the sinners," that is, among the group deliberately committing sin. It is said: 'khati'a' when one sins intentionally. He said "of the sinners" in the masculine form, giving precedence to males over females. The Aziz was only a forbearing man. It is related that he was of little jealousy.
