"So when he saw" — meaning Qitfir — "and knew Yusuf's innocence and her lying, he said: 'Indeed it is' — that is, your words — 'of your guile, which is what you say, the punishment of one who intends evil against your family, or the matter, namely her desire for Yusuf, is of your guile.' [Mahmud said: 'The pronoun refers to her words, "What is the punishment of one who intends evil against your family..."' Ahmad said: There is room for reflection in what this scholar said, for the verse in which the guile of Satan is mentioned is the speech of God, Exalted, not reported speech. But in this verse the guile of women is the speech of the Mighty, yet God reported it from him, so the reporting of it may be taken as affirmation of it, and it may be that the intention is not to approve it. Also, the guile of Satan is mentioned in the verse as opposed to the guile of God, so it is weak in comparison to it. Do you not see the beginning of the verse: 'Those who believe fight in the cause of God, and those who disbelieve fight in the cause of the Taghut. So fight against the friends of Satan; indeed the guile of Satan is ever weak.' Furthermore, the guile practised by women and others derives from Satan through his whispering and enticement, and the evidences of the Law stand on this, so it is not conceivable then that their guile is greater than his, and Allah knows best.] Or the matter, namely her desire for Yusuf, is of your guile. The address is to her and to her female servants. He magnified the guile of women because, although it exists in men, women are subtler in guile and more penetrating in stratagem. They have in this refinement and gentleness, and by it they overcome men. From this is His words: 'And from the evil of the blowers in knots' (113:4), and the adversities among them have what they do not have from other things. It is related from some scholars: 'I fear women more than I fear Satan, for God, Exalted, says: "Indeed the guile of Satan is ever weak," and He said to women: "Indeed your guile is great."'

"Yusuf" — the call particle is omitted from it, because he is a near addressee, present to the discussion, and in this there is nearness to him and gentleness toward his station. "Turn away from this matter and keep it secret, do not speak of it. And ask forgiveness, you, for your sin; indeed you were of the sinners," that is, among the group deliberately committing sin. It is said: 'khati'a' when one sins intentionally. He said "of the sinners" in the masculine form, giving precedence to males over females. The Aziz was only a forbearing man. It is related that he was of little jealousy.

And they raced each other to the door. Here the preposition is omitted and the verb is made to take a direct object, as in His words, "And Moses chose his people" (7:155), where "chose" is construed as implying a sense of "rushed". [He] "Yusuf fled, rushing towards the door in order to get out, and she hurried after him to stop him from going out." If you ask: why is "the door" singular, when He has used the plural in "and they locked the doors"? I say: he meant the outer door, the one which is the exit from the house and the escape from shame. For Ka'b related that when Yusuf fled, the bolt's catch began to fall away and drop until he went out through the doors. "And she tore his shirt from the back": she pulled him from behind and it was torn, that is, it was split as he fled from her towards the door and she followed him, trying to stop him. "And they met her lord at the door": they came upon her husband, who was Qitfir. The woman says to her husband, "My lord," [which is why He did not say "your lord" (sayyidahuma)] as Yusuf's dominion was not valid, so he was not truly her lord.

It is said that the reason He did not say "sayyidahuma" (their lord) is that Yusuf's ownership was not valid, so he was not truly her lord. It is said: [a poet said]:

"They found him coming, wishing to enter."

It is also said that he was sitting with a cousin of the woman. When her husband saw her in that suspicious state, and she was enraged at Yusuf because he had not complied with her, she devised a stratagem which combined two aims: clearing herself in her husband's eyes of suspicion and anger toward Yusuf, and frightening him, in the hope that he would comply out of fear of her and her scheming, and out of reluctance once she despaired of his compliance willingly. Do you not see her words: "And if he does not do what I order him, he will surely be imprisoned," where "ma" is negative, meaning: his punishment is nothing but prison. It may also be interrogative, meaning: what is his punishment but prison, as you say: "Who is in the house but Zayd?" If you ask: why did she not state Yusuf's name in her words, when he intended evil toward her? [Mahmud said: "If you say: why did she say what she said without explicitly mentioning Yusuf..." Ahmad said: By this vagueness she displayed modesty and decorum, so as not to tell her husband, "This man intended evil toward me." For this reason also she spoke of "evil" in general terms, to conceal what she had harboured of wrongdoing, out of exaggeration in scheming and plotting, and to remove suspicion from herself by avoiding anything that suggested wantonness and brazenness. The reverse of her aim, though it matched her purpose with modest vagueness, is the statement of the daughter of Shu'ayb praising Musa, peace be upon him, as Allah related: "One of them said, 'O my father, hire him; indeed the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy.'" She did not say "he is strong and trustworthy," out of modesty, reserve and shyness. But the disposition of shame prompted her to this courtesy, whereas the wife of the ruler was prompted to it by artifice and deliberate effort for that corrupt purpose of scheming. And Allah knows best.] I say:

She intended generality: whoever intends evil toward your family deserves to be imprisoned or tortured, for that is more effective for her aim of frightening Yusuf. It is said: "painful punishment" means flogging with whips. When she incited against him and exposed him to prison and torment, it became obligatory for him to defend himself, so he said: "It was she who sought to seduce me," and had it not been for that, he would have kept silent about her. "And a witness from her family testified." It is said he was a cousin of hers. Allah only placed the testimony on the tongue of one from her family so that it would be more binding as proof against her, more firm in establishing Yusuf's innocence, and more effective in removing suspicion from him. It is said: he was the one who had been sitting with her husband by the door. It is said he was a wise man to whom the king would return and consult. It is possible that one of her relatives was in the house and saw her without her noticing, and Allah angered her on Yusuf's behalf by the testimony and by standing for the truth. It is said: he was her maternal cousin, a child in the cradle. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ: "Four spoke while they were infants: the son of Pharaoh's hairdresser, the witness of Yusuf, the companion of Jurayj, and Jesus." [Related by al-Hakim, Ibn Hibban, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Bazzar and Abu Ya'la; al-Tabari and al-Bayhaqi in the sixteenth section of al-Shu'ab all narrated it through Hammad ibn Salamah, from 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, raised to the Prophet: "When I was taken on the night journey, a fragrant scent passed me..." — the hadith, in which is the story of the hairdresser, and at its end the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Four spoke in the cradle while they were infants: this one, the witness of Yusuf, the companion of Jurayj, and Jesus son of Mary." Also in al-Hakim, from the narration of Muslim ibn Ibrahim, from Jurayj ibn Hazim, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayrah, raised: "None spoke in the cradle except four while they were infants: Jesus, the witness of Yusuf, the companion of Jurayj, and the son of Pharaoh's hairdresser," and he mentioned it with the wording of three, and he mentioned the third as the son of the woman who was thrown into the fire, for she feared for her child, and he spoke. In the two Sahihs from another route from Abu Hurayrah, raised: "None spoke in the cradle except three: Jesus son of Mary, the companion of Jurayj, and an infant who was nursing, when a man rode past on a mount..." — the hadith. Al-Tibi limited himself to this, and was not correct, and on this reckoning they become five. Al-Tha'labi related from al-Dahhak that they were six, adding Yahya ibn Zakariyya.] If you ask: why did He call his words "testimony" when they are not in the form of testimony? [Mahmud said: "If you say: why did He call his words testimony when they are not in the wording of testimony..." Ahmad said: whatever is assumed of that in his following her, the same may be assumed of her following him, for she could have torn his shirt from the front by supposing that he pulled her until they faced each other, and she pushed him away from herself. This same possibility holds if she was the one who followed: she pulled him until they faced one another, then pulled his shirt toward herself from the front. Indeed, this is more evident here, because what usually causes a shirt to be torn is pulling, not pushing.] I say: when it fulfilled the function of testimony, in that Yusuf's words were established by it and her words were nullified, it was called testimony. If you ask: how is the conditional clause permissible to be reported after the act of testifying? I say: because it is a statement among statements, or with the intention of saying, as if it were said: "And a witness testified and said, 'If his shirt is torn from the front...'" If you ask: if the tearing of the shirt from behind shows that she is lying and that she is the one who followed him and pulled his garment toward herself until it tore, how does its tearing from the front show that she is truthful and that he was following her? I say: from two aspects. The first: if he was following her and she was pushing him away from herself, then his shirt would be torn from the front by her pushing. The second: he rushed after her to catch her and stumbled over the front of his shirt, so it tore. [His words continue: "The second: that he hurried after her to overtake her, and stumbled over the front of his shirt, and so it was torn." Ahmad said: this same possibility holds if she was the one following while he was fleeing from her, and his shirt was torn as he hurried to escape. And so Zamakhshari's discussion in this section is not that. The truth, and God is the granter of success, is that if the witness mentioned was a child in the cradle, as some hadith reports, then the verse concerns merely his speech before its time; even if he had said, "Yusuf spoke truly and she lied," that would have sufficed as proof of his truthfulness, just as the mere report of Jesus in the cradle was proof of Mary's truthfulness. Then there is no connection between the sign set up and what was based on it, for the foundation of the proof is the setting up of the sign, not its connection. If the witness was one of her relatives who was in the house and saw her without her noticing, then Allah angered her on Yusuf's behalf by the testimony and by establishing the truth, as Zamakhshari mentioned. In this case it was his duty to state plainly what he had seen, so that he would confirm Yusuf and refute her; but he wished not to be the one who exposed her, and he trusted that the tearing of the shirt was from behind, so he set it as a sign of his truthfulness and her lying. Then he mentioned the other case, the tearing from the front, knowing that it had not been torn from the front, so that he might clear himself of suspicion in the testimony and of intending disgrace, and be fair to both of them, mentioning a sign of her truthfulness whose absence is known, just as he mentioned a sign of his truthfulness whose presence is known. For this reason he placed the sign of her truthfulness before the sign of his truthfulness in mention, to remove suspicion, and because of his confidence that the second sign was the actual event, so its later mention did no harm. This very subtlety, and Allah knows best, is what the believer of Pharaoh's family observed in his words: "If he is a liar, then upon him is his lie; and if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you," where he put the case of lying before the case of truth, to remove the suspicion he feared might fall upon him regarding Musa, peace be upon him, and out of confidence that the second case, his truthfulness, was the actual one. Its later mention does no harm, for this purpose. For this reason he said "some of what he promises you," and did not say "all that he promises you," implicitly indicating that he was with them against him and was eager to deprive him of his right. This manner of delaying the mention, as with Yusuf's delay in uncovering his brother's bag, is similar, for had he begun with it they would have realized that he was the one who ordered the cup placed in it, and Allah knows best. So this witness intended only the latter sign.

The connection in it is established. As for the first sign, it is not the intended one; it was mentioned only as a preliminary, as previously stated. So no clear and certain connection was sought for it; it is rather like a supposition and assumption, and Allah knows best. It is as if he said: "If his shirt is torn from the front, then she is truthful." But he knew that the said sign did not occur, so he made her truthfulness depend on an impossibility, namely the existence of its tearing from the front in that state. This explanation is the correct and essential truth. As for if the wise witness, to whom the king would return and consult, as is reported in some exegeses, is meant, then the connection must be sought on both sides, since that is the responsibility of the wise man. The closest way to see the connection is that the tearing of the shirt from behind is evidence of his turning away from her, and its tearing from the front is evidence of his turning toward her with his face, and Allah knows best.]. It was read "min qubul" and "min dubur" with a damma, according to the doctrine of the ends of phrases, meaning: from the front of the shirt and from its back. As for the indefinite form, its meaning is from a direction called "front" and from a direction called "back." It is related from Ibn Abi Ishaq that he read "min qubul" and "min dubur" with a fatha, as though he made them proper names for the two directions, so they were not declined, owing to definiteness and femininity. And both were read with a sukun on the 'ayn. If you ask: how is it permissible to combine "in" which is for the future with "kana" (was)? I say: because the meaning is that it be known that his shirt was torn, and it is like your saying: "If you do good to me, then you have already done good to me before," to someone who reproaches you with his favour, meaning: if you reproach me, I will reproach you.

"So when he saw" — meaning Qitfir — "and knew Yusuf's innocence and her lying, he said: 'Indeed it is' — that is, your words — 'of your guile, which is what you say, the punishment of one who intends evil against your family, or the matter, namely her desire for Yusuf, is of your guile.' [Mahmud said: 'The pronoun refers to her words, "What is the punishment of one who intends evil against your family..."' Ahmad said: There is room for reflection in what this scholar said, for the verse in which the guile of Satan is mentioned is the speech of God, Exalted, not reported speech. But in this verse the guile of women is the speech of the Mighty, yet God reported it from him, so the reporting of it may be taken as affirmation of it, and it may be that the intention is not to approve it. Also, the guile of Satan is mentioned in the verse as opposed to the guile of God, so it is weak in comparison to it. Do you not see the beginning of the verse: 'Those who believe fight in the cause of God, and those who disbelieve fight in the cause of the Taghut. So fight against the friends of Satan; indeed the guile of Satan is ever weak.' Furthermore, the guile practised by women and others derives from Satan through his whispering and enticement, and the evidences of the Law stand on this, so it is not conceivable then that their guile is greater than his, and Allah knows best.] Or the matter, namely her desire for Yusuf, is of your guile. The address is to her and to her female servants. He magnified the guile of women because, although it exists in men, women are subtler in guile and more penetrating in stratagem. They have in this refinement and gentleness, and by it they overcome men. From this is His words: 'And from the evil of the blowers in knots' (113:4), and the adversities among them have what they do not have from other things. It is related from some scholars: 'I fear women more than I fear Satan, for God, Exalted, says: "Indeed the guile of Satan is ever weak," and He said to women: "Indeed your guile is great."'

"Yusuf" — the call particle is omitted from it, because he is a near addressee, present to the discussion, and in this there is nearness to him and gentleness toward his station. "Turn away from this matter and keep it secret, do not speak of it. And ask forgiveness, you, for your sin; indeed you were of the sinners," that is, among the group deliberately committing sin. It is said: 'khati'a' when one sins intentionally. He said "of the sinners" in the masculine form, giving precedence to males over females. The Aziz was only a forbearing man. It is related that he was of little jealousy.

And the women said, [a group of women, and they were five]: the wife of the cupbearer, the wife of the baker, the wife of the keeper of the animals, the wife of the jailer, and the wife of the chamberlain. "Niswah" (women) is a singular noun used as a collective plural of "imra'ah" (woman), and its feminine marking is not real, like the feminine marking of "lummah" (a group of companions); for this reason its verb did not take the feminine ta'. It has two dialects: the nun is pronounced with a kasra and with a damma. In the city, in Egypt, "imra'at al-'Aziz" [the wife of al-'Aziz], they mean Qitfir. "Al-'Aziz" means the king in the language of the Arabs. "Fata-hā" [her slave]: her male servant. It is said "fataya" and "fatatī," meaning my male servant and my female servant. "Shaghafahā" [pierced her love]: it split (kharaqa) her love through the "shaghaf" of her heart until it reached the heart (fu'ad). The "shaghaf" is the covering of the heart, and it is said to be a thin skin called the "tongue of the heart."

Al-Nabigha said:
"And a concern has come between me and that, penetrating
into the place of the shaghaf, which the fingers seek."

[The verse: "And a concern has come between me and that, penetrating into the place of the shaghaf, which the fingers seek. / And the threat of Abu Qabus, not in its full reality, came to me, while between me and him are the distant places of Rakish and Fala'ij." Al-Nabigha is apologising to al-Nu'man, king of the Arabs, for what the slanderers had charged him with. That is, a concern has prevented him from amorous pursuit of the beloved and other pleasures. "Waalij" means entering the place of the shaghaf. Another reading is "wa-luwuj al-shaghaf," meaning like its entering. The "shaghaf" is a disease of the heart on the right side, which physicians extract with their fingers, so "the fingers seek it" is a description of it as a state of the concern. It is also said that the shaghaf is the covering of the heart, or a thin skin called the tongue of the heart; then "which the fingers seek" is a description of the concern. He likened the fingers to one capable of seeking, by way of metaphor (makniyya) and imagination (takhyil); then he likened the intelligible concern to a perceptible thing and exaggerated, to the point of claiming that the fingers search for it and do not find it because of its intense penetration and hiddenness in the heart, or that they touch it and wish to remove it. He explains the concern with his words: "the threat of Abu Qabus," i.e. al-Nu'man's threat and menace, "not in its full reality," i.e. it had not reached me in its completeness; or because it arose without cause from me, rather the slanderers invented lies against me and came to me. "Dunawi": before me, these two places, which are a considerable distance; nevertheless fear overtook me, or the distance, indicating the king's exceedingly great anger with him.]

It was read "sha'afahā" with an ʿayn, from "sha'afa al-ba'ir" when one smears the camel with tar (hana'a), [the commentary note: his words "when he smears it" in al-Sihah: "I smeared the camel" means I daubed it with al-hanaʾ, which is tar], and burned it with tar. He said:

"As the man who smears the mangy camel with tar burns it."

[The verse: "Will you kill me, when you have burned her heart as the man who smears the mangy camel with tar burns it?" This is by Imru' al-Qays, and the interrogative is for denial and disbelief, or for wonder. "Sha'afa al-jamal" means when he burns it with boiling tar on the fire, and "hana'a" means he anointed it with that tar; so "sha'af" is used to mean burning in general, then it is used to mean burning with love, metaphorically and by sending (mursal), so that the comparison in his words is valid: as one burns the anointed camels, the one who anoints them. If it is read with a ghayn, "shaghafta," the meaning is: you struck the covering of her heart with love, which is the covering of the heart or its tongue or a black seed in its middle; as the man who anointed the camels frightened them and disturbed their hearts, because they fear him at first. It is also said: her love is likened to camels' delight in that tar after being anointed with it.]

"And love" is an accusative of specification (tamyiz). "In error" means in mistake and distance from the path of rightness. "With their guile": with their backbiting and evil speech. Their saying "the wife of al-'Aziz has fallen in love with her servant, the Canaanite, and we hate her" – they called backbiting "guile" because it is in secret and in a state of absence, as the schemer hides his scheme. It is also said: she had asked them to keep her secret, but they revealed it against her.

"She sent to them": she invited them. It is said: she invited forty women, among them the five mentioned. "And she prepared for them a *mutaka*": what they lean on, of cushions. She intended by that arrangement, while they were reclining with knives in their hands, that they would be astonished and bewildered at seeing him, and would be distracted from themselves, so their hands would fall upon their hands and cut them, because the one reclining who is bewildered by something lets his hand fall upon his hand. It is not far-fetched that she intended to combine the scheming against him and against them, placing the knives in their hands so they would cut their hands, and so she would rebuke them with the proof, and so that Joseph would be terrified by her guile when he came out before forty women gathered with knives in their hands, and she would imagine that they would attack him. It is also said: *mutaka* means a dining place, because they used to recline for food, drink and conversation, as is the custom of the affluent; and for this reason "he forbade a man to eat reclining" [from the narration of Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman from Ibn al-Zubayr from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade one of us to eat with his left hand and to eat reclining." In al-Tabari, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade two fasts, two prayers, two garments, two foods, two sales and two marriages..." – until he said: as for the two foods: that a man eats with his left hand, and with his right hand is sound; and that he eats reclining, its isnad is good. He has also in al-Awsat and in the Musnad of the Syrians, from the hadith of Abu al-Darda (may God be pleased with him), who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not eat reclining, and do not step over the necks of people on Friday." Ibn Hibban faulted it in al-Du'afa' through Zuraiq ibn Abd Allah, a narrator from 'Amr ibn al-Aswad from Abu al-Darda. And on this subject, from Ibn Abi Ihab. Al-Bazzar recorded it with the wording "he forbade that we eat reclining."] And "she gave them knives to cut with what they eat." It is also said *mutaka* means food, from your saying "we reclined at so-and-so's": we ate [his note: perhaps "i.e. we ate it"], by way of metonymy, because the one you invite to eat with you, you prepare for him a support to lean on. Jamil said:

"So we dwelt in favour and reclined, and drank the lawful from its jars."

[Attributed to Humayd ibn Thawr, and also to Jamil ibn Ma'mar. "Zalla" (to remain) is of the pattern 'alima. He says: we remained in favour, or in a state of being clothed in favour; "wa-ttakana" originally was "awtakana," its first ta' being a waw: i.e. we took a mutaka and lay upon it; and we drank lawful wine, meaning nabidh, "from its qulal," the plural of qullah, which is a great jar. In the mention of the jars there is an indication of the extravagance in drinking and of not being restricted in it.]

And from Mujahid: *mutaka* means food that is cut in slices, as if the meaning were "one leans on with the knife," because the cutter leans on what is cut with the knife. It was read *mutaka* without hamza. From al-Hasan: *mutaka'* with a long vowel, as if it were *iftiʿal*, owing to the lengthening of the fatha of the kaf, like his saying "bi-munтazah" [his note: "bi-muntazah" is from the words of the poet: "And you, from the calamities when they are thrown, and from the blame of men, from afar," the verse is by Ibn Harma mourning his son; al-ghawa'il are the events that seize souls and destroy them; nazaha means to be far away, and al-muntazah is a name for a place of distance, and its fatha was lengthened so that the alif arose from it, as in their saying "yinbaʿ" for "yanbaʿ" and "ʿaqrab" for "ʿaqrab"], meaning "bi-muntazah." Like it is "yunbaʿ" [his note: "yunbaʿ" is from the words of the poet: "It flows from the dhafra, a smooth, noble, sweating she-camel, like the stallion-camel that snorts," and the explanation of this verse was given earlier in surah al-A'raf in this part, page 122, so refer to it if you wish — its corrector], meaning "yanbaʿ." It was also read *matkah*, which is the citron, and he recited:

"So she sent a *matkah* to the sons of her father, which a hard, sturdy she-camel bore swiftly."

[The *matkah* is the citron; it seems to be what Abu Dawud mentioned in his Sunan, that it was split into two halves and carried like two panniers on a camel. *Khabb* is a kind of pace; *ʿuthmuthmah* is hard; *waqqah*, with fatha, is one whose hoof strikes the ground forcefully.]

She had sent a citron on a she-camel; and it may be the citron that Abu Dawud mentioned in his Sunan, that it was split into two halves and carried on a camel like two saddlebags. It is also said: *al-zamawird*, [his note: "al-zamawird" is thin bread stuffed with meat]. From Wahb: citron, bananas and melon.

It is also said: she prepared for them what cuts, from *mataka al-shay'* meaning *bataka*, if he cut it. Al-A'raj read *mutakan* as *mufʿalan*, from *takiʾa yatakaʾu*, if he reclined.

*"Akbarnahu"* — they exalted him, and they were overcome by that beauty, the marvellous elegance and surpassing comeliness.

It is said: Joseph's excellence over people in beauty was like the excellence of the full moon on the night of the full moon over the stars of the sky. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "I passed by Joseph on the night I was taken up to heaven, and I said to Gabriel: 'Who is this?' He said: 'Joseph.'" It was said: "O Messenger of God, how did you see him?" He said: "Like the moon on the night of the full moon." [Recorded by al-Tha'labi from the narration of Abu Harun al-Abdi from Abu Sa'id. Al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in the Dala'il and Ibn Mardawayh recorded it through this route at length.] It is also said that when Joseph walked in the alleys of Egypt, the radiance of his face was seen on the walls, as the light of the sun is seen on water upon them.

It is also said: no one could describe Joseph. It is said: he resembled Adam on the day his Lord created him. It is said: he inherited his beauty from his grandmother Sarah. It is also said: *akbarna* means menstruated, and the *ha'* is for pause. It is said: "the woman *akbarat*" when she menstruated; its essence is that she entered into the state of greatness, for by menstruation she leaves the limit of childhood for the limit of adulthood. It seems Abu al-Tayyib took from this interpretation his words:

"Fear God, and cover this beauty with a veil, for if it appears, the unwed maidens menstruate in their chambers."

[By Abu al-Tayyib. He says: fear God and cover this beauty that is in your face with a veil, for if you appear, the unwed maidens, that is the best of women, who are in their chambers, will menstruate because of what they see of your beauty. *Lah* and *yalih* means: appeared, appears.]

*"Qatta'na aydiyahunna"* — they wounded them, as you say: "I was cutting the meat, so I cut my hand," meaning: I wounded it.

*"Hashā"* is a word expressing exoneration in the matter of exception. You say: "The people did wrong, except Zayd." It is said:

"Hasha Abi Thawban, indeed in him is restraint from rebuke and reviling."

[The verse, by al-Munqidh ibn al-Tammah, who is al-Jumayh al-Asadi: "Hasha Abi Thawban, Amr ibn Abd Allah, indeed in him is restraint from rebuke and reviling." *Hasha* is a word of absolution and exoneration, standing in the place of a verbal noun and governing what follows it, like *subhan Allah*. It is permitted that it is the exceptive *hasha*, which is a prepositional particle according to most. The Dabbi transmitted it as *hasha Aba Thawban* with the accusative, so it is a verb; the possibility of the dialect of the restricted form is weak because of the fame of the dialect of inflection by particles. On the first view its building is because of its resemblance to the particle in form and meaning. *Bakuma al-rajul* (like taʿiba): when he was unable to speak. *Qadima* (like sahila and zarufa): when he was unable to argue, as if his mouth were blocked. *Al-dann* with kasra is stinginess. *Al-malhah* is a mafʿalah from *lahahu* when he blamed him. *Al-lihaʾ* (like *al-ridaʾ*) is a mufaʿalah from lahn and ʿadhl, from *lahawtu al-ʿud* when I peeled the wood. The repetition of Abu Thawban is for his exaltation and to mark his name; "laysa bi-bakmah" with damma, meaning: not one with dumbness, i.e. not dumb, nor *qadam*, i.e. incapable of speech. 'Amr: it is said he is a substitute for Abu Thawban, so his words "indeed Abu Thawban..." are a parenthetical sentence explaining the reason for exoneration. And in his words "indeed in him is restraint" is an explanation of the reason for his silence about punishing the base; the meaning: in him is refusal and exaltation above baseness and reviling.]

It is a particle of the prepositions, so it was placed in the position of exoneration and innocence, and the meaning of "hasha Allah" is the innocence of God and the exoneration of God. This is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, with *hasha* annexed to God as annexation of innocence. Whoever reads "hasha li-Allah," it is like your saying "saqyan laka," as if he said "baraʾah" (innocence), then said "li-Allah," to clarify who is declared innocent and exonerated.

The evidence that *hasha* is placed in the position of a verbal noun is the reading of Abu al-Simmal: *hashā lillāh*, with tanwin; and the reading of Abu ʿAmr *hasha lillahi*, with the final alif omitted; and the reading of al-A'mash *hasha lillahi*, with the first alif omitted. It was also read *hashsha lillahi* with the shin sukun, on the basis that the fatha followed the alif in dropping; this is weak because of the meeting of two sukuns against its rule. It was also read *hasha al-ilah*.

If you ask: why was it permissible in *hasha lillah* not to take tanwin, after treating it as "innocence for God"? I say: out of regard for its original form, which is the particle. Do you not see their saying "I sat from on his right" how they left "ʿan" uninflected in its original form? And [his note: his conjunction of "ʿala" in his words needs contrivance, i.e. and to his words "they went from upon him after a mourning, their thirst..." how he left "ʿala" in his words; it is possible the estimate is: do you not see their saying etc., and "ʿala" in his words, i.e. and do you not see "ʿala"...] the alif inverting to yā' with the pronoun in his words "ghadat min ʿalayhi"? The meaning: exalting God, exalted, above the attributes of incapacity, and marvelling at His power to create a beauty like this. As for His words *"hasha lillahi ma ʿalimna ʿalayhi min sawʾ"* [“God forbid! We know no evil in him”], the marvel is at His power to create a chaste one like him. *"Ma hadha basharan"* [“This is no mere mortal”]: they negated humanity from him, for the strangeness of his beauty and the remoteness of his comeliness, for the qualities of the forms of beauty; and they affirmed for him angelhood, and by it gave judgment. This is because God, mighty and majestic, established in human nature that there is nothing more beautiful than an angel, just as He established in it that there is nothing uglier than the devil; for this reason every extreme of beauty and ugliness is likened to them. He established that in them only because the reality is so, just as He established in human nature that there is nothing more inclined to evil than the devils, nor more gathered to good than the angels — except what the lost, rebellious group, the Jabriyya, hold concerning the preference of man over the angel; and this is nothing but their inversion of realities, their denial of necessary knowledge, and their obstinacy in every matter. [His note: "except what the lost group holds" means the people of the Sunna, and he has erred in his partisanship for the Mu'tazila, may God pardon him.] The use of *ma* in the manner of *laysa* is the ancient Hijazi dialect, and the Qur'an came in it. Among it is God's saying *"ma hunna ummahatihim"* [“they are not their mothers”]. Whoever reads by his natural dialect of the Banu Tamim reads *"bashar"* with a damma. It is in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. It was also read *"ma hadha bashariy"*, meaning: he is not a base, lowly, owned slave; *"in hadha illa malakun karim"* [“this is none but a noble angel”]. You say: *"hadha bashara"*, meaning: it is a gain for you, i.e. it is attainment of good news, in the sense of "this is a good" — and you say: "This is for you a good news, or a bakra?"

The reading (qira'a) with the singular is the preferable one, because it agrees with the Mushaf (the codified Qur'an), and because it matches "basharin" (a human) with "malak" (an angel). She said ﴿فَذَلِكُنَّ الَّذِي لُمْتُنَّنِي فِيهِ﴾ ("That is the one about whom you blamed me"), and she did not say "fa-hadha" ("this one"), though he was present. This is to raise his rank in beauty, to make him worthy of being loved and of being the object of infatuation, to exalt his condition, and to affirm the lofty status of his station. It is also possible that the demonstrative refers to the meaning expressed in their words: "She has fallen in love with her Canaanite slave." It is as if she said: "That is the Canaanite slave whom you pictured in your own selves, then you blamed me for him." She means: you did not picture him as he truly is. Had you pictured him as you have now seen him, you would have excused me for being infatuated with him.

Al-istis'am (﴿فَاسْتَعْصَمَ﴾, "he abstained") is a form of emphasis (intensive construction) indicating extreme refusal and intense self-restraint, as if he were in a state of protection while striving to increase it. It is similar to istamsaka ("he held fast"), istawsa'a al-fatq ("he widened the tear"), istajma'a al-ra'y ("he gathered his opinion"), and istafhala al-khatb ("the matter grew severe").

This is a clear statement of what Yusuf (peace be upon him) did, beyond which nothing more can be added, and a proof brighter than anything else, showing that he is innocent of what the people of hashw (the "padding" party, a term Zamakhshari uses for the literalist exegetes) have attributed to him in their explanations of "al-hamm" (the intention) and "al-burhan" (the proof).

If you say: does the pronoun in ﴿آمُرُهُ﴾ refer to the relative pronoun (alladhi), or to Yusuf? I say: it refers to the relative pronoun. The meaning is "what I command him," and the preposition has been omitted, as in your saying "amartuka al-khayr" ("I commanded you the good"). It is also permissible to make "ma" a verbal-noun (masdariyya) particle, in which case the pronoun refers to Yusuf, and the meaning is: "And if he does not carry out my command to him," that is, the requirement and consequence of my command.

It has been read as ﴿وَلَيَكُونًا﴾ with both the doubled (tashdid) and the single (takhfif) forms of the nun. The single form is preferable, because the nun was written in the Mushaf as an alif according to the rule of pausal pronunciation (waqf), and that happens only with the light nun (nun al-khafifa).

And the women said, [a group of women, and they were five]: the wife of the cupbearer, the wife of the baker, the wife of the keeper of the animals, the wife of the jailer, and the wife of the chamberlain. "Niswah" (women) is a singular noun used as a collective plural of "imra'ah" (woman), and its feminine marking is not real, like the feminine marking of "lummah" (a group of companions); for this reason its verb did not take the feminine ta'. It has two dialects: the nun is pronounced with a kasra and with a damma. In the city, in Egypt, "imra'at al-'Aziz" [the wife of al-'Aziz], they mean Qitfir. "Al-'Aziz" means the king in the language of the Arabs. "Fata-hā" [her slave]: her male servant. It is said "fataya" and "fatatī," meaning my male servant and my female servant. "Shaghafahā" [pierced her love]: it split (kharaqa) her love through the "shaghaf" of her heart until it reached the heart (fu'ad). The "shaghaf" is the covering of the heart, and it is said to be a thin skin called the "tongue of the heart."

Al-Nabigha said:
"And a concern has come between me and that, penetrating
into the place of the shaghaf, which the fingers seek."

[The verse: "And a concern has come between me and that, penetrating into the place of the shaghaf, which the fingers seek. / And the threat of Abu Qabus, not in its full reality, came to me, while between me and him are the distant places of Rakish and Fala'ij." Al-Nabigha is apologising to al-Nu'man, king of the Arabs, for what the slanderers had charged him with. That is, a concern has prevented him from amorous pursuit of the beloved and other pleasures. "Waalij" means entering the place of the shaghaf. Another reading is "wa-luwuj al-shaghaf," meaning like its entering. The "shaghaf" is a disease of the heart on the right side, which physicians extract with their fingers, so "the fingers seek it" is a description of it as a state of the concern. It is also said that the shaghaf is the covering of the heart, or a thin skin called the tongue of the heart; then "which the fingers seek" is a description of the concern. He likened the fingers to one capable of seeking, by way of metaphor (makniyya) and imagination (takhyil); then he likened the intelligible concern to a perceptible thing and exaggerated, to the point of claiming that the fingers search for it and do not find it because of its intense penetration and hiddenness in the heart, or that they touch it and wish to remove it. He explains the concern with his words: "the threat of Abu Qabus," i.e. al-Nu'man's threat and menace, "not in its full reality," i.e. it had not reached me in its completeness; or because it arose without cause from me, rather the slanderers invented lies against me and came to me. "Dunawi": before me, these two places, which are a considerable distance; nevertheless fear overtook me, or the distance, indicating the king's exceedingly great anger with him.]

It was read "sha'afahā" with an ʿayn, from "sha'afa al-ba'ir" when one smears the camel with tar (hana'a), [the commentary note: his words "when he smears it" in al-Sihah: "I smeared the camel" means I daubed it with al-hanaʾ, which is tar], and burned it with tar. He said:

"As the man who smears the mangy camel with tar burns it."

[The verse: "Will you kill me, when you have burned her heart as the man who smears the mangy camel with tar burns it?" This is by Imru' al-Qays, and the interrogative is for denial and disbelief, or for wonder. "Sha'afa al-jamal" means when he burns it with boiling tar on the fire, and "hana'a" means he anointed it with that tar; so "sha'af" is used to mean burning in general, then it is used to mean burning with love, metaphorically and by sending (mursal), so that the comparison in his words is valid: as one burns the anointed camels, the one who anoints them. If it is read with a ghayn, "shaghafta," the meaning is: you struck the covering of her heart with love, which is the covering of the heart or its tongue or a black seed in its middle; as the man who anointed the camels frightened them and disturbed their hearts, because they fear him at first. It is also said: her love is likened to camels' delight in that tar after being anointed with it.]

"And love" is an accusative of specification (tamyiz). "In error" means in mistake and distance from the path of rightness. "With their guile": with their backbiting and evil speech. Their saying "the wife of al-'Aziz has fallen in love with her servant, the Canaanite, and we hate her" – they called backbiting "guile" because it is in secret and in a state of absence, as the schemer hides his scheme. It is also said: she had asked them to keep her secret, but they revealed it against her.

"She sent to them": she invited them. It is said: she invited forty women, among them the five mentioned. "And she prepared for them a *mutaka*": what they lean on, of cushions. She intended by that arrangement, while they were reclining with knives in their hands, that they would be astonished and bewildered at seeing him, and would be distracted from themselves, so their hands would fall upon their hands and cut them, because the one reclining who is bewildered by something lets his hand fall upon his hand. It is not far-fetched that she intended to combine the scheming against him and against them, placing the knives in their hands so they would cut their hands, and so she would rebuke them with the proof, and so that Joseph would be terrified by her guile when he came out before forty women gathered with knives in their hands, and she would imagine that they would attack him. It is also said: *mutaka* means a dining place, because they used to recline for food, drink and conversation, as is the custom of the affluent; and for this reason "he forbade a man to eat reclining" [from the narration of Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman from Ibn al-Zubayr from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade one of us to eat with his left hand and to eat reclining." In al-Tabari, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade two fasts, two prayers, two garments, two foods, two sales and two marriages..." – until he said: as for the two foods: that a man eats with his left hand, and with his right hand is sound; and that he eats reclining, its isnad is good. He has also in al-Awsat and in the Musnad of the Syrians, from the hadith of Abu al-Darda (may God be pleased with him), who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not eat reclining, and do not step over the necks of people on Friday." Ibn Hibban faulted it in al-Du'afa' through Zuraiq ibn Abd Allah, a narrator from 'Amr ibn al-Aswad from Abu al-Darda. And on this subject, from Ibn Abi Ihab. Al-Bazzar recorded it with the wording "he forbade that we eat reclining."] And "she gave them knives to cut with what they eat." It is also said *mutaka* means food, from your saying "we reclined at so-and-so's": we ate [his note: perhaps "i.e. we ate it"], by way of metonymy, because the one you invite to eat with you, you prepare for him a support to lean on. Jamil said:

"So we dwelt in favour and reclined, and drank the lawful from its jars."

[Attributed to Humayd ibn Thawr, and also to Jamil ibn Ma'mar. "Zalla" (to remain) is of the pattern 'alima. He says: we remained in favour, or in a state of being clothed in favour; "wa-ttakana" originally was "awtakana," its first ta' being a waw: i.e. we took a mutaka and lay upon it; and we drank lawful wine, meaning nabidh, "from its qulal," the plural of qullah, which is a great jar. In the mention of the jars there is an indication of the extravagance in drinking and of not being restricted in it.]

And from Mujahid: *mutaka* means food that is cut in slices, as if the meaning were "one leans on with the knife," because the cutter leans on what is cut with the knife. It was read *mutaka* without hamza. From al-Hasan: *mutaka'* with a long vowel, as if it were *iftiʿal*, owing to the lengthening of the fatha of the kaf, like his saying "bi-munтazah" [his note: "bi-muntazah" is from the words of the poet: "And you, from the calamities when they are thrown, and from the blame of men, from afar," the verse is by Ibn Harma mourning his son; al-ghawa'il are the events that seize souls and destroy them; nazaha means to be far away, and al-muntazah is a name for a place of distance, and its fatha was lengthened so that the alif arose from it, as in their saying "yinbaʿ" for "yanbaʿ" and "ʿaqrab" for "ʿaqrab"], meaning "bi-muntazah." Like it is "yunbaʿ" [his note: "yunbaʿ" is from the words of the poet: "It flows from the dhafra, a smooth, noble, sweating she-camel, like the stallion-camel that snorts," and the explanation of this verse was given earlier in surah al-A'raf in this part, page 122, so refer to it if you wish — its corrector], meaning "yanbaʿ." It was also read *matkah*, which is the citron, and he recited:

"So she sent a *matkah* to the sons of her father, which a hard, sturdy she-camel bore swiftly."

[The *matkah* is the citron; it seems to be what Abu Dawud mentioned in his Sunan, that it was split into two halves and carried like two panniers on a camel. *Khabb* is a kind of pace; *ʿuthmuthmah* is hard; *waqqah*, with fatha, is one whose hoof strikes the ground forcefully.]

She had sent a citron on a she-camel; and it may be the citron that Abu Dawud mentioned in his Sunan, that it was split into two halves and carried on a camel like two saddlebags. It is also said: *al-zamawird*, [his note: "al-zamawird" is thin bread stuffed with meat]. From Wahb: citron, bananas and melon.

It is also said: she prepared for them what cuts, from *mataka al-shay'* meaning *bataka*, if he cut it. Al-A'raj read *mutakan* as *mufʿalan*, from *takiʾa yatakaʾu*, if he reclined.

*"Akbarnahu"* — they exalted him, and they were overcome by that beauty, the marvellous elegance and surpassing comeliness.

It is said: Joseph's excellence over people in beauty was like the excellence of the full moon on the night of the full moon over the stars of the sky. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "I passed by Joseph on the night I was taken up to heaven, and I said to Gabriel: 'Who is this?' He said: 'Joseph.'" It was said: "O Messenger of God, how did you see him?" He said: "Like the moon on the night of the full moon." [Recorded by al-Tha'labi from the narration of Abu Harun al-Abdi from Abu Sa'id. Al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in the Dala'il and Ibn Mardawayh recorded it through this route at length.] It is also said that when Joseph walked in the alleys of Egypt, the radiance of his face was seen on the walls, as the light of the sun is seen on water upon them.

It is also said: no one could describe Joseph. It is said: he resembled Adam on the day his Lord created him. It is said: he inherited his beauty from his grandmother Sarah. It is also said: *akbarna* means menstruated, and the *ha'* is for pause. It is said: "the woman *akbarat*" when she menstruated; its essence is that she entered into the state of greatness, for by menstruation she leaves the limit of childhood for the limit of adulthood. It seems Abu al-Tayyib took from this interpretation his words:

"Fear God, and cover this beauty with a veil, for if it appears, the unwed maidens menstruate in their chambers."

[By Abu al-Tayyib. He says: fear God and cover this beauty that is in your face with a veil, for if you appear, the unwed maidens, that is the best of women, who are in their chambers, will menstruate because of what they see of your beauty. *Lah* and *yalih* means: appeared, appears.]

*"Qatta'na aydiyahunna"* — they wounded them, as you say: "I was cutting the meat, so I cut my hand," meaning: I wounded it.

*"Hashā"* is a word expressing exoneration in the matter of exception. You say: "The people did wrong, except Zayd." It is said:

"Hasha Abi Thawban, indeed in him is restraint from rebuke and reviling."

The single form is preferable, because the nun was written in the Mushaf as an alif according to the rule of pausal pronunciation (waqf), and that happens only with the light nun (nun al-khafifa).

And the women said, [a group of women, and they were five]: the wife of the cupbearer, the wife of the baker, the wife of the keeper of the animals, the wife of the jailer, and the wife of the chamberlain. "Niswah" (women) is a singular noun used as a collective plural of "imra'ah" (woman), and its feminine marking is not real, like the feminine marking of "lummah" (a group of companions); for this reason its verb did not take the feminine ta'. It has two dialects: the nun is pronounced with a kasra and with a damma. In the city, in Egypt, "imra'at al-'Aziz" [the wife of al-'Aziz], they mean Qitfir. "Al-'Aziz" means the king in the language of the Arabs. "Fata-hā" [her slave]: her male servant. It is said "fataya" and "fatatī," meaning my male servant and my female servant. "Shaghafahā" [pierced her love]: it split (kharaqa) her love through the "shaghaf" of her heart until it reached the heart (fu'ad). The "shaghaf" is the covering of the heart, and it is said to be a thin skin called the "tongue of the heart."

Al-Nabigha said:
"And a concern has come between me and that, penetrating
into the place of the shaghaf, which the fingers seek."

[The verse: "And a concern has come between me and that, penetrating into the place of the shaghaf, which the fingers seek. / And the threat of Abu Qabus, not in its full reality, came to me, while between me and him are the distant places of Rakish and Fala'ij." Al-Nabigha is apologising to al-Nu'man, king of the Arabs, for what the slanderers had charged him with. That is, a concern has prevented him from amorous pursuit of the beloved and other pleasures. "Waalij" means entering the place of the shaghaf. Another reading is "wa-luwuj al-shaghaf," meaning like its entering. The "shaghaf" is a disease of the heart on the right side, which physicians extract with their fingers, so "the fingers seek it" is a description of it as a state of the concern. It is also said that the shaghaf is the covering of the heart, or a thin skin called the tongue of the heart; then "which the fingers seek" is a description of the concern. He likened the fingers to one capable of seeking, by way of metaphor (makniyya) and imagination (takhyil); then he likened the intelligible concern to a perceptible thing and exaggerated, to the point of claiming that the fingers search for it and do not find it because of its intense penetration and hiddenness in the heart, or that they touch it and wish to remove it. He explains the concern with his words: "the threat of Abu Qabus," i.e. al-Nu'man's threat and menace, "not in its full reality," i.e. it had not reached me in its completeness; or because it arose without cause from me, rather the slanderers invented lies against me and came to me. "Dunawi": before me, these two places, which are a considerable distance; nevertheless fear overtook me, or the distance, indicating the king's exceedingly great anger with him.]

It was read "sha'afahā" with an ʿayn, from "sha'afa al-ba'ir" when one smears the camel with tar (hana'a), [the commentary note: his words "when he smears it" in al-Sihah: "I smeared the camel" means I daubed it with al-hanaʾ, which is tar], and burned it with tar. He said:

"As the man who smears the mangy camel with tar burns it."

[The verse: "Will you kill me, when you have burned her heart as the man who smears the mangy camel with tar burns it?" This is by Imru' al-Qays, and the interrogative is for denial and disbelief, or for wonder. "Sha'afa al-jamal" means when he burns it with boiling tar on the fire, and "hana'a" means he anointed it with that tar; so "sha'af" is used to mean burning in general, then it is used to mean burning with love, metaphorically and by sending (mursal), so that the comparison in his words is valid: as one burns the anointed camels, the one who anoints them. If it is read with a ghayn, "shaghafta," the meaning is: you struck the covering of her heart with love, which is the covering of the heart or its tongue or a black seed in its middle; as the man who anointed the camels frightened them and disturbed their hearts, because they fear him at first. It is also said: her love is likened to camels' delight in that tar after being anointed with it.]

"And love" is an accusative of specification (tamyiz). "In error" means in mistake and distance from the path of rightness. "With their guile": with their backbiting and evil speech. Their saying "the wife of al-'Aziz has fallen in love with her servant, the Canaanite, and we hate her" – they called backbiting "guile" because it is in secret and in a state of absence, as the schemer hides his scheme. It is also said: she had asked them to keep her secret, but they revealed it against her.

"She sent to them": she invited them. It is said: she invited forty women, among them the five mentioned. "And she prepared for them a *mutaka*": what they lean on, of cushions. She intended by that arrangement, while they were reclining with knives in their hands, that they would be astonished and bewildered at seeing him, and would be distracted from themselves, so their hands would fall upon their hands and cut them, because the one reclining who is bewildered by something lets his hand fall upon his hand. It is not far-fetched that she intended to combine the scheming against him and against them, placing the knives in their hands so they would cut their hands, and so she would rebuke them with the proof, and so that Joseph would be terrified by her guile when he came out before forty women gathered with knives in their hands, and she would imagine that they would attack him. It is also said: *mutaka* means a dining place, because they used to recline for food, drink and conversation, as is the custom of the affluent; and for this reason "he forbade a man to eat reclining" [from the narration of Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Sulayman from Ibn al-Zubayr from Jabir, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade one of us to eat with his left hand and to eat reclining." In al-Tabari, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) forbade two fasts, two prayers, two garments, two foods, two sales and two marriages..." – until he said: as for the two foods: that a man eats with his left hand, and with his right hand is sound; and that he eats reclining, its isnad is good. He has also in al-Awsat and in the Musnad of the Syrians, from the hadith of Abu al-Darda (may God be pleased with him), who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not eat reclining, and do not step over the necks of people on Friday." Ibn Hibban faulted it in al-Du'afa' through Zuraiq ibn Abd Allah, a narrator from 'Amr ibn al-Aswad from Abu al-Darda. And on this subject, from Ibn Abi Ihab. Al-Bazzar recorded it with the wording "he forbade that we eat reclining."] And "she gave them knives to cut with what they eat." It is also said *mutaka* means food, from your saying "we reclined at so-and-so's": we ate [his note: perhaps "i.e. we ate it"], by way of metonymy, because the one you invite to eat with you, you prepare for him a support to lean on. Jamil said:

"So we dwelt in favour and reclined, and drank the lawful from its jars."

[Attributed to Humayd ibn Thawr, and also to Jamil ibn Ma'mar. "Zalla" (to remain) is of the pattern 'alima. He says: we remained in favour, or in a state of being clothed in favour; "wa-ttakana" originally was "awtakana," its first ta' being a waw: i.e. we took a mutaka and lay upon it; and we drank lawful wine, meaning nabidh, "from its qulal," the plural of qullah, which is a great jar. In the mention of the jars there is an indication of the extravagance in drinking and of not being restricted in it.]

And from Mujahid: *mutaka* means food that is cut in slices, as if the meaning were "one leans on with the knife," because the cutter leans on what is cut with the knife. It was read *mutaka* without hamza. From al-Hasan: *mutaka'* with a long vowel, as if it were *iftiʿal*, owing to the lengthening of the fatha of the kaf, like his saying "bi-munтazah" [his note: "bi-muntazah" is from the words of the poet: "And you, from the calamities when they are thrown, and from the blame of men, from afar," the verse is by Ibn Harma mourning his son; al-ghawa'il are the events that seize souls and destroy them; nazaha means to be far away, and al-muntazah is a name for a place of distance, and its fatha was lengthened so that the alif arose from it, as in their saying "yinbaʿ" for "yanbaʿ" and "ʿaqrab" for "ʿaqrab"], meaning "bi-muntazah." Like it is "yunbaʿ" [his note: "yunbaʿ" is from the words of the poet: "It flows from the dhafra, a smooth, noble, sweating she-camel, like the stallion-camel that snorts," and the explanation of this verse was given earlier in surah al-A'raf in this part, page 122, so refer to it if you wish — its corrector], meaning "yanbaʿ." It was also read *matkah*, which is the citron, and he recited:

"So she sent a *matkah* to the sons of her father, which a hard, sturdy she-camel bore swiftly."

[The *matkah* is the citron; it seems to be what Abu Dawud mentioned in his Sunan, that it was split into two halves and carried like two panniers on a camel. *Khabb* is a kind of pace; *ʿuthmuthmah* is hard; *waqqah*, with fatha, is one whose hoof strikes the ground forcefully.]

She had sent a citron on a she-camel; and it may be the citron that Abu Dawud mentioned in his Sunan, that it was split into two halves and carried on a camel like two saddlebags. It is also said: *al-zamawird*, [his note: "al-zamawird" is thin bread stuffed with meat]. From Wahb: citron, bananas and melon.

It is also said: she prepared for them what cuts, from *mataka al-shay'* meaning *bataka*, if he cut it. Al-A'raj read *mutakan* as *mufʿalan*, from *takiʾa yatakaʾu*, if he reclined.

*"Akbarnahu"* — they exalted him, and they were overcome by that beauty, the marvellous elegance and surpassing comeliness.

It is said: Joseph's excellence over people in beauty was like the excellence of the full moon on the night of the full moon over the stars of the sky. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "I passed by Joseph on the night I was taken up to heaven, and I said to Gabriel: 'Who is this?' He said: 'Joseph.'" It was said: "O Messenger of God, how did you see him?" He said: "Like the moon on the night of the full moon." [Recorded by al-Tha'labi from the narration of Abu Harun al-Abdi from Abu Sa'id. Al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in the Dala'il and Ibn Mardawayh recorded it through this route at length.] It is also said that when Joseph walked in the alleys of Egypt, the radiance of his face was seen on the walls, as the light of the sun is seen on water upon them.

It is also said: no one could describe Joseph. It is said: he resembled Adam on the day his Lord created him. It is said: he inherited his beauty from his grandmother Sarah. It is also said: *akbarna* means menstruated, and the *ha'* is for pause. It is said: "the woman *akbarat*" when she menstruated; its essence is that she entered into the state of greatness, for by menstruation she leaves the limit of childhood for the limit of adulthood. It seems Abu al-Tayyib took from this interpretation his words:

"Fear God, and cover this beauty with a veil, for if it appears, the unwed maidens menstruate in their chambers."

[By Abu al-Tayyib. He says: fear God and cover this beauty that is in your face with a veil, for if you appear, the unwed maidens, that is the best of women, who are in their chambers, will menstruate because of what they see of your beauty. *Lah* and *yalih* means: appeared, appears.]

*"Qatta'na aydiyahunna"* — they wounded them, as you say: "I was cutting the meat, so I cut my hand," meaning: I wounded it.

*"Hashā"* is a word expressing exoneration in the matter of exception. You say: "The people did wrong, except Zayd." It is said:

"Hasha Abi Thawban, indeed in him is restraint from rebuke and reviling."

[The verse, by al-Munqidh ibn al-Tammah, who is al-Jumayh al-Asadi: "Hasha Abi Thawban, Amr ibn Abd Allah, indeed in him is restraint from rebuke and reviling." *Hasha* is a word of absolution and exoneration, standing in the place of a verbal noun and governing what follows it, like *subhan Allah*. It is permitted that it is the exceptive *hasha*, which is a prepositional particle according to most. The Dabbi transmitted it as *hasha Aba Thawban* with the accusative, so it is a verb; the possibility of the dialect of the restricted form is weak because of the fame of the dialect of inflection by particles. On the first view its building is because of its resemblance to the particle in form and meaning. *Bakuma al-rajul* (like taʿiba): when he was unable to speak. *Qadima* (like sahila and zarufa): when he was unable to argue, as if his mouth were blocked. *Al-dann* with kasra is stinginess. *Al-malhah* is a mafʿalah from *lahahu* when he blamed him. *Al-lihaʾ* (like *al-ridaʾ*) is a mufaʿalah from lahn and ʿadhl, from *lahawtu al-ʿud* when I peeled the wood. The repetition of Abu Thawban is for his exaltation and to mark his name; "laysa bi-bakmah" with damma, meaning: not one with dumbness, i.e. not dumb, nor *qadam*, i.e. incapable of speech. 'Amr: it is said he is a substitute for Abu Thawban, so his words "indeed Abu Thawban..." are a parenthetical sentence explaining the reason for exoneration. And in his words "indeed in him is restraint" is an explanation of the reason for his silence about punishing the base; the meaning: in him is refusal and exaltation above baseness and reviling.]

It is a particle of the prepositions, so it was placed in the position of exoneration and innocence, and the meaning of "hasha Allah" is the innocence of God and the exoneration of God. This is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, with *hasha* annexed to God as annexation of innocence. Whoever reads "hasha li-Allah," it is like your saying "saqyan laka," as if he said "baraʾah" (innocence), then said "li-Allah," to clarify who is declared innocent and exonerated.

The evidence that *hasha* is placed in the position of a verbal noun is the reading of Abu al-Simmal: *hashā lillāh*, with tanwin; and the reading of Abu ʿAmr *hasha lillahi*, with the final alif omitted; and the reading of al-A'mash *hasha lillahi*, with the first alif omitted. It was also read *hashsha lillahi* with the shin sukun, on the basis that the fatha followed the alif in dropping; this is weak because of the meeting of two sukuns against its rule. It was also read *hasha al-ilah*.

If you ask: why was it permissible in *hasha lillah* not to take tanwin, after treating it as "innocence for God"? I say: out of regard for its original form, which is the particle. Do you not see their saying "I sat from on his right" how they left "ʿan" uninflected in its original form? And [his note: his conjunction of "ʿala" in his words needs contrivance, i.e. and to his words "they went from upon him after a mourning, their thirst..." how he left "ʿala" in his words; it is possible the estimate is: do you not see their saying etc., and "ʿala" in his words, i.e. and do you not see "ʿala"...] the alif inverting to yā' with the pronoun in his words "ghadat min ʿalayhi"? The meaning: exalting God, exalted, above the attributes of incapacity, and marvelling at His power to create a beauty like this. As for His words *"hasha lillahi ma ʿalimna ʿalayhi min sawʾ"* [“God forbid! We know no evil in him”], the marvel is at His power to create a chaste one like him. *"Ma hadha basharan"* [“This is no mere mortal”]: they negated humanity from him, for the strangeness of his beauty and the remoteness of his comeliness, for the qualities of the forms of beauty; and they affirmed for him angelhood, and by it gave judgment. This is because God, mighty and majestic, established in human nature that there is nothing more beautiful than an angel, just as He established in it that there is nothing uglier than the devil; for this reason every extreme of beauty and ugliness is likened to them. He established that in them only because the reality is so, just as He established in human nature that there is nothing more inclined to evil than the devils, nor more gathered to good than the angels — except what the lost, rebellious group, the Jabriyya, hold concerning the preference of man over the angel; and this is nothing but their inversion of realities, their denial of necessary knowledge, and their obstinacy in every matter. [His note: "except what the lost group holds" means the people of the Sunna, and he has erred in his partisanship for the Mu'tazila, may God pardon him.] The use of *ma* in the manner of *laysa* is the ancient Hijazi dialect, and the Qur'an came in it. Among it is God's saying *"ma hunna ummahatihim"* [“they are not their mothers”]. Whoever reads by his natural dialect of the Banu Tamim reads *"bashar"* with a damma. It is in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. It was also read *"ma hadha bashariy"*, meaning: he is not a base, lowly, owned slave; *"in hadha illa malakun karim"* [“this is none but a noble angel”]. You say: *"hadha bashara"*, meaning: it is a gain for you, i.e. it is attainment of good news, in the sense of "this is a good" — and you say: "This is for you a good news, or a bakra?"

The reading (qira'a) with the singular is the preferable one, because it agrees with the Mushaf (the codified Qur'an), and because it matches "basharin" (a human) with "malak" (an angel). She said ﴿فَذَلِكُنَّ الَّذِي لُمْتُنَّنِي فِيهِ﴾ ("That is the one about whom you blamed me"), and she did not say "fa-hadha" ("this one"), though he was present. This is to raise his rank in beauty, to make him worthy of being loved and of being the object of infatuation, to exalt his condition, and to affirm the lofty status of his station. It is also possible that the demonstrative refers to the meaning expressed in their words: "She has fallen in love with her Canaanite slave." It is as if she said: "That is the Canaanite slave whom you pictured in your own selves, then you blamed me for him." She means: you did not picture him as he truly is. Had you pictured him as you have now seen him, you would have excused me for being infatuated with him.

Al-istis'am (﴿فَاسْتَعْصَمَ﴾, "he abstained") is a form of emphasis (intensive construction) indicating extreme refusal and intense self-restraint, as if he were in a state of protection while striving to increase it. It is similar to istamsaka ("he held fast"), istawsa'a al-fatq ("he widened the tear"), istajma'a al-ra'y ("he gathered his opinion"), and istafhala al-khatb ("the matter grew severe").

This is a clear statement of what Yusuf (peace be upon him) did, beyond which nothing more can be added, and a proof brighter than anything else, showing that he is innocent of what the people of hashw (the "padding" party, a term Zamakhshari uses for the literalist exegetes) have attributed to him in their explanations of "al-hamm" (the intention) and "al-burhan" (the proof).

If you say: does the pronoun in ﴿آمُرُهُ﴾ refer to the relative pronoun (alladhi), or to Yusuf? I say: it refers to the relative pronoun. The meaning is "what I command him," and the preposition has been omitted, as in your saying "amartuka al-khayr" ("I commanded you the good"). It is also permissible to make "ma" a verbal-noun (masdariyya) particle, in which case the pronoun refers to Yusuf, and the meaning is: "And if he does not carry out my command to him," that is, the requirement and consequence of my command.

It has been read as ﴿وَلَيَكُونًا﴾ with both the doubled (tashdid) and the single (takhfif) forms of the nun. The single form is preferable, because the nun was written in the Mushaf as an alif according to the rule of pausal pronunciation (waqf), and that happens only with the light nun (nun al-khafifa).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 33–34:

It is also recited as "al-sijnu" (السِّجْنُ) with a fatha, as a verbal noun (مصدر). "He said, 'They invite me'" (يَدْعُونَنِي) is with the attribution of the invitation to all of them (the women), because they were advising him, and they had made the yielding to her seem appealing to him, and they said to him: "Beware of casting yourself into prison and humiliation." Thereupon he sought refuge with his Lord and said: "My Lord, imprisonment is dearer to me than committing disobedience." If you say: imprisonment is a severe hardship upon the soul, while what they invited him to is a great pleasure, so how could hardship be dearer to him than pleasure? I say: it was dearer to him and more preferred by him, looking to the goodness of patience in bearing it for the sake of God, and to the ugliness of disobedience, and to the outcome of each of the two, not looking at what the soul desires or dislikes. "And unless You turn away from me their guile" (وَإِلَّا تَصْرِفْ عَنِّي كَيْدَهُنَّ): he fled to the subtle kindnesses of God and His protection, as is the custom of the prophets and the righteous regarding what they have resolved upon and resolved their souls to endure patiently, not that he should seek compulsion toward chastity or be forced to it. "I would incline toward them" (أَصْبُ إِلَيْهِنَّ): I would lean toward them. The "ṣabwa" (الصبوة) is the inclination toward desire, and from it comes "al-ṣabā" (الصبا), because souls incline toward it for the pleasantness of its breeze and its spirit. It is also recited "aṣub ilayhinna," from "al-ṣabāba" (الصبابة). "Among the ignorant" (مِنَ الْجاهِلِينَ): among those who do not act upon what they know, because one whose knowledge is of no benefit is the same as one who does not know. Or among the foolish, because the wise does not commit ugliness. The response is mentioned without the supplication having preceded it, because his saying "unless You turn away from me" contains the meaning of asking for the turning away and supplicating for kindness. "He is the All-Hearing" (السَّمِيعُ) of the supplications of those who seek refuge in Him, "the All-Knowing" (الْعَلِيمُ) of their circumstances and what benefits them.
