Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 35:

The subject of بَدا لَهُمْ (*badā lahum*, "it appeared to them") is an implied pronoun, indicated by what explains it, namely ﴿ليسجننه﴾ ("that they imprison him"). The meaning is: *badā lahum bidā'* (a notion arose in them), that is, an opinion appeared to them to imprison him. The pronoun in *lahum* refers to the Governor and his household. ﴿مِنْ بَعْدِ ما رَأَوُا الْآياتِ﴾ ("after they had seen the signs") means the evidences of his innocence. This happened only because the woman had seduced her husband and turned him around, "in the crest and the back" (i.e., she managed him completely). [[Al-Zamakhshari's words "and turning him around in the crest" mean her circling around him by means of her deception. Reported by al-Sihah. (ع)]] He had become compliant with her, gentle and docile, his rein in her hand. Thus, what he had witnessed of the signs made him forget, and he acted on her opinion regarding his imprisonment and the humiliation he would suffer, as she had threatened him with it. This was because she had despaired of his obedience to her, or because she hoped that prison would subdue him and make him subservient to her.

In the recitation of al-Hasan (the recitation (*qira'a*) of al-Hasan), it is read *latasjununnahu* with a *tā'* (لَتَسْجُنُنَّهُ), in the second person. Some of them addressed the Governor and those around him with this, or it was addressed to the Governor alone as a mark of respect. ﴿حَتَّى حِينٍ﴾ ("for a time") means until a period of time. It is as if she proposed that he be imprisoned for a while, until she saw what would become of him.

In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, it is read *'atā ḥīn*, which is the dialect of Hudhayl (a tribe). It is related from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) that he heard a man reciting *'atā ḥīn*, and he said: "Who taught you this?" He said: "Ibn Mas'ud." So he wrote to him: "Allah revealed this Qur'an in Arabic and sent it down in the dialect of Quraysh. So teach the people in the dialect of Quraysh, and do not teach them in the dialect of Hudhayl. Peace."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 36:

"Ma'a" (with) indicates the meaning of companionship and its initiation. You say, "I went out with the prince," meaning as his companion, so their entering the prison must have been as his companions. Two young men (fatayan), slaves of the king: his baker and his cupbearer. It was reported to him that they intended to poison him, [[His saying "it was reported to him that they intended to poison him": in al-Sihah, "raqa ilayhi al-kalam tarqiyatan" means "it was raised to him," i.e., it was brought up to him. (ʿ)]] so he ordered them sent to prison. They were put in at the same time that Yusuf, peace be upon him, was put in. "Indi arani" (Indeed I see myself), meaning in a dream, and it is a narration of a past situation. "A'siru khamran" (I am pressing wine), meaning grapes, calling grapes by what they will become. It was also said that "khamr," in the dialect of Oman, is the name for grapes. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "a'siru 'inaban" (I am pressing grapes). "Min al-muhsinin" (of the good-doers): those who excel in interpreting dreams, i.e., those who do it well. They saw him being recounted the dream of some of the prisoners and interpreting it for him, so they said this to him. Or it means of the scholars, because they heard him speaking to people and knew that he was learned.

Or "of the good-doers" to the people of the prison. So be kind to us by relieving us of our distress through the interpretation of what we have seen, if you have any skill in interpreting dreams. It is related that whenever a man among them fell ill, he would attend to him; whenever one became poor, he would provide for him; and whenever one was in need, he would gather for him. It is also related from Qatadah: there were people in the prison who had lost hope and whose sorrow had lengthened, and he began to say, "Rejoice. Be patient and you will be rewarded, for indeed there is a great reward in this." They said, "May God bless you! How beautiful your face is and how beautiful your character! We have been blessed by your neighborhood. Who are you, young man?" He said, "I am Yusuf, son of the one chosen by God (Safiyy Allah) Ya'qub, son of the one sacrificed by God (Dhabih Allah) Ishaq, son of the friend of God (Khalil Allah) Ibrahim." The jailer said to him, "If I could, I would release you, but I will treat you well. Stay in whichever part of the prison you wish."

It is also related that the two young men said to him, "We love you from the moment we saw you." He said, "I beg you by God not to love me, for by God, no one has ever loved me without that love bringing me trouble. My aunt loved me, and her love brought me trouble. Then my father loved me, and his love brought me trouble. Then the wife of my master loved me, and her love brought me trouble. So do not love me, may God bless you both."

On the authority of al-Sha'bi: they both dreamed together to test him. The cupbearer said, "Indeed I see myself in a garden, and there is a grapevine stalk (habalah) with three bunches of grapes on it. I picked them and pressed them into the king's cup and gave it to him to drink." And the baker said, "Indeed I see myself, and on my head are three baskets containing various kinds of food, and birds of prey are pecking at them." [[His saying "fa-idha asila'?" ... "habalah" in al-Sihah: "al-habalah" with a damma is the fruit of the 'idah (thorny trees); and in it: "al-'idah" is every tree that grows large and has thorns; and "al-habalah" with a fatha is a shoot of a vine. Also in it: "sallat al-khubz" is the well-known bread basket. (ʿ)]]

If you ask: to what does the pronoun in His saying "nabbi'na bi-ta'wilihi" (inform us of its interpretation) refer? I answer: it refers to what they had related to him. The pronoun functions in the manner of a demonstrative in such constructions, as if it had been said, "Inform us of the interpretation of that."

When they had made him weep and described him as one of the good-doers, he seized the opportunity [[His saying "افترص ذلك" means he took it as an opportunity (فرصة), a turn, a share, and a portion, as al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) states. (ʿ)]]. He then linked to this by describing himself with what is beyond the knowledge of scholars: informing them of the unseen. He told them that he would inform them of the food that would be brought to them in prison before it came, describing it to them, saying, "Today there will come to you food of such and such a description." They found it just as he had told them. He made this a means of reaching the point of mentioning monotheism (tawhid) to them, presenting faith to them and making it appealing, and making polytheism (shirk) against God repugnant to them. This is the method that every scholar should follow with the ignorant and the sinners: when one of them asks him for a legal ruling, he should first offer guidance, direction, admonition, and advice, and call him to what is more important for him and more obligatory upon him than what he asked about, and only then give him the ruling.

In this there is the point that when a scholar's standing in knowledge is unknown, and he describes himself with what is relevant to the matter, his aim being that they take from him and benefit from him in religion, this does not fall under self-praise (tazkiya). His explanation of its nature and manner is like the explanation of an obscure matter and the clarification of its meaning. ﴿That is part of what my Lord has taught me﴾ refers to the interpretation (ta'wil, the explanation of the meaning and outcome of a matter) and to the reports of unseen things. That is, that interpretation and reporting of the unseen was taught to me and revealed to me, and I did not say it from soothsaying (takahhun) or astrology (tanajjum).

﴿Indeed I have forsaken﴾ may be an independent statement, or it may be a reason for what precedes it: that is, my Lord taught me that and revealed it to me, because I rejected the creed of those people and followed the creed of the prophets mentioned, which is the upright creed (al-milla al-hanifiyya). By "those" who do not believe he means the people of Egypt and those whose religion the two youths followed. Repeating them serves to show that they in particular are disbelievers in the Hereafter, and that others were people who believed in it, namely those who followed the creed of Abraham. It also serves to emphasize their disbelief in recompense, pointing to the injustice and grave sins they committed, which none would commit except one who disbelieves in the abode of recompense.

It may also contain an allusion to what he suffered at their hands when they imprisoned him, after they had seen the signs testifying to his innocence, and that such an act is not undertaken except by one who is extremely disbelieving in recompense. He mentioned his fathers to show them that he comes from a house of prophethood, after having informed them that he is a prophet to whom revelation is sent, through what he mentioned of his reports of unseen things, so that their desire to listen to him and follow his words would be strengthened.

﴿It is not for us﴾, that is, it is not proper for us, the company of prophets, ﴿to associate anything with God﴾, whatever it might be, whether an angel, a jinn, or a human, let alone associating with Him an idol that neither hears nor sees. Then he said, ﴿That [monotheism] is from the bounty of God upon us and upon mankind﴾, that is, upon the messengers and upon those to whom they were sent, because they alerted them to it and guided them to it. ﴿But most people do not give thanks﴾, meaning the people to whom they were sent do not give thanks for God's bounty, so they associate others with Him and do not take heed.

It has also been said that this is a bounty of God upon us, because He set up for us the proofs by which we reflect and draw inferences. He has set up similar proofs for all people without any difference, but most people do not reflect or draw inferences, following their desires, and so they remain disbelievers, not thankful.

When they had made him weep and described him as one of the good-doers, he seized the opportunity [[His saying "افترص ذلك" means he took it as an opportunity (فرصة), a turn, a share, and a portion, as al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari) states. (ʿ)]]. He then linked to this by describing himself with what is beyond the knowledge of scholars: informing them of the unseen. He told them that he would inform them of the food that would be brought to them in prison before it came, describing it to them, saying, "Today there will come to you food of such and such a description." O my two fellow prisoners! (Literally, "O my two companions of the prison," that is, "O my two companions in the prison.") He attributed them to the prison just as one says "O thief of the night," for just as the night is not what is stolen, but rather the thing stolen is in it, so too the prison is not what is accompanied; rather, the one accompanied is someone else, namely Yusuf, peace be upon him. A similar usage is your saying to your two companions, "O my two companions of truth," attributing them to truth, and you do not mean that they accompanied truth; rather, it is like saying "a man of truth." And you name them "two companions" because they accompanied you.

It is also permissible that he meant: "O inhabitants of the prison," like His saying: ﴿companions of the Fire and companions of Paradise﴾ [al-Hashr 59:20 / al-Ma'ida 5:29 type usage], and ﴿Are separate lords better, or God, the One, the Subduer?﴾ [Yusuf 12:39]. He means the dispersion in number and multiplicity: "Is it better for you to have many lords, each enslaving you in this way and that way, or for you to have one Lord, Subduer, who is not overcome and has no partner in lordship? Rather, He is al-Qahhar, the Overpowering." This is an example He struck for the worship of God alone and the worship of idols.

﴿What you worship besides Him are only names﴾: this is addressed to the two of them and to whoever holds their religion among the people of Egypt. It means that you have named what does not deserve divinity as "gods," and then you began to worship them, so it is as if you worship nothing but empty names with no named realities beneath them. The meaning of ﴿you have named them﴾ is: you have named them with these names. It is said: "I named him Zayd" and "I named him as Zayd." ﴿Which God has not sent down any authority for﴾, that is, for their naming, meaning no proof. ﴿Judgment belongs only to God﴾, concerning matters of worship and religion. Then He explained what He has ruled, saying: ﴿He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion﴾, the firm one, which the proofs have indicated.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 41:

As for one of you two, he will give his lord (sayyidahu) to drink. Ikrimah recited: "fa-yusqa rabbahu", meaning: he will be given to drink, that is, what he is irrigated with, in the passive form (al-bina' lil-maf'ul). It is narrated that he said to the first one: "What you saw of the vine and its beauty, the king is [your] lord, and your condition with him is good. As for the three branches, they are three days that pass while you are in prison; then you will come out and return to what you were." And he said to the second: "What you saw of the baskets, three days, then you will come out and be crucified." ﴿The matter has been decided﴾ means: cut off and completed the matter about which you two inquire, concerning your affair and your situation.

If you ask: the two did not inquire about one matter but about two different matters, so what is the reasoning for the singular (tawhid)? I say: the intended "matter" is what they were accused of, the poisoning of the king, and for which they were imprisoned. They thought that what they had seen had the same meaning as what had befallen them, so it was as if they were asking him about the matter that had befallen them: whether its outcome would be deliverance or destruction. So he said to them: "The matter about which you inquire has been decided," that is, the outcome it leads to, which is the destruction of one of them and the deliverance of the other.

It was also said: they denied and said, "We saw nothing," according to what is narrated, that they made an oath to him, so he informed them that this was going to happen, "whether you spoke the truth or lied."

The Ḍann (the one who thought) was Yusuf if his interpretation was by way of ijtihad (independent reasoning, *ijtihād*). If it was by way of wahy (revelation), then the one who thought was the cupbearer, and ẓann would then mean certainty (yaqīn).

*Udhkurnī ʿinda rabbika* (Mention me to your lord): mention me to the king by my description, and relate my story to him, so that perhaps he will show mercy to me and rescue me from this predicament. *Fa-ansāhu al-shayṭānu dhikra rabbihi* (So Satan made him forget the mention of his lord): Satan made the cupbearer forget to mention him to his lord. It is also said that *fa-ansāhu* means that Yusuf forgot the remembrance of God when he entrusted his affair to someone other than God. *Biḍʿa sinīn* (a few years): the *bidʿ* (a term for an indefinite small number) is between three and nine. Most of the reports hold that he remained there for seven years.

If you ask: how can Satan have power over a human being? I answer: he whispers to the servant things that distract him from something, through the causes of forgetting, until it leaves him and his remembrance slips from his heart. As for causing forgetfulness from the outset, only God, the Mighty and Majestic, has power over that: *mā nansakh min āyatin aw nunsihā* (We do not abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten).

If you ask: what is the justification for attributing the remembrance to his lord when what is meant is the king? And it is not an annexation of a verbal noun to its subject or to its object? I answer: he is connected to it in your saying "Satan made him forget the remembrance of his lord" or "with his lord," so it is permissible to attribute it to him, because annexation may occur with the slightest connection. Or the phrase is to be understood as "Satan made him forget the remembrance of the news of his lord," so the governing noun, which is *al-ikhbār* (the news), has been omitted.

If you ask: why was Yusuf rebuked for seeking help from other than God in removing what he was suffering? God the Exalted has said: *wa-taʿāwanū ʿalā al-birri wa-al-taqwā* (And cooperate in righteousness and piety), and He said, relating from ʿIsā (peace be upon him): *man anṣārī ilā Allāh* (Who are my helpers in (the cause of) God?). And in the hadith: "God is in the aid of the servant as long as the servant is in the aid of his Muslim brother," and: "Whoever relieves a believer of a distress, God will relieve him of a distress of the distresses of the Hereafter." And from ʿĀʾisha, may God be pleased with her: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was not overtaken by sleep one night, and he was asking for someone to guard him, until Saʿd came, and she heard his snoring. [Agreed upon (*mutafaq ʿalayhi*, reported by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim) from the route of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir ibn Rabīʿa from her, with the wording: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) could not sleep one night. He said: 'Would that a righteous man of my companions would guard me tonight.' He said: I heard the sound of weapons, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood up. Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ said: 'O Messenger of God, I have come to guard you.' ʿĀʾisha said: He then slept until I heard his snoring." Al-Ḥākim neglected this and added it as a supplement (*istadrakahu*).] Is that not merely like seeking treatment with medicines and gaining strength through drinks and food? And if it was because the king was an unbeliever, then there is no disagreement about the permissibility of seeking help from unbelievers in repelling oppression, drowning, burning and similar harms?

I answer: just as God the Exalted chose the prophets above His creatures, He also chose for them the best, most excellent and most fitting affairs. The better and more fitting course for a prophet, when he is afflicted with a trial, is not to entrust his affair to anyone but his lord, and not to lean on anyone but Him, especially when the one he leans on is an unbeliever, lest the unbelievers rejoice over him and say: "If this man were upon the truth, and had a lord who would relieve him, he would not have sought our help." It is reported from al-Ḥasan that he used to weep when he recited it and would say: "When a matter befalls us, we turn to people for help."

When the time of Joseph's release drew near, the king of Egypt, al-Rayyan ibn al-Walid, saw a strange dream that alarmed him. He saw seven fat cows coming out of a dry river, and seven lean cows, and the lean ones swallowed the fat ones. He also saw seven green ears of grain whose grain had formed, and seven others that were dry, having ripened and become ready for harvest, so the dry ones twisted around the green ones until they overcame them. He asked for its interpretation, but he found no one among his people who could interpret it well. *Simān* is the plural of *samīn* (masculine) and *samīna* (feminine), and likewise *rijāl* and *niswa kirām* (noble men and women).

If you say: is there a difference between placing *simān* as an adjective of the specified noun, *baqarāt* (cows), rather than of the specifying term, *sabʿa* (seven), and saying *sabʿa baqarāt samānā*? I say:

If you make it an adjective of *baqarāt*, you intend to specify the seven by a kind of cows, namely the fat ones among them, not by their genus. If you describe *sabʿa* with it, you intend to specify the seven by the genus of cows rather than by a kind of them, and then you return and describe the specifying noun, which is a genus, with fatness. If you say: why not say *sabʿ ʿijāf* as an *idāfa* (construct phrase)?

I say: *tamyīz* (specification) is meant to clarify the genus, and *ʿijāf* (lean) is a description by which clarification alone is not achieved. If you say: they do say *thalāthat furasān* (three knights) and *khamsat aṣḥāb* (five companions)?

I say: *al-fāris* (the knight), *al-ṣāḥib* (the companion), *al-rākib* (the rider) and similar words are descriptions that have taken the course of nouns, so they take the rulings of nouns, and things are permitted in them that are not permitted in others. Do you not see that you do not say: *ʿindī thalāthat ḍikhām wa arbaʿat ghilāẓ* (I have three big men and four coarse men)?

If you say: that is problematic, whereas what we are concerned with has no problem. Do you not see that he did not say *baqarāt sabʿ ʿijāf* (seven lean cows), because it is known that the intended meaning is cows?

I say: abandoning the original form is not permissible when one can dispense with what is not original, and you can dispense with your saying *sabʿun ʿijāfun* (seven lean) without the specification by description that you propose. *Al-ʿajf* is extreme emaciation beyond which there is nothing, and the reason why *ʿijāf* occurs as the plural of *ʿajfāʾ* is that *afʿal* and *faʿlāʾ* are not pluralized as *fiʿāl*; it was modeled on *simān*, because it is its opposite, and it is their practice to model the similar on the similar and the opposite on the opposite.

If you say: is there evidence in the verse that the dry ears were seven like the green ones? I say: the discourse is built on the focus on this number in the fat cows, the lean cows, and the green ears, so it was necessary that it encompass the meaning of the other seven, and his saying *wa ukhara yābisāt* (and other dry ones) is in the sense of *wa sabʿan ukhar* (and seven others).

If you say: is it permissible that his saying *wa ukhara yābisāt* be conjoined to *sunbulāt khuḍr* (green ears), so that it is in the genitive position? I say: this leads to a contradiction, which is that conjoining them to *sunbulāt khuḍr* requires that they enter its ruling, so they would be together a specification of the mentioned seven, whereas the word *ukhar* (others) requires that they be other than the seven. Its explanation: you say *ʿindī sabʿat rijāl qiyām wa quʿūd* (I have seven men standing and sitting) in the genitive, and it is correct, because you have specified the seven by men described as standing and sitting, with some of them standing and some sitting. But if you said *ʿindahu sabʿat rijāl qiyām wa ākharīn quʿūd* (he has seven men standing and other men sitting), it would be contradictory and invalid.

*Yā ayyuhā al-malaʾ* (O assembly) — it is as if he meant the notables among the scholars and the wise.

The *lām* in his saying *lil-ruʾyā* (for the dream) is either for clarification, like His saying *wa kānū fīhi min al-zāhidīn* (and they were among those who had no desire for it), or it is inserted, because when the governing word precedes its object, it is not as strong in acting upon it as when the object follows it. So it is strengthened by *lām*, just as the active participle is strengthened by it, when you say *huwa ʿābirun lil-ruʾyā* (he is an interpreter of dreams), because it falls short of the verb in strength.

It is permissible that *lil-ruʾyā* be the predicate of *kāna* (was), as you say *kāna fulān li-hādhā al-amr* (so-and-so was for this matter) when he is independently in charge of it and empowered over it. And *taʿburūna* (you interpret) is another predicate, or a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). Or *taʿburūna* may be taken to imply a verb that is transitive with *lām*, as if it were said: *in kuntum tantadibūna li-ʿibārat al-ruʾyā* (if you are appointed for the interpretation of the dream).

The real meaning of *ʿabarat al-ruʾyā* (he interpreted the dream) is that he mentioned its outcome and final end, just as you say *ʿabarat al-nahr* (I crossed the river) when you cross it until you reach the far end of its width, and that is its *ʿabr* (crossing point). Similar to it: *awwaltu al-ruʾyā* (I interpreted the dream) when you mention its *maʾāl* (outcome), which is its return.

*ʿAbarat al-ruʾyā* with the light form is what the reliable authorities have adopted, and I have seen them reject *ʿabbarat* with the doubled form, as well as *al-taʿbīr* (interpretation) and *al-muʿabbir* (interpreter). I have come across a verse that al-Mubarrad recited in his book *al-Kāmil*, attributed to some Bedouin:

*raʾaytu ruʾyā thumma ʿabbartuhā*
*wa kuntu lil-aḥlāmi ʿabbārā*

I saw a dream, then I interpreted it,
and I was an interpreter of dreams.

*Note: al-Mubarrad recited it in his book. "Ru'yā" with alif is the verbal noun of seeing in sleep, and its use with a tāʾ is rare; the verbal noun of seeing with the eyes is the reverse. "ʿAbarat al-ruʾyā" with the light form and with doubling as here means: she mentioned its outcome and reached its end, like "awwaltahā" when you mention its outcome and return. "Al-aḥlām" is the plural of "ḥulm" with a ḍamma, which is what a sleeper sees. "Al-ʿabbār" is an intensive form of "al-muʿabbir" or "al-ʿābir." The lām is added to the object to strengthen the governing word when it is weakened by being placed after its object, or by being a derivative of the verb; both of these apply here, so the lām was added.*

Confused dreams (aḍghāth aḥlām): their jumbled and false contents, and whatever of them comes from the promptings of the self or the whisperings of Satan.

The root meaning of aḍghāth is what is gathered and bundled from mixed herbs; its singular is ḍighth. The term was then borrowed for this sense. The construct phrase (iḍāfa) here carries the meaning of "min" (from), so that aḍghāth aḥlām means "bundles of dreams." The sense is: "They are confused dreams." If you ask: it was only one dream, so why did they say "confused dreams" in the plural? I answer: it is like your saying, "So-and-so rides horses and wears silk turbans," said of someone who rides only one horse and owns only one turban. This is an exaggeration in description. Likewise, they exaggerated in describing the dream as false, calling it "confused dreams." It is also possible that he had recounted to them, along with this vision, other visions. And their words, "We are not learned in the interpretation of dreams" (wa-mā naḥnu bi-ta'wīl al-aḥlām bi-ʿālimīn), may mean either: (1) that they intend by "dreams" specifically false dreams, so they would say: "there is no interpretation for them with us, for interpretation applies only to sound and righteous dreams"; or (2) that they acknowledge the deficiency of their knowledge and that they are not masters (naḥārīr) in the interpretation of dreams.

[[Al-Zamakhsharī's statement: "It is possible that their intended meaning by 'dreams' is dreams in general..." Etc. Commentator Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This is the apparent meaning. Reading the phrase the other way makes it like the line of verse: "upon a loving one whose beacon is not followed," as if they said: "there is no interpretation for false dreams, so that we would be knowledgeable in it." The king's statement to them at first, "If you are able to interpret dreams" (in kuntum lil-ru'yā ta'burūn), is evidence that in his judgment they were not knowledgeable in them, since he used the particle of doubt; and their admission of deficiency came in accordance with the king's doubt, which he phrased as a question about whether they were knowledgeable in dreams. The youth's statement, "I will inform you of its interpretation... so that I may return to the people, that they may know," is also evidence of this, and God knows best.]]

Note: "naḥārīr" is the plural of naḥrīr, meaning the expert who is thoroughly proficient, as in the Ṣiḥāḥ.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 45:

It is recited "wa-dda-kara" with the dal, and this is the eloquent (fasih) reading. And it is narrated from al-Hasan: "wa-dhdhakara," with the dhal marked with a dot. The original is "tadhakkara," meaning: he remembered, the one who was saved of the two youths from being killed, Yusuf, and what he had witnessed from him "after a period" (ba'da ummatin), after a long time. This is because when he [the king] asked about his dream and the chiefs (al-mala') could not interpret it, the one who was saved remembered Yusuf and his interpretation of his dream and the dream of his companion, and he had asked him to mention him to the king. Al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read "ba'da ummatin" with a kasra on the hamza, and al-Ummah means blessing (ni'mah). 'Adi said:

[[Where is Kisra, the king of kings, Abu Sasan, and where before him is Sabur?

After prosperity and kingship and blessing, the graves have covered them there.

Then they became like dry leaves, so the breeze and the south wind blew upon them.

By 'Adi ibn Zayd. Kisra, Sasan and Sabur are names of kings, and Sasan is the father of the Akasira. It is also narrated as "Anushirvan" instead of "Abu Sasan," so it is one word. The second Kisra is a substitute for the first, in construct with what follows it, as one says "malik al-muluk" (king of kings). It is a Persian arabized word, its origin being Khusraw, which Arabic altered. If it is Arabic, derived from "al-kasr" (breaking), the meaning is that he used to break the power of kings. What follows is an explanatory apposition (bayan) to it, and "qablahu" is connected to an omitted element as a circumstantial clause (hal) from Sabur. The word "bal" indicates that Sabur was greater than both of them. "Thumma" with a fatha is an adverb whose predicate is an omitted element, meaning "they are then." If it is with a damma, it is a conjunction coordinating with an omitted element, meaning "they prospered, then after prosperity," that is, survival, or success and kingship. In another narration "al-rushd" (right guidance) is used instead. "Al-immah" with a kasra is blessing, and with a damma is a great army. "Warathum" means their graves covered them in that place, a metaphor for their death, so they are buried in the depths of the earth after their greatness upon its surface. Then he compared them to the leaf that dried, so that the breeze and the south wind blew upon it, this one in one direction and that one in another. "Alwat" means "iltawat" (twisted), or in the sense of "awqa'at bihi" (struck it), meaning that time stretched over them until their bones crumbled and became like that.]] That is, after he had been blessed with deliverance. It is also recited "ba'da ummatin" as "after forgetfulness" [[His saying "it is recited ba'da ummatin as after forgetfulness" perhaps means "ba'da" (after). (Editor)]]. It is said: "amihahu ya'mahu amhan" when he forgot. Whoever reads it with a sukun on the mim has erred [[His saying "whoever reads it with a sukun on the mim has erred" means sinned, from "khata'" with a kasra, which is sin, as stated in al-Sihah. (Editor)]]. "Ana unabbi'ukum bita'wilihi": I will inform you of its interpretation, from one who has knowledge of it.

In the recitation of al-Hasan: "Ana atikum bita'wilihi," I will bring you its interpretation. "Fa-arsilun," so send me to him that I may ask him, and [let me go] to him for its interpretation.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: the prison was not in the city.

The meaning: "So they sent him to Yusuf, and he came to him and said: Yusuf, O man of truth (al-Siddiq), the one eminent in truthfulness." He addressed him in this way because he had tested his circumstances and recognized his truthfulness in the interpretation of his dream and the dream of his companion, when it came about just as he had interpreted. For this reason he spoke to him in guarded speech, saying: "Perhaps I may return to the people, perhaps they will know," because he was not certain of returning, for he might die before that, and not certain of their knowing, for perhaps they would not know. Or the meaning of "perhaps they will know" is: perhaps they will know your merit and your standing in knowledge, so that they seek you out and free you from your ordeal.

The phrase "تزرعون" is a report in the sense of a command, like His saying: ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in Allah's cause﴾. The command comes in the form of a report only for the sake of emphasis on the obligation of what is commanded, so that it is treated as though it already exists, and so it is reported about.

The evidence that it carries the meaning of a command is His saying: ﴿So leave it in its ear﴾. "Daaban" is read with the hamza both unvocalized and vocalized, and both are verbal nouns of "da'aba fi al-'amal" (he persisted in the work). It is a circumstantial state (hal) of those addressed, meaning persistently: either as a state of "tad'abuna da'aban" (you shall persevere with perseverance), or as the verbal noun placed in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning "dhawi da'ab" (possessors of persistence). ﴿So leave it in its ear﴾ so that it does not become infested. "Ya'kulna" is a figurative ascription (al-isnad al-majazi): the eating of its people is ascribed to the lean cows. ﴿You store up﴾ means you keep and hoard. ﴿Mankind will be given relief﴾ comes from al-ghawth (relief) or from al-ghayth (rain). It is said: "ghiyatha al-bilad" when the lands received rain, and from it is the saying of the Bedouin woman: "We were given rain as much as we wished."

﴿They will press﴾ is read with the ya' and with the ta': they press grapes, olives and sesame. It is also said: they milk the udders.

It is also read "yu'sarun" in the passive voice, from "a'sarahu" meaning he rescued him, which agrees with relief. It is permissible for it to be in the active voice with the meaning "yanjun" (they will be saved), as if it were said: in it mankind will be given relief, and in it they will give relief to themselves; that is, Allah will give them relief and some of them will give relief to others. It is also said that ﴿ya'surun﴾ means "they will be rained upon," from "a'sarat al-sahabah" (the cloud rained). There are two possibilities for this: either "a'sarat" is taken to include the meaning of "matarat" (it rained) and so is construed with its transitive form, or it is said that the original is "a'sarat 'alayhim" and the preposition was dropped and the verb was made to reach its object directly.

He interpreted the fat cows and the green ears as years of abundance, and the lean and the dry as years of drought. Then, after finishing the interpretation of the dream, he gave them the good news that the eighth year would come blessed, fertile, abundant in good and plentiful in blessings, and that this was from the side of revelation. It is narrated from Qatadah: "Allah increased him in knowledge of a year."

If you say: it is known that when years of drought end, their ending is by fertility, otherwise they would not be described as ending, so why do you say that this knowledge came from revelation? I say: that is known in a general way, not in detail. And His saying ﴿in it mankind will be given relief, and in it they will press﴾ is a detailing of the condition of that year, and that is not known except through revelation.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verses 50–51:

He delayed and deliberated before answering the king, and he put forward the question of the women so that his innocence of the accusation brought against him might become clear, "for which he was accused and imprisoned," lest the envious use it as a ladder (*tasallu*, i.e., a means) to disparage his position in the king's eyes and to bring down his rank with him, and lest they say that he remained in prison for seven years only because of a great matter and a grave crime that deserved his imprisonment, torment, and the restraint of his evil.

[[Al-Zamakhshari said: "He delayed and deliberated before answering the king so that his innocence of the accusation brought against him... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: The Prophet ﷺ praised him for this forbearance by saying: "If I had remained in prison as long as Yusuf remained, I would have answered the summoner." Within the praise of his forbearance and deliberation lay the clearing and exoneration of him from what might come to the mind of a doubter, that he had inclined toward Zulaykha, for which he would be held to account. For if he was patient and deliberate in the matter that was due to him, namely not to remain in prison, though the motives to leave it were abundant, then being patient in what was due to him to be patient in, namely the inclination (of the heart), is more fitting and more worthy. And God knows best.

"His saying 'for which he was accused, etc.' means: he was charged with it. And *tasallu* means: seeking a means (*tawassul*). (Ibn ʿAbbas? — noted as (ʿ))]]

This passage also shows that striving to refute accusations is obligatory, in the way that one must avoid standing in the places of suspicion. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him not stand in places of suspicion." [[This will come in al-Ahzab.]] Among this is what the Messenger of God ﷺ said to those who passed by him while he was in seclusion (*iʿtikaf*) and some of his wives were with him: "She is so-and-so." [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim), from the narration of Ali ibn al-Husayn from Safiyya bint Huyayy, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ was in seclusion, so I came to visit him at night, I talked with him, then I got up to return, and he got up with me to accompany me. Her dwelling was in the house of Usama ibn Zayd. Two men of the Ansar passed by, and when they saw him they hastened. So he said: "Slow down, both of you, she is only Safiyya..." — the hadith.]] This was to avoid suspicion. And it is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ: "I have been amazed at Yusuf, his generosity and his patience, may God forgive him, when he was asked about the lean cows and the fat ones. Had I been in his place, I would not have informed them until I stipulated that they bring me out. And I have been amazed at him when the messenger came to him and he said: 'Return to your lord.' Had I been in his place and had I remained in prison as long as he remained, I would have hastened to answer, and I would have rushed to the door, and I would not have sought an excuse, were he truly forbearing and possessed of deliberation." [[Abd al-Razzaq and al-Tabari reported it through his chain from Ibn ʿUyayna from ʿAmr from ʿIkrima with this wording, without the phrase "truly forbearing and possessed of deliberation." Ishaq transmitted it from the narration of Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Jawzi from ʿAmr ibn Dinar from ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbas with the same meaning, and he added: "Had it not been for the word he said, he would not have remained in prison until he sought relief from other than God, meaning his saying: 'Mention me to your lord' (12:42)." Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported it through the chain of Ishaq. As for the phrase "truly forbearing and possessed of deliberation," al-Tabari reported from the narration of Abu Ishaq from a man not named, from Abu al-Zinad, from al-Aʿraj, from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "May God have mercy on Yusuf. If I had been the one imprisoned and then the summons came to me, I would have come out quickly. He is truly forbearing and possessed of deliberation." Ibn Mardawayh reported it through the chain of Ibn Ishaq from ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Bakr from al-Zuhri, and from al-Aʿraj from Abu Hurayra.]] and he hastened to the door, and he sought the excuse.

He said: "Ask the king about the condition of the women," and he did not say "ask him to investigate their affair," because a question stirs a person and moves him to search into what he is asked about. So he wished to put the question to him so that he would strive in the inquiry into the reality of the story and its details (*fass al-hadith*), until his innocence became clear to him in an openly manifest way, in which truth is distinguished from falsehood. [[His saying "its details" (*fass al-hadith*): in al-Sihah, "fass al-amr" means its detail (*mufassaluhu*). (ʿ)]]

It is read *al-niswati* with a damma on the nun. And from his generosity and good manners is that he did not mention his mistress, despite what she had done to him and the imprisonment and torment she had caused him, and he confined himself to mentioning the women who had cut their hands. *Inna rabbi bi-kaydihinna ʿalim*, meaning: indeed my Lord knows their scheming. He intended that it is a great scheme which none knows but God, because of its depth. Or he invoked God's knowledge as a witness that they had schemed and that he was innocent of what he had been accused of. Or he intended a warning to them, i.e., He knows their scheming, so He will requite them for it.

*Ma khatbukunna*: what is your affair, *idh rawadtunna Yusuf*: when you sought Yusuf to yield, *hal wajadtunna minhu maylan ilaykunna*: did you find from him any inclination toward you? They said: *Hasha li-Llah*, "God forbid!", in wonder at his chastity, and at how he had put aside any trace of suspicion, and at his purity from it. The wife of the chieftain said: *Al-an hasḥas al-haqq*: now the truth has become firm and established. It is also read *ḥuṣḥiṣa* in the passive form, and it is from *ḥuṣḥiṣa al-baʿir* when he cast his knees (*thafanatahu*) down for kneeling. [[His saying "he cast his knees for kneeling": the *thafanat* are the parts of the camel that fall on the ground when it kneels and that are thick, like the two knees and others, as in al-Sihah. (ʿ)]] He said:

*Fa-ḥaṣḥaṣa fi ṣumm al-ṣafa thafanatahu / wa-nāʾa bi-Salmā nawʾatan thumma ṣammamā* [[Humayd ibn Thawr, describing a camel that cast its limbs, on which it kneels when it kneels down, onto hard stones. *Ṣumm* is the plural of *ṣammāʾ* or *aṣamm*, meaning hard. *Nāʾa* means it rose heavily with my beloved Salma in one rising and one movement, without hesitation, then it resolved and determined to continue on its way.]]

It is related that Samura ibn Jundab was brought a man who was impotent, so he bought a slave-girl for him from the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*) and put her in with him for a night. When morning came he said to him: "What did you do?" He said: "I did until I (*hasḥastu*) was roused in her." So he asked her, and she said: "He did nothing." So he said: "Release her path (her way)."

And there is no addition to their testimony to his innocence and purity, and to their confession against themselves that he had not been implicated in anything of what they had accused him of, because they were his adversaries. When the adversary acknowledges that his companion is in the right and he himself is in the wrong, nothing remains for anyone to say. But the Mujbira and the Hashwiyya [[His saying "the Mujbira and the Hashwiyya said: We still have a point to make, and we must strike at the scalp of one whose innocence is established." He means the people of the Sunna. His saying "We still have a point..." means that their position regarding the interpretation of the *hamm* and the *burhan* is represented by this. The *farwa* is the skin of the head. (ʿ)]] said: "We still have a point to make, and we must strike at the scalp of one whose innocence is established."

*Ma khatbukunna*: what is your affair, *idh rawadtunna Yusuf*: when you sought Yusuf to yield, *hal wajadtunna minhu maylan ilaykunna*: did you find from him any inclination toward you? They said: *Hasha li-Llah*, "God forbid!", in wonder at his chastity, and at how he had put aside any trace of suspicion, and at his purity from it. The wife of the chieftain said: *Al-an hasḥas al-haqq*: now the truth has become firm and established. It is also read *ḥuṣḥiṣa* in the passive form, and it is from *ḥuṣḥiṣa al-baʿir* when he cast his knees (*thafanatahu*) down for kneeling. [[His saying "he cast his knees for kneeling": the *thafanat* are the parts of the camel that fall on the ground when it kneels and that are thick, like the two knees and others, as in al-Sihah. (ʿ)]] He said:

*Fa-ḥaṣḥaṣa fi ṣumm al-ṣafa thafanatahu / wa-nāʾa bi-Salmā nawʾatan thumma ṣammamā* [[Humayd ibn Thawr, describing a camel that cast its limbs, on which it kneels when it kneels down, onto hard stones. *Ṣumm* is the plural of *ṣammāʾ* or *aṣamm*, meaning hard. *Nāʾa* means it rose heavily with my beloved Salma in one rising and one movement, without hesitation, then it resolved and determined to continue on its way.]]

It is related that Samura ibn Jundab was brought a man who was impotent, so he bought a slave-girl for him from the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*) and put her in with him for a night. When morning came he said to him: "What did you do?" He said: "I did until I (*hasḥastu*) was roused in her." So he asked her, and she said: "He did nothing." So he said: "Release her path (her way)."

And there is no addition to their testimony to his innocence and purity, and to their confession against themselves that he had not been implicated in anything of what they had accused him of, because they were his adversaries. When the adversary acknowledges that his companion is in the right and he himself is in the wrong, nothing remains for anyone to say. But the Mujbira and the Hashwiyya [[His saying "the Mujbira and the Hashwiyya said: We still have a point to make, and we must strike at the scalp of one whose innocence is established." He means the people of the Sunna. His saying "We still have a point..." means that their position regarding the interpretation of the *hamm* and the *burhan* is represented by this. The *farwa* is the skin of the head. (ʿ)]] said: "We still have a point to make, and we must strike at the scalp of one whose innocence is established."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 52:

﻿[[Resumes the speech. He said: "His saying, 'That, so that he may know that I did not betray him in secret,' etc.: it is from the speech of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the meaning is that this diligence in showing innocence is so that he may know ... etc." Ahmad said: His understanding it as covering all circumstances is more fitting for his purification, and more indicative that the purpose of this statement is his humility and his disavowal of praising himself. So it is more indicative of this meaning than taking it to refer to the particular incident. And Allah knows best.]] That is, that deliberation and exertion in showing innocence is so that al-Aziz may know that "I did not betray him in secret," in respect of his honour. The phrase "bil-ghayb" (in secret) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) [[His saying, "and bil-ghayb is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the agent," is perhaps "the position of a circumstantial clause" or "the accusative of circumstance." (ʿAyn)]] from the agent or the object, in the sense of: "while I was absent from him, hidden from his sight," or "while he was absent from me, hidden from my sight." It is also permissible that it be an adverb of place, meaning "in the place of the unseen," which is concealment and hiding behind the seven locked doors. "And that Allah does not guide the scheme of the treacherous" means He does not make it succeed or set it right. This seems to be an allusion to his wife's betrayal of her husband's trust, and to the betrayal of the one who helped her, after the signs had appeared, in imprisoning him, which was a betrayal of Allah's trust. It is also permissible that this be an affirmation of his own trustworthiness, meaning that had he been treacherous, Allah would not have guided his scheme or set it right.

Then he wished to be humble before God and to diminish himself, lest he should attest to his own purity and be self-satisfied and boastful about his trustworthiness, as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and there is no boasting" [[Muslim transmitted it from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, without the words "and there is no boasting." Abu Nu'aym mentioned it with those words in al-Dala'il, from the narration of Suhayl from his father, from him, within a longer hadith. Ibn Abi 'Asim transmitted it in his al-Adab from the hadith of 'A'isha with those words. Ibn Hibban transmitted it from the hadith of Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, Wathila, and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. al-Tirmidhi transmitted it from the narration of Abu Nadra, from Abu Sa'id, with the wording "I am the master of the children of Adam on the Day of Resurrection, and there is no boasting," the hadith, and he said: hasan (good). Some transmitted it from Abu Nadra as Ibn 'Amir. It is in Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi's al-Dala'il. Both of them, through Abu Nadra, said: Ibn 'Abbas addressed us from the pulpit of Basra and mentioned it. The hadith of Ibn 'Abbas has another route, which al-Daraqutni recorded in al-Afrad through the narration of Kharija ibn Mus'ab, who is weak, from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Ata', from Ibn 'Abbas; and another from Ibn Mardawayh within a hadith of the Night Journey, with a very weak chain. On this topic there is also a report from 'Ubada ibn al-Samit in al-Hakim, whose chain is disconnected (munqati'); and from Anas in al-Bazzar, in which is Mubarak ibn Suhayma, who is abandoned (matruk). In Abu Ya'la's version there is an addition by Ziyad ibn Maymun al-Bakhtari. There is also from Abdullah ibn Salam, recorded by Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani through the narration of Bishr ibn Shaffaf from him; it is defective (ma'lul). The well-preserved version from Bishr ibn Shaffaf is from Abdullah ibn 'Amr. There is also from Jabir, recorded by al-Hakim, in which is al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn 'Aqil, who is abandoned.]] And to make clear that the trustworthiness in him was not his alone, but was by God's grace, kindness, and protection, He said: ﴿And I do not absolve myself﴾, and I do not testify to my complete innocence nor declare myself pure. The statement may be understood in one of two ways: either it refers to this particular incident, because of the concern (hamm) mentioned above, which is the inclination of the soul along the path of human desire and not along the path of deliberate resolve; or it refers to the general state of affairs: ﴿Indeed, the soul is most certainly one that commands evil, except that on which my Lord has mercy﴾. Here "soul" is generic, meaning that this kind commands evil and drives toward it through its desires, ﴿except that on which my Lord has mercy﴾, that is, except for the part which my Lord has shown mercy to through protection, such as the angels. It is also permissible that "what" (ma) here means "time," that is: except at the time of my Lord's mercy, meaning that the soul commands evil at every time and moment, except the time of protection. It is also permissible that this is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: but the mercy of my Lord is what turns away the evil, as in His words ﴿nor will they be saved, except by mercy﴾. It has also been said that the meaning is: "That is so that he may know that I did not betray him, because disobedience is a betrayal." It has also been said that this is the speech of the wife of the Aziz [[Returning to his words. He said: "It has also been said that all of this is the speech of the wife of the Aziz, i.e., that which I said..." etc. Ahmad said: This manner of reading is only adopted when a necessity compels it, as in His words ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, since it is impossible to attribute it to the council in any way, so the pronoun must be turned away from them toward Pharaoh. As for this verse, it follows His words ﴿and he is most certainly among the truthful﴾ and the pronouns before it, all of which definitely refer to Joseph, peace be upon him. There is no necessity to take the pronoun in ﴿li-ya'lam﴾ as referring to the Aziz and to make it the speech of Joseph, especially since the verse introduced by the words of Zulaykha is encompassing it: ﴿The wife of the Aziz said﴾. The context of the verse indicates that this statement was made by her while Joseph, peace be upon him, was still in prison and had not been brought before the king; and when his innocence was made certain by her words, the king sent for him to be released from prison. This is His words ﴿And the king said: Bring him to me, I will take him for myself﴾.]]: that is, "That which I said was so that Joseph would know that I did not betray him and did not lie about him in his absence, and I came with the truth and sincerity regarding what I was asked about. And yet I do not absolve myself of betrayal, for I did betray him when I accused him and said: 'What is the penalty for one who intended harm to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?' and I put him in prison"—she intends by this an apology for what she had done [[His words "when I accused him" mean "when I charged him." (ʿ)]]. ﴿Indeed, the soul is most certainly one that commands evil, except that on which my Lord has mercy﴾: except a soul which God has shown mercy to through protection, like the soul of Joseph. ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: she sought forgiveness from her Lord and asked Him for mercy for what she had committed. If you ask: How is it correct to make this the speech of Joseph when there is no evidence for that?

I answer: The meaning itself is sufficient as a guiding proof [[His words "a guiding proof" mean "leading" or "directing." (ʿ)]] to make it his speech. A similar case is His words: ﴿He said to the chiefs around him: Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer, who wants to drive you out of your land with his sorcery﴾, and then He said: ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, which is the speech of Pharaoh addressing them and consulting them. It is reported from Ibn Jurayj that this is an instance of the Qur'an's rearrangement (taqdim wa ta'khir) and that "That is so that he may know" is connected to His words ﴿So ask him: What is the matter with the women who cut their hands?﴾. The one who speaks falsely has fabricated fabricated narrations [[His words "the one who speaks falsely has fabricated fabricated narrations" mean the People of the Sunna, whom he called the Mujbira (Predestinarians) earlier. (ʿ)]]. [[Returning to his words. He said: "The one who speaks falsely has fabricated narrations..." etc. Ahmad said: He was indeed right in describing as slander (bahť) their transmission of these additions, which is the way of falsifiers in every sect, just as the Qadariyya fabricated concerning the story of Moses, when he asked to see God and fell down unconscious, that the angels began to strike him with their feet and say: "O son of the menstruating women, have you aspired to see the Lord of Majesty?"—all this so that their aim would be achieved, namely that he sought something impossible for the intellect concerning God Most High. But God establishes the truth by His words and nullifies falsehood, and God is the Granter of success.]] They claimed that when Joseph said ﴿that I did not betray him in his absence﴾, Gabriel said to him: "Nor when you intended with her," and the wife of the Aziz said to him: "Nor when you untied the cord of your trousers, O Joseph." This is because of their eagerness to slander God and His messengers [[His words "because of their eagerness to slander God and His messengers" mean accusing them of what they did not do. This is what the Sihah states. (ʿ)]].

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 54:

It is said: istakhlasahu and istakhassahu, when one makes him pure for himself (khalis) and special to himself (khass). ﴿So when he spoke to him and he witnessed from him what he had not expected, he said: "O truthful one, today you are with us established (makin), possessing standing and rank, trusted (amin), entrusted with everything."﴾ It is narrated that the messenger came to him and said: "The king loves you," so he left the prison and prayed for his family: "O God, turn the hearts of the good toward them, and do not conceal from them the news, for they are the most knowledgeable of people about news of events."

And he wrote on the door of the prison: "This is the abode of affliction [[His words "al-balwa" are, in the version of al-Nasafi, al-balwa'. (ʿAynī)]], the graves of the living, the gloating of enemies, and the testing of friends." Then he bathed and cleaned himself of the filth of the prison, and put on new clothes.

When he entered upon the king, he said:

"O God, I ask You by Your goodness for its good, and I seek refuge in Your might and power from its evil."

Then he greeted him and blessed him in Hebrew. He said: "What is this tongue?" He replied: "It is the tongue of my forefathers." The king used to speak seventy tongues, so he spoke to him in them, and he answered him in all of them. He was amazed at him and said: "O truthful one, I wish to hear my dream from you." So he said:

"You saw cows," and he described their color, their conditions, and the place from which they emerged, and he described the ears of grain and what was among them in the form which the king had seen, not omitting a single letter. He said to him: "It is your right to gather the food into the granaries [[His words "to gather the food into the granaries" (al-ahra') are likewise in al-Nasafi's version, but it is not in al-Sihah. Rather, what is there is harrahu al-bard, meaning the cold intensified upon him until it nearly killed him; and hurri al-mal and hurri al-qawm, so they are muhraun. So the root of al-ihra' is places where the cold is intense. (ʿAynī)]], so people will come to you from all directions seeking grain from you, and treasures will gather for you that have not gathered for anyone before you."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 55:

﴿Appoint me over the treasuries of the land; indeed I am a knowledgeable guardian.﴾ Ulanī khazā'in al-ardi wa-lī khazā'in arḍika. Innī ḥafīẓun ʿalīm, amīn: "I will guard what you entrust to me, and I know the ways of managing it." He described himself with trustworthiness and capability, the two qualities that kings seek in those whom they appoint. He said this so that he could reach the enforcement of God the Exalted's rulings, the establishment of truth, the spreading of justice, and the authority by which prophets are sent to people. He knew that no one other than himself could fill that role, so his request for appointment was made seeking the face of God, not out of love for kingship or worldly life.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "May God have mercy on my brother Joseph. Had he not said, 'Appoint me over the treasuries of the land,' he would have been put in charge immediately, but he delayed it, as a practice [[Al-Tha'labi related it from Ibn ʿAbbas through the transmission of Ishaq ibn Bishr from Juwaybir from al-Ḍaḥḥāk from him, and this chain is fallen (sāqiṭ)]]."

If you say: how was it permissible for him to take up a position from the hand of a disbeliever and to be a subordinate under his command and obedience?

I say: Mujahid reported that he had embraced Islam, and it is also related from Qatada. This is evidence that a person may take up a position from the hand of an unjust ruler, and the early generation (al-salaf) used to accept judgeship from rebellious rulers and considered it permissible. And if a prophet or a scholar knows that there is no way to judge by God's command and remove injustice except by empowering a disbelieving or wicked king, then he may seek support through him. It was also said: the king would defer to his opinion and would not object to anything he decided, so he was in the position of one who follows and obeys him.

And thus did We establish Joseph in the land of Egypt: the same kind of manifest establishment. It is reported that it was forty farsakhs by forty. ﴿He could take up residence in it wherever he willed﴾ — it is read with the nun and with the ya'. That is: every place he wished to make his dwelling and his place of settling, he was not prevented from it, since he had gained mastery over all of it and it had come under his dominion and authority. It is reported that the king invested him, sealed him with his ring, and clothed him with his sword. He placed for him a throne of gold, adorned with pearls and rubies. It is reported that he said to him: "As for the throne, I strengthen your kingship with it; as for the ring, you will manage your affairs with it; and as for the crown, it is not from my garments nor the garments of my forefathers." He said: "I have placed it out of reverence for you and in acknowledgment of your merit." So he sat upon the throne, and the kings submitted to him, and the king entrusted his affairs to him and dismissed Qitfir. Then he died after him, and the king married him to his wife Zulaykha. When he went in to her, he said: "Is this not better than what you sought?" He found her a virgin, and she bore him two sons: Ifraithim and Maysha. He upheld justice in Egypt, and men and women loved him. The king and many people accepted Islam at his hands. In the years of drought he sold the food to the people of Egypt: in the first year for dinars and dirhams, until none of them remained with them; then for jewelry and gems; then for livestock; then for lands and property; then for their persons, until he had enslaved them all. They said: "By God, we have never seen a king more majestic or greater than him." He said to the king: "How do you see the way God has dealt with me in what He entrusted to me? What is your opinion?" He said: "The opinion is yours."

He said: "Indeed I call God and call you to witness that I have freed the people of Egypt, every one of them, and returned their possessions to them." He would not sell to any of the grain-buyers more than one camel-load, distributing it fairly among the people. The land of Canaan and the lands of the Levant were struck by a famine similar to that which struck the land of Egypt, so Jacob sent his sons to buy grain, and he detained Benjamin.

﴿By Our mercy﴾ — by Our bounty in this world, of kingship, wealth and other blessings — ﴿to whom We will﴾ — whom the wisdom required that We should will this for; ﴿and We do not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾ — that We would reward them in this world.

﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is better for them.﴾ Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: "The believer is rewarded for his good deeds in this world and in the Hereafter, while the wicked person is hastened to receive good in this world, and ﴿he has no share in the Hereafter.﴾" Then he recited this verse.

Did not recognize him, due to the long time elapsed [[Mahmud said: "They failed to recognize him only because of the long lapse of time and the change in his appearance..." etc. Ahmad said: The fact that the brothers arrived one after another when entering upon him, and that he recognized them at that moment, indicates that the mere act of their entering upon him was immediately followed by recognition, without delay, and God knows best.]] and his having parted from them while still young, and because they believed he had perished, and because he had slipped from their thoughts due to their little consideration of him and their lack of concern for his affair, and because the state he had now attained of kingship and authority was far removed from the state in which they had left him, lying prostrate in the well, sold for a few counted dirhams, so that even if it had occurred to them that he was he, they would have dismissed themselves and their own suppositions. Also, kingship changes one's garb and clothes its bearer with a awe and grandeur that makes familiar features unrecognizable. It was also said: they saw him in the garb of Pharaoh [[Regarding his saying "It was said they saw him in the garb of Pharaoh": if by Pharaoh is meant the Pharaoh of Moses, then he had not yet been born. The phrasing of al-Khazin: "the garb of the kings of Egypt, upon him garments of..." etc. (Ghurar)]], upon him garments of silk, seated on a throne, with a gold collar around his neck and a crown upon his head, so it did not occur to them that he was he. It was also said: they saw him only from afar, with a distance and a screen between them and him, and they stood only where those seeking needs stand. He recognized them because he had parted from them when they were men, and he saw their garb close to their own garb at that time, and because his resolve was fixed upon them and upon recognizing them, so he would scrutinize and perceive. And it is related from al-Hasan: he did not recognize them until they made themselves known to him.

When he had equipped them with their provisions, he said: "Bring me a brother of yours from your father." (Al-Zamakhshari explains: "He prepared them with their supplies," meaning he readied them with their provisions, which are the necessities of travel such as food and what travelers need. "And he loaded their camels with what they had come for," meaning the grain. It is also read bijihāzihim with a kasra on the jim.)

Before the discussion of this matter, there must be a preface that preceded it with them, until the speech drew on to this point.

It is related that when he saw them and they spoke to him in Hebrew, he said to them: "Tell me who you are and what your affair is, for I do not recognize you." They said: "We are a people from the land of Syria, herdsmen. Hardship has befallen us, so we have come to obtain provisions." He said: "Perhaps you have come as spies, to look for the weak points of my land?" They said: "God forbid! We are brothers, sons of one father, who is an aged, truthful man and a prophet among the prophets, named Ya'qub (Jacob)." He said: "How many are you?" They said: "We were twelve, and one of us perished." He said: "How many are you here?"

They said: "Ten." He said: "Where is the eleventh brother?" They said: "He is with his father, who consoles himself with him for the one who was lost." He said: "Then who will bear witness for you that you are not spies, and that what you say is true?" They said: "We are in a land where no one knows us, so no one can testify for us." He said: "Leave one of your number with me as a pledge, and bring me your brother from your father, for he carries a message from your father, so that I may believe you." So they cast lots among themselves, and the lot fell upon Shim'un, who was the best of them in opinion regarding Yusuf, and they left him with him. He had treated them well in hospitality and lodging.

As for "wa-la taqrabun" (and do not come near me), there are two possibilities. The first is that it is included in the conditional judgment and is in the jussive mood, being conjoined to the position of "fa-la kayla lakum" (so there is no measure for you), as if it were said: "If you do not bring him to me, you will be deprived, and you will not draw near." The second is that it carries the sense of a prohibition.

(Al-Zamakhshari explains: "He prepared them with their supplies," meaning he readied them with their provisions, which are the necessities of travel such as food and what travelers need. "And he loaded their camels with what they had come for," meaning the grain. It is also read bijihāzihim with a kasra on the jim.)
