Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 61:

﴿We will seek to coax him away from his father﴾: We will deceive him into parting with him, and we will strive and devise a plan until you take him out of his hand. ﴿And indeed we will do it﴾: And indeed we are capable of that and will not be unable to accomplish it. Or: ﴿and indeed we will do it﴾ without doubt; we will not neglect it and we will not be slack.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 62:

[Joseph said to] "his servants" (li-fityanihi). It is also read li-fityanihi (with a different vowelling in the final syllable). Both are plurals of fata (young man, servant), like ikhwa and ikhwan for akh (brother). The form fi'lah (fityah) is used for the paucity (plural of few), and the form fi'lan (fityan) is used for the abundance (plural of many), meaning: to his servants who were in charge of the measuring (al-kayyalin).

"So that they may recognise it" (la'allahum ya'rifunaha): so that they may recognise the right of its return and the right of the generosity in giving the two portions (al-badlayn).

"When they return to their family" (idha ingalabu ila ahlihim) and have emptied their sacks (wa-farraghu zuruafahum): "so that they may come back" (la'allahum yarji'un): so that their knowledge of that may move them to return to us. Their merchandise (bidha'atuhum) was leather shoes (al-ni'al) and hides (al-adam).

It has been said: he feared that his father would not have among the goods anything with which they could return. It has also been said: he did not consider it generous to take a price from his father and brothers. It has also been said: he knew that their religious devotion would compel them to return the merchandise, since they would not consider it lawful to keep it, so they would come back for its sake.

And it has been said: the meaning of "so that they may come back" (la'allahum yarji'un) is "so that they may return it" (yaruddunaha).

"Measure is withheld from us" — they mean Yusuf's words: "If you do not bring him to me, there will be no measure for you with me." For when they were warned that measure would be withheld, then measure was in fact withheld. "We will measure" — we will remove the obstacle to measuring, and measure out the food we need. "Yaktal" is also read, with the same meaning as "naktal." "Our brother" — so that his measuring is added to our measuring. Or let him be a cause of measuring, since its withholding is due to him.

Will I trust you with him as I trusted you with his brother before? You said of Joseph, "We will surely guard him," and yet you betrayed your pledge. So what assurance do I have against the like of that? Then he said: "God is better at guarding" (فَاللَّهُ خَيْرٌ حافِظاً), meaning: I put my trust in God regarding him and entrust him to them.

"Ḥāfiẓan" (حافِظاً) is a tamyīz (specification, a noun clarifying the comparison), as in your saying: "He is the best of them as a man" (هو خيرهم رجلا), and "God bless his horsemanship" (ولله درّه فارساً). It is also permissible for it to be a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the action).

It is read as "ḥifẓan" (حفظا). Al-A'mash read: "fa-llāhu khayrun ḥāfiẓ" (فالله خير حافظ). Abu Hurayra read: "khayru l-ḥāfiẓīn" (خير الحافظين). "Wa huwa arḥamu r-rāḥimīn" (وَهُوَ أَرْحَمُ الرَّاحِمِينَ): so I hope that He will bless me by guarding him, and will not gather two calamities upon me.

And it was read *ruddat ilayna* with a kasra (رُدَّتْ إِلَيْنا), on the basis that the kasra of the assimilated dal (the *idgham*, assimilation of one consonant into the next) was transferred to the rā', as in *qīla* and *bī'a* (قيل وبيع), and Qutrub (قطرب) related *ḍuriba Zaydun* (ضرب زيد). As for transferring the kasra of the rā' to the ḍād according to those who pronounce it with a sukūn: ﴿مَا نَبْغِي﴾ ("we seek nothing") is a negation, i.e., "we do not exaggerate in speech, and we do not add to what we have described to you of the king's kindness and honour." They had said to him: "We have come to the best of men, who lodged us and honoured us with a hospitality such that, if he had been a man of the family of Yaʿqūb, he would not have honoured us as he did." Or it means: "we do not seek anything beyond what he has done for us of kindness." Or it is an interrogative, meaning: "What do we seek beyond this?"

In the reading of Ibn Masʿūd, *mā tabghī* (ما تبغى), with the tā' addressing Yaʿqūb, the meaning is: "What do you seek beyond this kindness, or beyond the witness of our truthfulness?" It was also said that the meaning is: "We do not want from you any other merchandise."

His saying ﴿هَذِهِ بِضَاعَتُنَا رُدَّتْ إِلَيْنَا﴾ ("This is our merchandise, returned to us") is a resumptive clause (*jumla mustaʾnafa*, a new sentence) explaining his saying ﴿مَا نَبْغِي﴾, and the clauses after it are conjoined to it, with the meaning: "Indeed our merchandise has been returned to us, so we will be strengthened by it, ﴿وَنَمِيرُ أَهْلَنَا﴾ ("and we will provide for our family") upon our return to the king, ﴿وَنَحْفَظُ أَخَانَا﴾ ("and we will guard our brother"), so that nothing of what you fear befalls him, and we will gain, by taking our brother along, ﴿كَيْلَ بَعِيرٍ﴾ ("a camel-load") in addition, or [we will gain] the load of our camels. So what could we seek beyond these benefits by which we improve our circumstances and widen our means?"

They only said ﴿وَنَزْدَادُ كَيْلَ بَعِيرٍ﴾ because, as we mentioned, he would not give a man more than one camel-load for rationing.

If you say: this is when you interpret *al-baghy* as "seeking," but if you interpret it as "lying and exaggeration in speech," then the first clause, ﴿هَذِهِ بِضَاعَتُنَا رُدَّتْ إِلَيْنَا﴾, becomes an explanation of their truthfulness and the absence of exaggeration in their statement; so what do you make of the remaining clauses? I say: I conjoin them to ﴿مَا نَبْغِي﴾, with the meaning: "We do not exaggerate in what we say, and [we say] ﴿وَنَمِيرُ أَهْلَنَا﴾ and we do such-and-such and such-and-such." It is also permissible that it be an independent statement, like your saying: "It is incumbent that we provide for our family," just as you say: "I strove in the need of so-and-so, and exerted myself in achieving his aim. It is necessary that I strive, and it is fitting for me not to fall short."

It is also permissible that the meaning be: "We do not seek, and we speak nothing but the truth regarding what we advise you concerning our equipping with our brother," then they said: "This is our merchandise, by which we are strengthened, and we provide for our family, and we act and manage," as an explanation that they do not seek [anything] in their opinion, and that they are correct in it. This is a good and clear view.

﴿ذَلِكَ كَيْلٌ يَسِيرٌ﴾ ("That is an easy measure"): i.e., that is a small measure which does not suffice us. They mean: what is measured out for them. So they wanted to add to it what would be measured out for their brother. Or it may refer to the load of one camel: i.e., that measure is a small thing which the king grants us and does not trouble us about, or something easy for him, which does not burden him.

It is also permissible that it be from the words of Yaʿqūb, and that the load of one camel is a small thing for which one does not risk the son, like His saying ﴿ذَلِكَ لِيَعْلَمَ﴾ ("That he may know," Q. 12:52).

[[His saying "like His saying 'That he may know'": Is the intended meaning that it is permissible for it to be from the words of Yaʿqūb, because the meaning leads to it, just as it was permissible in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿ذَلِكَ لِيَعْلَمَ﴾, for it to be from the words of Yūsuf, because the meaning leads to it? So reflect. (ʿ)]]

﴿I will never send him with you﴾ — contradicts my state, [Mahmud said: "Its meaning is that sending him with you is contrary to..." etc.] Ahmad said: *lan* is for emphatic negation. As for al-Zamakhshari's claim regarding its contradiction (*munafat*), he has a purpose beyond this, which only one who has thoroughly studied his words will perceive. He relied, in denying the vision of God, on the verse ﴿You will never see Me﴾, holding that its meaning is that vision contradicts my state, and he made this contradiction a requirement of *lan*. He then held to this in every occurrence of this word, all to accustom minds to the idea that this is what *lan* requires. The refutation of this has already been given.

﴿And you have seen what you have seen﴾ [of you] — sending him with you ﴿until you give me a solemn covenant from God﴾, i.e., until you give me what I can rely upon from God. He meant that they should swear to him by God. He made swearing by God a "covenant from Him" only because swearing by Him is what covenants are confirmed and strengthened with. God has permitted this, so it is a permission from Him. ﴿That you will surely bring him back to me﴾ is the answer to the oath, because the meaning is: until you swear that you will surely bring him back to me, ﴿unless you are encompassed﴾ — unless you are overpowered — [Mahmud said: "His saying ﴿you will surely bring him back to me unless you are encompassed﴾ means: unless you are overpowered, so that you are unable to bring him." Ahmad said: This type of exception is specific to negation, because the excepted element is left unstated, and the negation is general, since the negation of bringing him, for example, necessarily entails the negation of all the circumstances attached to it. So, because of its generality, it is as if it were accompanied by mention of the excepted element. This is not the case with "bringing," for it does not imply generality of circumstances, since it depends only on one of them. And God knows best. This story has indeed confirmed the well-known proverb, which is their saying: "Calamity is entrusted to speech." For Ya'qub (peace be upon him) first said concerning Yusuf: ﴿and I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾, and he was afflicted from the direction of that statement. Here he said secondly: ﴿unless you are encompassed﴾, i.e., overpowered by it, and he was afflicted by that too, when they were encompassed and overpowered.]

— so you were unable to bring him. Or: unless you are destroyed.

If you ask: explain to me the reality of this exception, for it is problematic? I say: ﴿encompassed with you﴾ (*an yuhata bikum*) is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), and the affirmative statement, which is ﴿you will surely bring him back to me﴾, is in the sense of a negation. Its meaning: you will not refrain from bringing him except because of being encompassed, i.e., you will not refrain from it for any reason except one single reason: that you be encompassed. So it is an exception from the most general of the general in the object of purpose, and an exception from the most general of the general can only occur in negation alone, so it must be interpreted as negation. Its parallel from affirmation interpreted in the sense of negation is the saying: "I swear by God, that you did it, unless you did it," meaning: I do not ask of you anything except the doing.

﴿Over what we say﴾ — of seeking the covenant and giving it — ﴿is a Guardian﴾, a watchful Overseer.

In the commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verses 67–68:

He only forbade them to enter by one gate because they were people of splendour and fine appearance [[His words, "they were people of splendour and fine appearance, ishtahurahum (made them famous)": in al-Sihah (al-Jawhari's lexicon), al-shara means clothing and bearing. Also, "ishtahara al-amr" means it became clear, and "li-fulan fadila ishtharaha al-nas" means a person has a virtue that people have made known. (Ε)]]. The people of Egypt had made them famous for their nearness to the king and for a special honour that was not granted to others. So they were likely to draw people's gaze from among the delegations, and to be pointed at with fingers. It would be said: "These are the guests of the king. Look at them, how handsome these youths are, and how deserving of honour. The king must have honoured them, brought them near, and preferred them over the other visitors for some reason." He therefore feared that if they entered as one group, they would be struck by the evil eye (yu'anu) because of their beauty and the greatness of their position in people's hearts, and something that would grieve them would befall them. For this reason he did not instruct them to separate in the first trip, because they had been unknown and unnoticed among people.

If you say: Is there any sense in which the evil eye (al-'ayn) can be real? I reply: It is possible that God, exalted is He, causes, at the moment of looking at a thing and admiring it, a deficiency and defect in it in some respect, and that this is a trial from God and a test for His servants, so that those who verify the truth (al-muhaqqiqun) may be distinguished from the literalists (ahl al-hashw) [[His words, "so that those who verify the truth may be distinguished from the literalists": if he means the People of the Sunna (ahl al-Sunna), they say that the influence of the evil eye belongs to the category of linking causes to effects, like linking fire to burning. The cause is effective in appearance, while God is the true agent. Al-Nasafi said: "al-Jubba'i denied the evil eye," and he was one of the shaykhs of the Mu'tazila. (Ε)]]. The verifier says: "This is the act of God," while the literalist says: "It is the effect of the evil eye," as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We made their number only a trial for those who disbelieved﴾ [74:31], and the verse continues.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he used to seek refuge for al-Hasan and al-Husayn, saying: "I seek refuge for you both in the perfect words of God, from every eye that strikes, and from every devil and venomous creature." [[Reported by al-Bukhari and the authors of the Sunan from the narration of al-Minhal ibn 'Amr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is more complete than this.]]

﴿And I cannot avail you anything against God. The command belongs only to God.﴾ That is, if God intends harm for you, my advice to you to separate will not benefit you nor prevent from you what I have advised against, and it will certainly befall you. ﴿The command belongs only to God.﴾ Then He said: ﴿And when they entered from the gate their father had commanded them, it did not avail them against God at all﴾, that is, separately. The opinion of Ya'qub did not benefit them in any way, nor did their entering separately, since what grieved them befell them despite their separation: the attribution of theft to them, their disgrace because of it, the taking of their brother when the bowl was found in his bag, and the doubling of the calamity upon their father. ﴿Except a need in the soul of Ya'qub which he fulfilled﴾. This is a disconnected exception, meaning: but there was a need in the soul of Ya'qub which he fulfilled, and it was his compassion for them, shown through what he said to them and the advice he gave them. ﴿And he was indeed a possessor of knowledge﴾, that is, of His words "I cannot avail you anything," and of his knowledge that precaution does not avail against destiny.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 69:

آوى إِلَيْهِ أَخاهُ ضم إليه بنيامين. وروى أنهم قالوا له: هذا أخونا قد جئناك به، فقال لهم: أحسنتم وأصبتم، وستجدون ذلك عندي، فأنزلهم وأكرمهم، ثم أضافهم وأجلس كل اثنين منهم على مائدة. فبقى بنيامين وحده فبكى وقال: لو كان أخى يوسف حياً لأجلسنى معه، فقال يوسف: بقي أخوكم وحيداً، فأجلسه مع على مائدته وجعل يؤاكله، قال: أنتم عشرة فلينزل كل اثنين منكم بيتاً، وهذا لا ثانى له فيكون معى، فبات يوسف يضمه إليه ويشم.

Translation:

"He took his brother to himself" (آوى إِلَيْهِ أَخاهُ): he drew Benjamin to himself, embracing him. It is narrated that they said to him, "This is our brother, whom we have brought to you." He said to them, "You have done well and you have been right, and you will find that with me." He lodged them and honoured them, then hosted them and seated every two of them at a table. Benjamin was left alone, so he wept and said, "If my brother Joseph were alive, he would have seated me with him." Joseph said, "Your brother has been left alone," so he seated him with himself at his table and began to eat with him. He said, "You are ten. Let every two of you lodge in one room, and this one has no second, so he will be with me." So Joseph spent the night holding him to himself and smelling his scent until morning. He asked him about his children, and he said, "I have ten sons, whose names I derived from the name of a brother of mine who perished." He said to him, "Would you like me to be your brother in place of your perished brother?" He said, "Who would find a brother like you? But Jacob and Rachel did not bear you." Joseph wept, rose to him, embraced him, and said to him, "Indeed, I am your brother Joseph, so do not be distressed (فَلا تَبْتَئِسْ) by what they used to do (بِما كانُوا يَعْمَلُونَ) to us in the past, for God has been good to us and gathered us together in the best way. Do not inform them of what you have been informed." It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "He made himself known to him." It is reported from Wahb: "He only said to him, 'I am your brother in place of your missing brother, so do not be distressed by what you used to suffer from them of envy and harm, for I have secured you from them.'"

It is also reported that he said to him, "I will not leave you." He said, "You know the grief of my father over me; if I detain you, his grief will increase, and there is no way to that except that I attribute to you something that is not becoming." He said, "I do not mind; do what you wish." He said, "I will place my cup in your baggage, then call out after you that you have stolen it, so that I can have you returned to me after I release you with them."

He said, "Do it."

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verses 70–72:**

*al-siqaya* (the drinking-cup): a vessel from which one drinks, and it is the *sawwa'* (the measuring cup). It is said that the king used to drink from it, and then it was made into a measure by which grain was measured. It is also said that the animals were watered with it and grain was measured with it. It is also said that it was a long vessel resembling the *mikwak* (a measure).

It is said that it is the Persian *mikwak*, whose two ends meet, from which non-Arabs drink. It is said that it was silver overlaid with gold, and it is said that it was gold. It is said that it was set with jewels. Then ﴿a crier called out﴾, ﴿then a caller called out﴾. It is said *adhdhanahu* meaning *a'lamahu* (he informed him). *Adhdhana* means to inform much, and from it comes *mu'adhdhin* (the caller), because of how much he does so. It is related:

That they departed, and Yusuf gave them respite until they had set off. Then he ordered that they be pursued, caught and detained, and then this was announced to them.

*al-'ir* (the caravan): the camels that carry loads, so called because they go and come (*ta'ir*, from *'ara*, to go back and forth). It is also said it is a caravan of donkeys, and then the term became widespread until every caravan was called *'ir*. It is as if it were the plural of *'ir*, and its original form is *fa'l*, like *saqf* and *suqf*, and it was treated as *bayd* and *'ayd* were treated (the grammatical note: the text reads *wa'ayd*; perhaps it is *wa-ghayd*, with a ghayn, the plural of *ghaydā'* meaning delicate; or *aghyad*, meaning drowsy with a bent neck, as in the *Sihah*; so the author's wording should be verified). The intended meaning is the people of the caravan, as in the saying: "O horsemen of God, mount!"

Ibn Mas'ud read *wa-ja'ala al-siqaya* (and he placed the cup), by omitting the response to *lamma* (when), as if it were said: "When he had equipped them with their provisions and placed the cup in his brother's baggage, he gave them respite until they had set off, then a caller called out."

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read *tafqidun* (you miss), from *afqadtuhu* when you find him missing (*faqid*).

It has been recited as *sawā'*, *sā'*, and *sawa'*, with the *sad* vowelled with a fatha or a damma, and the *'ayn* pointed or unpointed.

*Wa-ana bihi za'im* (and I am its guarantor): said by the caller. He means: I am a guarantor for the camel's load, which I will deliver to the one who brings it. He intended the load of a camel of grain as a reward for whoever retrieves it.

Tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) of al-Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf, on Surah Yusuf (12), verse 73:

﴿By God!﴾ It is an oath which carries the sense of astonishment at what is attributed to them. They said ﴿You know well﴾ and so they called their knowledge to witness, because of what was established among them from the evidences of their religion and their trustworthiness during their two previous trips and their dealings with the king. Also, they had entered with the mouths of their riding-beasts muzzled [[His words "and the mouths of their riding-beasts muzzled": it is said ka'amtu al-ba'ir (I muzzled the camel) when one tightens its mouth with a ka'am, which is an object placed on a camel's mouth when it becomes agitated; this is in al-Sihah (Lexicon of al-Jawhari). (Gh.)]], so that they would not graze on the crops or take food from anyone in the market.

Also, they returned their merchandise, which they had found in their saddlebags, and said ﴿We were never thieves.﴾ They had never been described as thieves, and theft is incompatible with their condition.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verses 74–75:**

﴿Then what shall be its recompense (fa-ma jaza'uhu)?﴾ The pronoun in *jaza'uhu* refers to the *sawa'* (the king's drinking cup). That is, "what is the recompense for its theft, if you are lying?" in your denial and your claim of innocence concerning it.

They said: ﴿Its recompense is: he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself is its recompense﴾. That is, the recompense for its theft is that the one in whose saddlebag it was found is seized. The ruling on a thief in the family of Ya'qub was that he be enslaved for a year, and for this reason they gave a ruling on its recompense.

Their words ﴿so he himself is its recompense﴾ affirm the ruling. That is: the seizing of the thief himself is his recompense and nothing else, like your saying: "It is Zayd's right to be clothed, fed and shown kindness," so that is his right, meaning: he has this right, to confirm what I have mentioned of his entitlement and its binding force [[The phrase "from his entitlement and its binding force. It is permissible that jaza'uhu be a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence)" — he will mention that the ruling on a thief under the law of the king of Egypt is that he must pay back twice what he took, not that he be bound and enslaved. (Ea.)]].

It is also permissible that *jaza'uhu* be a *mubtada'* (grammatical subject), with the conditional clause as its *khabar* (predicate) as it stands, by placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun. The original would be: "its recompense is: he in whose saddlebag it is found, so he is it," and the recompense was put in the place of "he is it," as when you say to your companion: "Who is Zayd's brother?" and he answers: "His brother is whoever sits beside him, so he is it." The first pronoun refers back to *man* (whoever), and the second to the brother. Then you say "so he is his brother," placing the explicit noun in the position of the pronoun.

It is also possible that *jaza'uhu* is the *khabar* of an omitted *mubtada'*, meaning: "the matter asked about is its recompense," and then they gave their ruling with their words: "whoever is found in his saddlebag, he is its recompense." This is like someone asked about the recompense for the game killed by a pilgrim in the state of ihram, saying "the recompense of the game of the pilgrim," and then saying: ﴿And whoever among you kills it intentionally, the recompense is the like of what he killed from the livestock﴾.

So he began with their bags, before the bag of his brother. It was said: the one appointed over them said, "There must be a search of your bags." So he took them to Joseph, and Joseph began searching their bags, before the bag of Benjamin, to dispel suspicion, until he reached his bag, and he said: "I do not think this one took anything." They said: "By God, you will not leave him until you search his baggage, for that is better for your own heart and for ours." So they brought it out of it. Al-Hasan read "wiʿāʾ akhīhi" (the bag of his brother) with a ḍammah on the wāw, and this is a dialect form. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr read "iʿāʾ akhīhi," changing the wāw into a hamzah.

If you ask: why did He mention the pronoun referring to the drinking-cup several times and then make it feminine? I say: it was said that he referred to it as feminine because of al-Siqāyah (the drinking vessel), or he made ṣuwāʿ (the cup) feminine because it may be masculine or feminine. Perhaps Joseph called it siqāyah and his servants called it ṣuwāʿ, for in what was connected to him in speech there occurred "siqāyah," and in what was connected to them from it there occurred "ṣuwāʿ."

Thus did We plan for Joseph (kadhālika kidnā li-Yūsuf): such a great plan, We devised it for Joseph, meaning We taught it to him and inspired it to him. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law (mā kāna li-yaʾkhudha akhāhu fī dīn al-malik): this is an explanation and clarification of the plan, because under the law of the king of Egypt, the penalty for a thief was to pay back double what he took, not to be held and enslaved. Except that God wills (illā an yashāʾ Allāh): that is, he could not have taken him except by God's will and permission. We raise in degrees whom We will (narfaʿu darajātin man nashāʾ): in knowledge, just as We raised Joseph's degree in it. It is also read "yarfaʿu" with the yāʾ, and "darajātin" with tanwīn. And above every possessor of knowledge is One who knows (wa fawqa kulli dhī ʿilmin ʿalīm): above him is one whose degree is higher than his in knowledge, or above all the scholars is the All-Knowing, whom they fall short of in knowledge, and He is God, Mighty and Exalted.

If you ask: what God permits must be good, so in what respect is this plan good? It is nothing but slander, and accusing one who did not steal, and calling liars those who did not lie, namely His saying "You are surely thieves" and "What is the penalty for it if you are liars?" I say: it is in the form of slander, but it is not slander in reality, because His saying "You are surely thieves" is an allusion to what was done like theft, namely their conduct toward Joseph. It was also said that this statement came from the caller, not from Joseph. And His saying "if you are liars" is a supposition for the negation of their innocence. A supposition of lying is not lying. Moreover, even if he had openly called them liars just as he openly called them thieves, it would have had a basis, because they were lying in their saying: "We left Joseph by our belongings, and the wolf devoured him." This plan follows the rule of the lawful stratagems by which one reaches religious benefits and interests, such as God's saying to Job, peace be upon him: "Take in your hand a bundle and strike with it" (so that he would be freed from his oath and not break it), and Abraham's saying, peace be upon him: "She is my sister," so that he would be safe from the hand of the disbeliever. All the sacred laws are nothing but interests and paths to escaping falling into corruption. God, exalted is He, knew in this stratagem that Joseph was taught great interests, so He made it a ladder and a means to them, and it became good and beautiful, and the aspects of ugliness were removed from it for the reason we have mentioned.

Brother of his: they wanted Yusuf. It is related that when they brought out the drinking bowl (sa') from Benjamin's saddlebag, his brothers lowered their heads in shame and turned to him and said: "What have you done? You have disgraced us and blackened our faces. Sons of Rachel, there is always some calamity from you! When did you steal this bowl?" He replied: "The sons of Rachel, from whom calamity never ceases for you, you took my brother and destroyed him, and this bowl was put in my saddlebag just as the merchandise was put in your saddlebags."

Scholars differed about the theft they attributed to Yusuf. It was said that in his youth he took an idol belonging to his maternal grandfather, broke it, and threw it among the carcasses on the road. It was also said that he entered a church and took a small golden statue that they worshipped, and buried it. It was also said that there was a she-goat or a hen in the house, and he gave it to a beggar. It was further said that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) had a belt which the eldest of his descendants inherited in turn; Ishaq inherited it, then it came to his daughter, who was the eldest of his children. She had raised Yusuf, being his paternal aunt, after his mother's death, and she could not bear to be parted from him. When he grew up, Ya'qub wanted to take him from her, so she resorted to the belt and tied it around Yusuf under his clothes, and said: "The belt of Ishaq has been lost; search for whoever took it." They found it tied on Yusuf, and she said: "He is mine; I will do with him as I please." So Ya'qub left him with her until she died.

﴿فَأَسَرَّها يوسف في نفسه﴾ (So Yusuf concealed it within himself). The pronoun "hā" (it, feminine) refers to the statement, because his words ﴿أَنْتُمْ شَرٌّ مَكاناً﴾ (You are worse in position) form a sentence or a phrase, and they call a group of speech a "word" (kalimah). It is as if it were said: he concealed the sentence or word which is his saying ﴿أَنْتُمْ شَرٌّ مَكاناً﴾. The meaning is: he said in himself: ﴿أَنْتُمْ شَرٌّ مَكاناً﴾. This is because his saying ﴿قالَ أَنْتُمْ شَرٌّ مَكاناً﴾ is a substitute (badal, in grammar, an apposition) for the pronoun of "concealed it" in what is called the explanatory condition (shart al-tafsir), i.e., the pronoun is explained by what follows it.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, it is ﴿فأسرَّه﴾ (he concealed it) in the masculine, meaning the saying or the speech.

The meaning of ﴿شَرٌّ مَكاناً﴾ (worse in position) is: you are worse in rank regarding theft, because you are indeed thieves, for your stealing of your brother from your father. ﴿وَاللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِما تَصِفُونَ﴾ (And Allah knows best what you allege). He knows that no theft was proven against me or against my brother, and the matter is not as you describe it.

They appealed to him by reminding him of the right of their father Ya'qub (Jacob), and that he was an elderly man, aged or of great standing, and that Binyamin (Benjamin) was dearer to him than they were. They had informed him that a son of his had perished, and that he was bereaved over him [[His words "قد هلك وهو عليه ثكلان" mean: he was grieved and sorrowful over the loss of his son. (ʿA.)]], and that he was comforted by his brother. So, ﴿take one of us in his place﴾: take him instead, by way of holding him as a pledge or as a slave. ﴿Indeed, we see you to be among the doers of good﴾ to us, so complete your kindness. Or, it is your custom to do good, so continue in your custom and do not change it.

Ma'adha Allah ("God forbid") is a directive expression, its apparent meaning being: since the ruling of your verdict requires seizing the one in whose saddlebag the bowl was found and enslaving him, then to take anyone else would be an injustice by your own school of thought. So why do you seek [to take someone else], when you yourselves know that it is injustice? Its inner meaning is: God commanded me and revealed to me to seize Benjamin and detain him for a purpose, or for many purposes, which He knows in this matter; so if I were to take someone other than the one whom He commanded me to take, I would be an unjust person, acting contrary to the revelation.

The meaning of ma'adha Allah an nakhudha ("God forbid that we should take") is: we seek refuge in God, a seeking of refuge from taking [anyone other than him]. The verbal noun is therefore annexed to its object, and min is omitted. Idhan ("then") is the answer and the conditional response to their statement, "Take one of us in his place," because the meaning is: if we took his replacement, we would be wrongdoers.

[[His statement "Idhan is the answer and the conditional response" refers to their saying "Take one of us in his place." (ʿ)]]

**istay'asū** (they despaired): *yaʾisū*. The addition of the *sīn* and *tāʾ* here is for intensification (*mubālagha*), as in what has already been said about *istaʿṣama*.

*Al-najī* (confidant, one in private consultation) has two meanings. It may mean *al-munājā* (one who is conferred with), like *al-ʿashīr* and *al-samīr* meaning *al-muʿāshir* (companion) and *al-msāmir* (one who converses in the evening). From this is the verse ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾. It may also mean the verbal noun *al-tanājī* (secret conferring), just as *al-najwā* is said to have the same meaning. From this comes the expression "a people *najī*," as in the verse ﴿when they were in secret consultation﴾, treating the verbal noun as a descriptive. It is also permissible to say "they are *najī*," just as one says "they are *ṣadīq*" (friend), because it follows the pattern of verbal nouns, and its plural is *anjiyah*. The poet said:

*Indeed, when the people become confidants (of one another),*
*and the people are stirred like the well-ropes,*
*and they are bound one upon another with the ropes of drawing water;*
*there, advise me, and do not advise another with it.*

These are from the verses of *al-Ḥamāsa*. The *mā* is superfluous (*zāʾida*). *Al-anjiyah* is the plural of *najī* in the sense of *munājā*, like *al-samīr*, *al-jalīs* and *al-ʿashīr*, in the sense of *mufāʿil*.

Alternatively, *al-najī* is a verbal noun like *al-dawī*, *al-azīz*, *al-nashīj*, *al-naʾīj* and *al-ṣahīl*, all of which are kinds of sound. It then follows the pattern of "Zayd is *ʿadl*" (Zayd is a just person). If you say that it is the plural of *najāʾ*, the verbal noun of *nājāhu* (he conferred with him), like *qitāl* is the verbal noun of *qātalahu* (he fought him), that would also be permissible, and it would be like *al-arshiyah*, the plural of *rishāʾ*, which is the rope for drawing water, and *al-arwiyah*, the plural of *riwāʾ*, which is also the rope for drawing water and for quenching thirst. That is: they were groups conferring secretly and consulting about what had befallen them, and they were agitated, standing, sitting, going and coming, like the agitation of the well-ropes over the water. It is related: "and their necks were agitated like the well-ropes." *Shudda* is passive: some of them were bound to others, tied and bundled with the ropes for drawing water, as a metaphor for their readiness for war. It is unlikely that it is a metaphor for readiness to draw water in a time of drought there, that is, in that time or place.

It is said: "Or in both (of these) I shall be brave and patient; so advise me, not another, and do not advise another with it." The apparent sense of the verse permits the predicate of *inna* to be an imperative clause, but this is not the case; rather it is by interpretation, as you see. The address is to a feminine person, but it may also be to a masculine one. The retention of the *yāʾ* in the two verbs is for lengthening (*ishbāʿ*), and the *hāʾ* in *bīh* is for pausal ending (*sakt*). This is a metaphor for his bravery and endurance, or a metaphor for his generosity from afar.

The meaning of **khalaṣū** (they withdrew) is that they withdrew and separated themselves from the others, sincerely, with no one else mixing with them. **Najiyyan** means possessors of secret conference, or a group in secret conference, that is, conferring with one another. Better than this is that they were purely in secret conference, because they had gathered for it and were immersed in it with diligence and concern, as if they themselves embodied conferring and its reality. Their conference was about arranging their affair: in what manner should they go, and what should they say to their father about their brother?—like a people who were baffled by the calamity that had struck them, and so needed consultation.

**Kabīruhum** (their eldest) in age, who was Rubeel. It is also said: their leader, who was Shamʿūn. It is also said: their eldest in intellect and judgment, who was Yahūdhā.

**Mā farraṭtum fī Yūsuf** (you neglected Joseph) has several possibilities. The *mā* may be a connecting particle (*ṣila*), meaning: "and before this you were negligent concerning Joseph, and did not keep your father's covenant."

It may be a verbal-nominal particle (*maṣdariyya*), with the verbal noun in the nominative position as subject, and its predicate being the adverbial phrase **min qablu** (before), meaning: "and there occurred before this your neglect of Joseph." Or it may be in the accusative, coordinated with the object of **alam taʿlamū** (did you not know), which is **anna abākum** (that your father), as if it were said: "Did you not know that your father took a covenant from you, and that you had been negligent concerning Joseph before?"

It may also be a relative pronoun (*mawṣūla*), meaning: "and before this, what you had done with regard to Joseph of the great crime," its position being nominative or accusative according to the two possibilities.

**Fa-lan abraḥa al-arḍa** (so I will not leave the land), that is, I will not depart from the land of Egypt, **ḥattā yaʾdhana lī abī** (until my father permits me to return to him), **aw yaḥkuma Allāhu lī** (or God judges for me) to leave it, or to obtain justice against the one who took my brother, or to free him from his hand by some means. **Wa-huwa khayru al-ḥākimīn** (and He is the best of judges), because He never judges except with justice and truth.

Also read sariqa (he was accused of theft), meaning: he was attributed to theft. "And we did not testify to him as a thief except by what we knew of his theft" [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "Its meaning is: 'And we did not testify against him as a thief except by what we knew of him, of his theft...' etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munir) said: Either the legal practice of their law at that time was that the mere presence of an item in the possession of the accused, after his denial, entailed for him the rulings of a thief, in which case "knowledge" is to be taken in its literal sense. Or it is not so, in which case this mere fact of its being found in his baggage does not entail knowledge that he is a thief. At most it yields a clear presumption, so the intended meaning of "knowledge" here is "presumption." A similar usage has occurred, and their saying "And we were not guardians of the unseen" serves as an indication that their basis for what they said was a presumption according to the apparent state of affairs. As for uncovering the inner reality, which would produce certain knowledge, they do not claim that.]] and we were certain of it, for the cup was extracted from his bag, and nothing is clearer than this. "And we were not guardians of the unseen" meaning: we did not know that he would steal when we gave you the covenant [[The text resumes from al-Zamakhshari: "Their saying 'And we were not guardians of the unseen' means: we did not know that he would steal when we gave you the covenant..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munir) said: The two readings are only harmonious under the interpretation you mentioned, namely that they attributed the theft to him only as a presumption according to the apparent state of affairs, and they guarded against the belief that they knew it for certain, so they said: "And we were not guardians of the unseen." Thus, under the stated interpretation, the two readings imply their exoneration from the claim of definite knowledge against him. As for the other interpretations mentioned, the two readings do not fit together, since the first implies a definite judgment of theft as knowledge, while the second implies disavowal of certainty. And God knows best.]]. Or: we did not know that you would be afflicted with him as you were afflicted with Joseph. As for the one who reads sariqa, its meaning is: "And we did not testify except to the extent of what we knew of the concealment (of the cup), and we were not guardians of the unseen matter: whether he stole in truth, or whether he placed the cup in his baggage without his knowing."

The town in which we were is Egypt, meaning: send to its people and ask them about the real facts of the story. ﴿And the caravan in which we came﴾, and the members of the caravan, who were a people from Canaan, neighbours of Ya'qub (Jacob). It was also said that they were from the people of Sanaa. The meaning is: they returned to their father and told him what their brother had told them. ﴿He said: "Nay, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you"﴾, a matter you had wished for.

[[Mahmud said: "Indeed, this is a thing you had wished for… etc." Ahmad said: This is an anticipatory answer by al-Zamakhshari to a question, as if someone were to say: In the first incident their souls had made a matter seem fair to them, beyond any doubt. But in this second incident they did not intend any wrong against Binyamin, nor did they inform their father except of the reality in its clear form, and they did not leave him in Egypt except as men overpowered in bringing him back. So what is the reason for His saying to them a second time, "Nay, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you," as He said to them the first time? If the question is posed in this way, then the answer requires further elaboration. We say: At that time they were under suspicion in the eyes of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and they were fit to be accused of it, because of what they had previously done concerning Yusuf, peace be upon him. And there was with him a circumstantial indication that strengthened and confirmed the suspicion, namely the king's taking him for theft. That was only in accordance with the religion of Ya'qub alone, not the religion of other people, nor their custom. To this the Exalted One alluded in His saying, ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾, as a warning from God Most High regarding the way in which Ya'qub suspected them. It is known that the king did that only on their legal opinion (fatwa) to him, and he thought that they had given him that verdict after the theft was discovered, deliberately, so that their brother would be detained. In reality they had been asked for a ruling before the accusation of theft was made against them, so they stated what they had, and they did not realise that the aim was to hold them to what they had said and to accuse one whose position makes accusation possible, which is not objectionable, especially regarding a father and a son. And it is possible, and God knows best, that the basis that justified this statement concerning them is that they made the mere presence of the goblet in the baggage of whoever is found with it a theft, without making the ruling depend on the establishment of his being a thief in a known manner. In our sacred law (shar') this does not establish theft against the one accused. If their law was like ours in this, then their verdict was not precise. This is an indication that they were eager to establish the theft against him. This is confirmed by their saying, ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾, by which they affirm that the theft is established against him. God knows best. His saying to them, "Nay, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you," fits their situation, even if their law required that differently from our law. The main reliance is on the first answer, and God is the one sought for help.]]

Otherwise, I do not know whether that man would take the thief for his theft, were it not for your verdict and your instruction. ﴿Perhaps God will bring them all to me﴾, meaning Yusuf, his brother, and Ruwbil or someone else. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Knowing﴾ of my condition in grief and sorrow, ﴿the All-Wise﴾, who did not afflict me with this except for a wisdom and a benefit.

The town in which we were is Egypt, meaning: send to its people and ask them about the real facts of the story. ﴿And the caravan in which we came﴾, and the members of the caravan, who were a people from Canaan, neighbours of Ya'qub (Jacob). It was also said that they were from the people of Sanaa. The meaning is: they returned to their father and told him what their brother had told them. ﴿He said: "Nay, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you"﴾, a matter you had wished for.

[[Mahmud said: "Indeed, this is a thing you had wished for… etc." Ahmad said: This is an anticipatory answer by al-Zamakhshari to a question, as if someone were to say: In the first incident their souls had made a matter seem fair to them, beyond any doubt. But in this second incident they did not intend any wrong against Binyamin, nor did they inform their father except of the reality in its clear form, and they did not leave him in Egypt except as men overpowered in bringing him back. So what is the reason for His saying to them a second time, "Nay, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you," as He said to them the first time? If the question is posed in this way, then the answer requires further elaboration. We say: At that time they were under suspicion in the eyes of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and they were fit to be accused of it, because of what they had previously done concerning Yusuf, peace be upon him. And there was with him a circumstantial indication that strengthened and confirmed the suspicion, namely the king's taking him for theft. That was only in accordance with the religion of Ya'qub alone, not the religion of other people, nor their custom. To this the Exalted One alluded in His saying, ﴿He could not have taken his brother under the king's law﴾, as a warning from God Most High regarding the way in which Ya'qub suspected them. It is known that the king did that only on their legal opinion (fatwa) to him, and he thought that they had given him that verdict after the theft was discovered, deliberately, so that their brother would be detained. In reality they had been asked for a ruling before the accusation of theft was made against them, so they stated what they had, and they did not realise that the aim was to hold them to what they had said and to accuse one whose position makes accusation possible, which is not objectionable, especially regarding a father and a son. And it is possible, and God knows best, that the basis that justified this statement concerning them is that they made the mere presence of the goblet in the baggage of whoever is found with it a theft, without making the ruling depend on the establishment of his being a thief in a known manner. In our sacred law (shar') this does not establish theft against the one accused. If their law was like ours in this, then their verdict was not precise. This is an indication that they were eager to establish the theft against him. This is confirmed by their saying, ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾, by which they affirm that the theft is established against him. God knows best. His saying to them, "Nay, your souls have made a matter seem fair to you," fits their situation, even if their law required that differently from our law. The main reliance is on the first answer, and God is the one sought for help.]]

Otherwise, I do not know whether that man would take the thief for his theft, were it not for your verdict and your instruction. ﴿Perhaps God will bring them all to me﴾, meaning Yusuf, his brother, and Ruwbil or someone else. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Knowing﴾ of my condition in grief and sorrow, ﴿the All-Wise﴾, who did not afflict me with this except for a wisdom and a benefit.

And he turned away from them and withdrew from them, out of aversion for what they had brought. "Alas for Joseph!" (Yā asafā): he attributed the grief (asaf), which is the most intense sorrow and regret, to himself, and the alif is a substitute for the ya' of the first-person possessive. The paronomasia (tajanus) between the words asaf (grief) and Yusuf (Joseph) is of the kind that occurs naturally and unforced, so it is graceful and striking. Similar to it is: ﴿What, are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ (ithaqaltum ila al-ard, aradiytum), and ﴿they forbid it and keep away from it﴾ (wa-hum yanhawna 'anhu wa-yana'awna 'anhu), and ﴿they think they are doing good﴾ (yahsabuna annahum yuhsinuna), and "from Saba' with a true report" (min saba' bi-naba').

And it is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No nation has been given — 'Indeed we belong to God and to Him we return' — at the time of calamity, except the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ)." [[Al-Tha'labi related it from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Sa'id al-Hadi, from Ishaq ibn al-Rabi' ibn Sufyan ibn Ziyad al-Mu'sfari, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, with this wording traced to the Prophet. al-Tabarani related it in al-Du'a' by another route from Sufyan ibn Ziyad. 'Abd al-Razzaq related it through al-Tabari, from al-Thawri, from Sufyan, from Ziyad al-Mu'sfari, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. I say: al-Bayhaqi likewise related it in al-Shu'ab from the narration of Abu 'Amir from al-Thawri. He said: "Some weak narrators raised it (to the Prophet), and it is nothing."]] Consider Ya'qub: when what befell him befell him, he did not say "We belong to God." Rather he said, "Alas for Joseph!"

If you ask: How could he grieve over Joseph rather than over his brother, and over the third, when the most recent calamity is heavier on the soul and more evident in its effect? I answer: this shows the persistence of his grief over Joseph, that nothing lost had filled his place in his heart, and that the calamity concerning him, though its time had long passed, remained fresh and raw for him.

"And the most grievous of misfortunes did not make me forget him after him" (wa-lam tunsini awfa al-musibat ba'dahu). [[Hisham ibn 'Uqba al-'Udhri said, lamenting his brother Dhu al-Rummah, whose name was Ghaylan ibn 'Uqba, and also lamenting Awfa ibn Dalham. It is said he lamented his two brothers.

"Ta'azzaytu 'an Awfa bi-Ghaylan ba'dahu / 'Azaa'an wa-jafna al-'ayni mala'un matra'u" / "Fa-lam tunsini awfa al-musibat ba'dahu / wa-lakin nakka' al-qarha bi-l-qarhi awja'u."

He says: I consoled myself, that is, I was distracted, concerning Awfa by the death of Ghaylan after him; that is, what befell me was of a kind that would cause the earlier grief to be forgotten, yet I did not forget it, while the eyelid of my eye was full of tears. Or the meaning: I forced myself to be consoled but was unable. It is said atra'a al-hawd when it is filled with water; al-mutra' is an emphasis. It is permissible to liken the eyelid to a pool by way of metaphor (makniyya), and itra' is an imaginative representation (takhyil). So: the afflictions that struck me after him, the death of my brother Ghaylan, did not make me forget, but they increased my grief upon my grief. Al-qarh is the wound once it has healed and its scab has dried; al-nakka' is scraping off that scab. It is also related as wa-lakin nakka' with the nun doubled. The verb nakka' is the one from which the measure of the "striking" derives. So the state of his first calamity, to which another was added that increased it, is likened to the state of that wound, by way of allegorical representation (tamthiliyya): that is, "but the scraping of the wound hurt more than the first state." The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun to display the pain and anguish. Or the meaning: but the scraping of the first wound by the wound of another hurt the person more than before. The phrase bi-l-qarh is connected to awja'u or to nakka'.]]

Because the calamity concerning Joseph was the foundation of the afflictions that followed for his son, his grief over him was grief over whoever was joined to him. "And his eyes turned white" (wa-abyadhdhat 'aynahu): when weeping is abundant, the tears erase the blackness of the eye and turn it into a dull whiteness. It is said that his sight had become blind. It is also said that he could perceive only weakly. It is read as "from grief" (min al-huzn).

"From grief": grief was the cause of the weeping which produced the whiteness, so it is as if it arose from grief. It is said that Ya'qub's eyes did not dry from the time of Joseph's separation until the time of their reunion, eighty years, and that on the face of the earth there was none more honored by God than Ya'qub. It is related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he asked Jibril (peace be upon him): "What was the extent of Ya'qub's longing for Joseph?" [[I have not found it traced to the Prophet. al-Tabari related it from the narration of 'Isa ibn Yazid from al-Hasan al-Basri that it was said to him: "What was the extent..." and then mentioned it.]] He said: "The longing of seventy bereaved mothers." He asked: "What reward did he have?" He said: "The reward of a hundred martyrs, and he never thought ill of God even for a moment."

If you ask: How was it permissible for a prophet of God to be carried by grief to that degree?

I answer: a human being is created such that he cannot master himself at the time of hardships from grief, and for this reason his patience was praised, and that he should restrain himself so that he does not go out to what is unseemly. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) wept over his son Ibrahim and said: "The heart grieves, the eye weeps, and we do not say what displeases the Lord. Indeed, we are saddened by you, O Ibrahim." [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Anas.]] What is blameworthy is only the grief of the ignorant: shrieking and wailing, striking the chest and face, and tearing garments. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he wept over the son of one of his daughters while he was in his last breaths, and it was said: "O Messenger of God, you weep though you have forbidden us from weeping?" He said: "I did not forbid you from weeping; I forbade you from two foolish sounds: a sound at joy and a sound at sorrow." [[The compiler said: al-Tibi attributed it to the two Sahihs, but was not correct. This does not occur concerning the son of one of his daughters; it occurs concerning his son Ibrahim, as related by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ishaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and others, from the hadith of Jabir. al-Hakim related it from the hadith of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf in similar wording. What is related concerning one of his daughters is agreed upon from the hadith of Usama, and in it: "His eyes overflowed, and Sa'd said to him: 'What is this, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'This is mercy which God placed in the hearts of His servants.'" I say: the former is in the wording: "'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf said: 'Do you weep, though you had forbidden weeping?' He said: 'No, but I forbade two foolish sounds: a sound at a calamity, scratching of faces, the wailing of Satan, and tearing of collars; and a sound of the tune of play, amusement, and the flutes of Satan.'"]] It is related from al-Hasan that he wept over a son or someone else, and when he was asked about it, he said: "I have not seen that God made grief a disgrace for Ya'qub."

﴿So he was filled with grief﴾ (fa-huwa kazim): he was full of suppressed anger [[His words "full of anger" mean the concealed rage. Explained in al-Sihah. His words "and he did not show what grieved them" mean concerning what they had done to Joseph and his brother. (ʿ)]] toward his sons, and did not show what distressed them. Here fa'il has the sense of maf'ul, as evidenced by ﴿and he was suppressing it (wa-huwa makzum)﴾, from kazama al-siqa' when one tightens a water-skin when it is full. The word kazm, with the zay vowelled with fatha, means the outlet of the breath. It is said: "He seized him by his throat (bi-akzamihi)."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 85:

﴿تَفْتَؤُا﴾ — he intended: لا تفتؤ (lā taftu, "you will not cease"), so the negative particle was dropped, because it is not confused with the affirmative, for if it were affirmative, the lam and the nun (of emphasis) would have been necessary. Similar to it is:

فَقُلْتُ يَمِينَ اللَّهِ أَبْرَحُ قَاعِداً ... وَلَوْ قَطَعُوا رَأْسِي لَدَيْكَ وَأَوْصَالِي

[[سَمَوْتُ إِلَيْهَا بَعْدَ مَا نَامَ أَهْلُهَا ... سُمُوَّ حَبَابِ الْمَاءِ حَالاً عَلَى حَالِ

fa-qultu yamīna Allāhi abraḥu qāʿidan ... wa-law qaṭaʿū raʾsī ladayka wa-awṣālī

By Imru' al-Qays. He says: I ascended toward my beloved Salma after her people had slept, and no one heard my voice, and she did not perceive me until I was with her, like the rising of water bubbles upon it with ease. Ḥubāb al-māʾ, with a ḍammah, is the name of a water serpent; ḥubāb al-māʾ, with a fatḥah, is its froth which rises above it. His saying "ḥālan ʿalā ḥāl" stands in the position of an emphasizing circumstantial clause for the simile, i.e., a state fitting upon another state and equal to it, like your saying "sawāʾan bi-sawāʾ." Here there is an ellipsis: i.e., "you frightened me with the people, so I said: by God's oath I will not cease sitting," i.e., lā abraḥu qāʿidan.

The deletion of the negative lā before the present-tense verb after an oath is common, owing to the absence of confusion, and because, were it not for its implied presence, the verb would have had to be joined with the lam of the answer of the oath or with the nun of emphasis, or with both. Yamīn is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, i.e., uqsimu yamīna Allāh, so it is like the verbal noun standing in for its verb.

The rest of the story has already passed.]] The meaning of ﴿تَفْتَؤُا﴾ is "you will not cease." It is reported from Mujāhid: "you will not slacken in your love," as if he made fatʾ and futūr (slackening) two brothers.

It is said: mā fati'a yafʿalu ("he did not cease doing"). Aws said:

فَمَا فَتِئَتْ خَيْلٌ تَثُوبُ وَتَدَّعِي ... وَيَلْحَقُ مِنْهَا لَاحِقٌ وَتُقَطَّعُ

[[By Aws ibn Ḥajar; he used "horses" as a metonymy for their riders. It is said: thāba and thawwaba, when one waves the edge of his garment at a call from afar. Tadaʿā is a form of tafaʿʿala from du'ā', i.e., some of them call to one another. It may be that tathūbu means "returns," i.e., goes and returns.

The meaning of "tadaʿī" is: they follow one another and are attributed to one another, metaphorically; it is permissible that the horses are meant literally, or the horses are likened to people by way of metaphor in the mode of implicit comparison, and the "ideda'" (calling) in the sense of calling out is imaginative; these two aspects are more fitting to his saying "wa-yalḥaqu," i.e., one of them that is ahead overtakes. And tuqaṭṭaʿ: i.e., they are cut off, and some of them are cut off from others, piece by piece; thus they gather and disperse. The images of war from its beginning to its end are in this verse, i.e., the horses have not ceased doing thus until the war ended.]]

﴿حَرَضاً﴾: "consumed, brought close to death by illness." One says aḥraḍahu al-marḍ (the illness wore him down), and it is used the same for the singular and plural, masculine and feminine, because it is a verbal noun. The adjective is ḥaraḍ, with a kasrah on the rāʾ. Similar to it are danaf and danif, and both readings have come down. al-Ḥasan read ḥaraḍan with two ḍammahs; similarly among adjectives: rajulun junub and gharib.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 86:

Al-Bathth (البث): the most difficult grief, which its bearer cannot bear patiently, so he spreads it (yabuthhu) among the people, i.e., he makes it public. From the same root: "baththa amrahu" and "abthathahu iyyahu" (he disclosed it to him). The meaning of "innama ashku" (﴿إِنَّمَا أَشْكُو﴾):

"I do not complain to anyone among you or others. I only complain to my Lord, calling upon Him and seeking refuge in Him, so leave me and my complaint." This is the meaning of "tawallaa 'anhum" (﴿وَتَوَلَّىٰ عَنْهُمْ﴾), i.e., he turned away from them to God and complained to Him.

It is said: a neighbour of his came to Ya'qub and said: "O Ya'qub, I have become broken and worn out, and have reached the age your father reached!" He said: "What has broken me and worn me out is the grief with which God has tested me concerning Yusuf." Then God revealed to him: "O Ya'qub, do you complain to Me about My creation?" He said: "O Lord, a sin I committed; forgive me." So He forgave him, and after that, whenever he was asked, he would say: "I only complain of my distress and sorrow to God."

It is also narrated that God revealed to Ya'qub: "I was displeased with you because you slaughtered a sheep and a poor man stood at your door and you did not feed him. The dearest of My creation to Me are the prophets, then the poor. So prepare food and invite the poor to it."

It is said: he bought a slave-girl together with her son; he sold her son, and she wept until she went blind.

"A'lamu min Allahi ma la ta'lamun" (﴿أَعْلَمُ مِنَ اللَّهِ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾): i.e., I know from God His action, His mercy, and that I think well of Him, that He will bring me relief from where I do not expect.

It is narrated that he saw the Angel of Death in his dream and asked him: "Have you taken the soul of Yusuf?" He said: "No, by God, he is alive, so seek him."

Al-Hasan recited "wa huzni" with two fathas (وَحَزَنِي). "Wa huzni" with two dammas (وَحُزْنِي) is the reading of Qatada.

So seek out news of Yusuf and his brother, get to know from them, and look for their news. It was also recited with a jim (*tajassasu*), as it was recited with both readings in *al-Hujurat*. Both forms are *tafa'ul* from *al-ihsas*, which means knowledge, and from *al-jass*, which means seeking. From the same root comes their word for the faculties of human perception: *al-hawass* (the senses) and *al-jawwas* (the scouts). ﻿Then when Isa perceived disbelief from them, and from *al-jass*, which means seeking. ﻿From the mercy of God means from His relief and ease. Al-Hasan and Qatada recited *min rawh Allah* with a damma on the *ra'*, meaning from His mercy by which His servants live.

Commentary of al-Zamakhsharī (*al-Kashshāf*) on Sūrah Yūsuf (12), verse 88:

﴿The harm (al-ḍurr)﴾ means emaciation from hardship and hunger. ﴿Poor goods (muzjāt)﴾ means goods that are pushed away: every merchant pushes them off out of disinterest in them and contempt for them. It comes from *azjaytuhu*, "I pushed him and drove him away," as in "the wind drives (tuzjī) the clouds." It is said that the goods were wool and clarified butter from the Bedouins' possessions. It is also said they were pine nuts and *ḥabbat al-khaḍrā'* (a green seed). It is also said they were barley-meal and dried curds.

It is also said they were debased dirhams that are accepted only at a discount. ﴿So give us full measure﴾ means give us our full right of measure, ﴿and be charitable to us﴾ means show us favour by overlooking the inferiority of the goods, or add to our share. They called the surplus and extra, which is not obligatory, "charity" (ṣadaqah), because charity is forbidden to the prophets. It is also said that it was permitted for someone other than our Prophet. Ibn ʿUyayna was asked about this and said: "Have you not heard ﴿and be charitable to us﴾?" He meant that it was lawful for them.

The apparent meaning is that they humbled themselves before him and asked him to give them charity. For this reason he was moved with pity for them, and compassion overcame him, so he could not restrain himself from making himself known to them. His words ﴿Indeed, God rewards those who give charity﴾ are evidence for this, since they mention God and His reward. Charity (ṣadaqah) is the gift by which one seeks reward from God. From this is the saying of al-Ḥasan, to a man he heard say: "O God, be charitable to me": "God Most High does not give charity; only one who seeks reward gives charity. Say: 'O God, give me,' or 'show me favour,' or 'have mercy on me.'"

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 89:

He said, "Do you know [the thing] came to them from the direction of religion, and he was forbearing and successful,»"

So he addressed them in the form of a question, about the aspect of ugliness that the one who repents must take into account, and said: ﴿Do you know the ugliness of what you did to Joseph and his brother, when you were ignorant?﴾ That is, ﴿you were ignorant﴾ of its ugliness, so you undertook it. He means: "Did you know its ugliness, so that you would repent to God for it?" For knowledge of ugliness calls for finding it ugly, and finding it ugly leads to repentance. So his speech was out of compassion for them and sincere advice to them in religion, not reproach and rebuke, preferring the right of God over his own right, in the situation in which the distressed person breathes out, the one with a wound in his chest [[his note: "the one with a wound in his chest" (al-masdur) is the one whose chest is afflicted. "Al-mahnaq" is the enraged one. "Al-mawtur" is the one whose slain relative has not been avenged, as in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari).]] pours out his grief, and the enraged one seeks relief, and the one who has been wronged obtains his vengeance. How gentle and easy are the morals of the prophets, and how mild! And how steady and sound are the minds of those people. [[his note: "How gentle and easy": that is, how easy and how kind. Al-Sihah has: so-and-so has a "ḥaṣāh", meaning intellect and understanding, so "ḥaṣā ʿuqūlihim" is an explanatory genitive.]]

It has also been said that the verse does not intend to deny them knowledge, for they were learned men, but because they did not do what knowledge requires, and nothing like that is undertaken except by an ignorant person [[his note: "and nothing like that is undertaken except by an ignorant person": perhaps this is a coordination on the meaning, since his words "they did not do ..." mean they did what knowledge does not require.]], he called them ignorant.

It has also been said that the meaning is: "when you were children in the bounds of foolishness and recklessness, before you reached the time of forbearance and steadiness." It is narrated that when they said, "Adversity has touched us and our family," and pleaded with him, his eyes shed tears, and then he said this statement.

It has also been said: they delivered to him the letter of Jacob: "From Jacob, Israel of God, son of Isaac, the sacrificed of God, son of Abraham, the friend of God, to the Governor of Egypt. To proceed: we are a household upon whom trials have been decreed. As for my grandfather, his hands and feet were bound and he was thrown into the fire to be burned, but God saved him and made the fire cool and safe for him. As for my father, a knife was placed on his nape to be slaughtered, but God ransomed him. As for me, I had a son, and he was the dearest of my children to me. His brothers took him to the wilderness, then they came back to me with his shirt smeared with blood and said, 'The wolf has eaten him,' so my eyes were lost from weeping for him. Then I had another son, who was his full brother, and I was consoled by him. They took him away, then returned and said, 'He has stolen, and you have imprisoned him for that. We are a household that does not steal, nor do we give birth to a thief. If you return him to me, well and good; otherwise I will invoke upon you a supplication that will reach the seventh of your offspring. Peace.'" When Joseph read the letter, he could not contain himself, and his patience gave way, and he said that to them. It is also narrated that when he read the letter he wept, and he wrote the reply: "Be patient as they were patient, and you will prevail as they prevailed."

If you ask: what did they do to his brother?

I say: they caused him grief and bereavement [[his note: "Al-thakl" is a woman's losing her child, as in al-Sihah. Here it means sorrow.]] by separating him from his brother of the same father and mother, and they treated him harshly, so that he could not speak to any of them except as a humble person speaks to a powerful one, and they harmed him in various kinds of harm.

"Read as an interrogative, أَإِنَّكَ (ʾa-innaka, "Are you indeed..."). And read as an affirmation, وأنك (wa-annaka, "and that you..."). In the reading of Ubayy: أإنك أو أنت يوسف, with the meaning "Are you indeed Yusuf, or are you Yusuf?" The first (إنك) is omitted because the second (أنت) indicates it. This is the speech of one who is amazed and astonished at what he hears, so he repeats the request for confirmation. If you ask: how did they recognize him? I say: they saw in his appearance (رواء, rawāʾ, "appearance, outward bearing") and his characteristics, when he spoke to them in this way, something that made them feel that he was he, while knowing that what he addressed them with could only come from a ḥanīf Muslim of the lineage of Ibrahim, and not from some noble of Egypt. It has also been said: he smiled at that moment, and they recognized him by his front teeth, which were like strung pearls. It has also been said: they did not recognize him until he lifted the crown from his head, and they saw a mark on his forehead that belonged to Yaʿqub and Sarah, resembling a white mole (shāmah). If you ask: they asked him about himself, so why did he answer about them and about his brother, when his brother was known to them? I say: because mention of his brother was an explanation of what they had asked about, [namely] "Whoever is mindful of God (yattaqi) — that is, fears God and His punishment — and is patient (yaṣbir) — that is, refrains from sins and persists in obedience — indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers (al-muḥsinīn)." So he placed "the good-doers" in place of the pronoun, because it includes those who are mindful and patient. ﴿God has certainly preferred you over us﴾, that is, He has favoured you over us with piety, patience and the conduct of the good-doers. And our state and condition is that we were sinners, deliberately committing wrongdoing; we did not guard ourselves and we did not endure patiently. Undoubtedly God has exalted you with kingship and abased us through our humbling ourselves before you.

﴿No reproach shall be upon you today﴾: there is no rebuke or blame upon you. The root of tathrīb is from ths-r-b, which is the fat that covers the stomach (thurb). Its meaning is the removal of the thurb, just as tajlīd (flaying) and taqrīʿ (scolding) mean removing the skin and the scab (qaraʿ). This is because when it is removed, that is the ultimate in emaciation and wasting, so it is struck as an image for the scolding that tears apart reputations and takes away the honour of faces. If you ask: with what is "today" connected? I say: with tathrīb, or with the implied element in ʿalaykum (the sense of "settling"), or with yaghfiru. The meaning: there is no blame upon you today, which is the day that is the very occasion for blame, so what do you think of other days? Then he began, saying: ﴿May God forgive you﴾, so he invoked forgiveness for them for what they had committed. It is said: "Ghafara Allāhu laka" and "Yaghfiru Allāhu laka," using both the past and present forms. From this is the phrase of one who blesses someone who sneezes: "Yahdīkumu Allāhu wa-yuṣliḥu bālakum." And "today God forgives you" is a glad tidings of the swift forgiveness of God, because of their repentance and remorse for their sin that renewed on that day.

It is related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took hold of the two posts of the door of the Kaʿbah on the day of the Conquest, and said to the Quraysh: "What do you think I will do with you?" They said: "We expect good: a noble brother and the son of a noble brother, and you have power." He said: "I say what my brother Yusuf said: ﴿No reproach shall be upon you today﴾." [Narrated by al-Nasāʾī and al-Bayhaqī from the narration of Thābit from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Rabāḥ from Abū Hurayrah with similar meaning and more complete. Al-Thaʿlabī narrated it from the narration of Samʿān from ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbās with this wording and more complete. Likewise Ibn Isḥāq mentioned it from some scholars and said in it "you have power, so forgive," and likewise al-Wāqidī narrated it in al-Maghāzī from the hadith of Barrah bint Tajrāh. Abū ʿUbayd narrated it in al-Amwāl from Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Ḥusayn.]

It is also related that when Abū Sufyān came to embrace Islam, al-ʿAbbās said to him: "When you come to the Messenger, recite to him: ﴿No reproach shall be upon you﴾," and he did so. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "May God forgive you and whoever taught you." [I have not found it.]

It is also related that when his brothers recognized him, they sent to him: "You invite us to your food morning and evening, and we are ashamed before you because of what we committed against you." Yusuf said: "The people of Egypt, even though you have ruled over them, look at me with the first eye, and they say: 'Glory be to Him who raised a slave sold for twenty dirhams to what he has reached.' Indeed you have now become noble through being with you, and I have become great in the eyes when people know that you are my brothers and that I am a descendant of Ibrahim."

﴿Go with this shirt of mine﴾: it is said it is the inherited shirt which was in the amulet of Yusuf, and it was from Paradise. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verses 94–96:

فَصَلَتِ الْعِيرُ (So when the caravan set out) means it departed from the outskirts (ʿarīsh) of Egypt. It is said: faṣala min al-balad fuṣūlan (فصل من البلد فصولا) when one separates from the town and passes beyond its walls. Ibn ʿAbbas recited: فلما انفصل العير (When the caravan had separated), قالَ لولد ولده ومن حوله من قومه (he said to his grandchildren and those around him among his people):

إِنِّي لَأَجِدُ رِيحَ يُوسُفَ (﴿Indeed, I find the scent of Yusuf﴾). God caused him to find the smell of the shirt when it arrived from a distance of eight (days' journey).

Al-tafnīd (التفنيد) means attributing to someone al-fand (الفند), which is senility, and loss of reason due to old age. It is said: shaykh mufannad (شيخ مفند), an aged man who has lost his reason; one does not say ʿajūz mufannada (عجوز مفندة) for a woman, because she was never possessed of judgment in her youth that could be lost in her old age. The meaning of لَوْلا أَنْ تُفَنِّدُونِ (﴿Were it not that you think me senile﴾) is: لَصَدَّقْتُمُونِي (﴿you would have believed me﴾), لَفِي ضَلالِكَ الْقَدِيمِ (﴿You are surely in your old error﴾), that is, in your departure from the right course, in ancient times, in excessive love for Yusuf, in your constant mention of him, and in your hope of meeting him, while they thought he had died.

أَلْقاهُ (﴿He cast it﴾): the bearer of good tidings cast the shirt upon the face of Yaʿqub.

Or, it was Yaʿqub who cast it. فَارْتَدَّ بَصِيراً (﴿and he regained his sight﴾): he returned seeing. It is said: radda-hu fa-ertadda (ردّه فارتد) and irtadda-hu (ارتده) when he took it back.

أَلَمْ أَقُلْ لَكُمْ (﴿Did I not tell you﴾): this refers to his saying إِنِّي لَأَجِدُ رِيحَ يُوسُفَ (﴿Indeed, I find the scent of Yusuf﴾), or to his saying وَلا تَيْأَسُوا مِنْ رَوْحِ اللَّهِ (﴿and do not despair of relief from God﴾), and to his saying إِنِّي أَعْلَمُ (﴿Indeed, I know﴾), which is a fresh statement not governed by the preceding speech. You may take it as governed by it, and read it together with his saying إِنَّما أَشْكُوا بَثِّي وَحُزْنِي إِلَى اللَّهِ وَأَعْلَمُ مِنَ اللَّهِ ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ (﴿I only complain of my anguish and grief to God, and I know from God what you do not know﴾).

It is narrated: he asked the bearer of good tidings, "How is Yusuf?" He said, "He is king of Egypt." He said: "What do I care for kingship? Has he left a religion?" He said, "On the religion of Islam." He said: "Now the blessing is complete."
