It is said: faṣala min al-balad fuṣūlan (فصل من البلد فصولا) when one separates from the town and passes beyond its walls. Ibn ʿAbbas recited: فلما انفصل العير (When the caravan had separated), قالَ لولد ولده ومن حوله من قومه (he said to his grandchildren and those around him among his people):

إِنِّي لَأَجِدُ رِيحَ يُوسُفَ (﴿Indeed, I find the scent of Yusuf﴾). God caused him to find the smell of the shirt when it arrived from a distance of eight (days' journey).

Al-tafnīd (التفنيد) means attributing to someone al-fand (الفند), which is senility, and loss of reason due to old age. It is said: shaykh mufannad (شيخ مفند), an aged man who has lost his reason; one does not say ʿajūz mufannada (عجوز مفندة) for a woman, because she was never possessed of judgment in her youth that could be lost in her old age. The meaning of لَوْلا أَنْ تُفَنِّدُونِ (﴿Were it not that you think me senile﴾) is: لَصَدَّقْتُمُونِي (﴿you would have believed me﴾), لَفِي ضَلالِكَ الْقَدِيمِ (﴿You are surely in your old error﴾), that is, in your departure from the right course, in ancient times, in excessive love for Yusuf, in your constant mention of him, and in your hope of meeting him, while they thought he had died.

أَلْقاهُ (﴿He cast it﴾): the bearer of good tidings cast the shirt upon the face of Yaʿqub.

Or, it was Yaʿqub who cast it. فَارْتَدَّ بَصِيراً (﴿and he regained his sight﴾): he returned seeing. It is said: radda-hu fa-ertadda (ردّه فارتد) and irtadda-hu (ارتده) when he took it back.

أَلَمْ أَقُلْ لَكُمْ (﴿Did I not tell you﴾): this refers to his saying إِنِّي لَأَجِدُ رِيحَ يُوسُفَ (﴿Indeed, I find the scent of Yusuf﴾), or to his saying وَلا تَيْأَسُوا مِنْ رَوْحِ اللَّهِ (﴿and do not despair of relief from God﴾), and to his saying إِنِّي أَعْلَمُ (﴿Indeed, I know﴾), which is a fresh statement not governed by the preceding speech. You may take it as governed by it, and read it together with his saying إِنَّما أَشْكُوا بَثِّي وَحُزْنِي إِلَى اللَّهِ وَأَعْلَمُ مِنَ اللَّهِ ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ (﴿I only complain of my anguish and grief to God, and I know from God what you do not know﴾).

It is narrated: he asked the bearer of good tidings, "How is Yusuf?" He said, "He is king of Egypt." He said: "What do I care for kingship? Has he left a religion?" He said, "On the religion of Islam." He said: "Now the blessing is complete."

Surah 12, verses 97–98:

﴿سَوْفَ أَسْتَغْفِرُ لَكُمْ﴾ ("I will ask forgiveness for you"). It was said: he delayed the seeking of forgiveness until the time of the pre-dawn (al-sahar). It was also said: until the night of Friday, so that he would deliberately seek it at the time of answered supplication. It was said: [he delayed it] to learn their condition regarding the sincerity and purity of their repentance. It was also said: he intended to persist in seeking forgiveness for them. It is related that he used to seek forgiveness for them every Friday night for some twenty-odd years.

It was said: he stood up to pray at the time of the pre-dawn, and when he had finished he raised his hands and said: "O Allah, forgive me my anguish over Yusuf and my lack of patience with regard to him, and forgive my sons for what they did to their brother." So Allah revealed to him: "Indeed Allah has forgiven you and them all."

It is related that they said to him, when the sorrow had overtaken them: "Our pardon from you would avail us nothing, if our Lord does not pardon us. If you are not inspired with forgiveness for us, may our eyes never be comforted." So the Shaykh (Ya'qub) faced the qiblah standing and supplicating, and Yusuf stood behind him saying "Amin," and they stood behind the two of them, humbled and submissive, for twenty years, until their exertion reached its limit and they thought it was destruction. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended and said: "Indeed Allah has answered your supplication concerning your son, and has bound their covenants after you to prophethood, though there has been disagreement about whether they were prophets."

When they entered upon Yusuf, he took his parents to himself. It is said that he sent to his father a gift (jihaz) and two hundred mounts (rahila), so that he might equip himself with those who were with him. Yusuf went out with the king in four thousand troops, along with the nobles and all the people of Egypt, and they met Ya'qub as he walked leaning on Yahudha. He looked at the horses and the people and said: "O Yahudha, is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said: "No, this is your son." When he met him, Ya'qub, peace be upon him, said: "Peace be upon you, O remover of sorrows."

It is said that when they met, Yusuf said to him: "O father, you wept for me until your sight was lost. Did you not know that the Resurrection will gather us?" He said: "Yes, but I feared that your religion would be taken from you, and then I would be separated from you."

It is also said that Ya'qub and his children entered Egypt when they were seventy-two, men and women, and they left it with Musa, and their fighting men were six hundred thousand, five hundred and some seventy men, apart from the offspring and the aged; and the offspring were one million and two hundred thousand.

﴿He took his parents to himself﴾: he drew them to himself, embraced them. Ibn Abi Ishaq said: "His mother was alive." It is also said: "They were his father and his maternal aunt. His mother had died, so he married her, and she was counted as one of the two parents, because a stepmother is called a mother, due to her standing in the place of the mother, or because a maternal aunt is a mother just as a paternal uncle is a father." From this is His saying: ﴿the God of your fathers, Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq﴾.

If you ask: what is the meaning of their entering upon him before their entering Egypt? I say: as if, when he met them, he descended to them in a tent (madrib) [[His phrase "in a tent": al-Nasafi's wording: a tent pitched for shelter. (ʿ)]] or a house, then they entered upon him and he took his parents to himself, then he said to them: ﴿Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security﴾. When he entered Egypt and sat in his council, seated upright on his throne, and they gathered to him, he honored his parents and raised them upon the throne, and ﴿they fell down before him in prostration﴾, meaning the eleven brothers and the two parents. It is also possible that he went out in a dome of the royal domes carried on mules, and he commanded that his parents be brought up to him, and they both entered upon him in the dome. He drew them to himself by embracing them and brought them near to him, and after that said: "Enter Egypt."

If you ask: to what is the will (mashi'a) attached? I say: to entering, qualified by security, because the intention is that they be characterized by security in their entering, so it is as if it was said to them: "Be safe and secure in your entering, if God wills." Its parallel is your saying to the warrior: "Return safe and laden with spoil, if God wills." The will is not attached to returning absolutely, but restricted to safety and spoil, qualified by them. The estimate is: "Enter Egypt secure, if God wills you enter secure," then the response was omitted because the speech indicates it, then the conditional clause was inserted between the circumstantial phrase and its subject. Among the bizarre interpretations is that His saying ﴿if God wills﴾ is by way of anticipation and postponement, and that its place is after His saying ﴿I will ask my Lord for forgiveness for you﴾ in the speech of Ya'qub, and I do not know what to say about it and its like.

If you ask: how was it permissible for them to prostrate to other than God? I say: prostration among them was in the manner of greeting and honor, like standing, shaking hands, and kissing the hand, and similar acts that the custom of people has established, of deeds famous for exalting and honoring. It is also said: it was only a bowing without placing the foreheads on the ground, and their falling in prostration denies that. It is also said: its meaning is that they fell down prostrate to God, for the sake of Yusuf, in thanks. This too has a figurative sense.

It is said: "He did good to him and by him," and likewise "he did evil to him and by him." A poet said:

"Harm us or do us good, there is no blame"

﴿from the desert﴾: from the badiya, because they were people of tents and owners of livestock, moving among the waters and pastures. ﴿Shaytan had incited (nazagha) discord between us﴾: he corrupted between us and stirred up enmity; its origin is the trainer's goading of the animal and urging it to run. It is said: "nazaghahu" and "nasaghahu," when he pricked him. ﴿Gracious to what He wills﴾: subtle in arranging for it, gentle, so that it comes about in the manner of wisdom and rightness.

It is related that Yusuf took Ya'qub by the hand and walked him through his treasuries, causing him to enter the treasuries of silver and gold, the treasuries of jewelry, the treasuries of garments, the treasuries of weapons, and other things. When he brought him into the treasury of papers, he said: "O my son, what is this disobedience? You have these papers, and what you wrote to me from eight stages away?"

He said: "Jibril commanded me." He said: "Did you not ask him?" He said: "You are closer to him than I am, so ask him." Jibril, peace be upon him, said: "God Most High commanded me to do so, because of your saying ﴿and I fear that the wolf will devour him﴾." He said: "Would that you had feared Me instead."

It is related that Ya'qub stayed with him for twenty-four years, then died. He had bequeathed that he be buried in Syria beside his father Ishaq. So Yusuf himself went and buried him there, then returned to Egypt, and he lived after his father twenty-three years. When his affair was complete and he knew that it would not last for him, his soul sought the everlasting, eternal kingdom, and his soul longed for it, so he wished for death. It is said: no prophet before him or after him wished for it, and God caused him to die pure and pristine. The people of Egypt disputed and quarreled over his burial, each wanting to be buried in their own quarter, until they were about to fight. They judged it right to make for him a coffin of marble and placed him in it, and buried him in the Nile in a place where the water passes over him and then reaches Egypt, so that they would all share in him equally [[His phrase "so that they would all share in him equally": in al-Sihah: people in this matter are a share (shirʿ), meaning equal, vocalized either way. (ʿ)]]. And there were born to him Ifraithim and Misha. To Ifraithim was born Nun, and to Nun was born Yusha', the young man of Musa. The Pharaohs after him inherited Egypt from the Amalekites, and the children of Israel remained under their hands upon the remnants of the religion of Yusuf and his fathers, until God sent Musa, ﷺ.

"Min" in "min al-mulk" and "min ta'wil al-ahadith" is for partitive (tab'id), because he was only given some of the kingdom of this world, or some of the kingdom of Egypt, and some of the interpretation.

Anta waliyyi (You are my Protector): You are the One who takes care of me with blessings in both abodes, and who joins the transient kingdom to the enduring kingdom.

Tawaffani musliman (Cause me to die in submission): a request to die in a state of Islam, and so that he may be concluded with goodness and the best end, just as Ya'qub said to his sons: ﴿And do not die except as Muslims﴾. It is also permissible that it be a wish for death, as has been said, ﴿and join me with the righteous﴾, [meaning] among my forefathers, or it may be in general.

It is related from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that Maymun ibn Mihran spent the night at his house, and he saw him weeping much and asking for death. He said to him: "May God make much good come through your hands: you have revived sunnas and extinguished innovations, and your life is good and a relief for the Muslims." He said: "Shall I not be like the righteous servant, whom God gladdened the eye of and whose affair He gathered for him?" [Then he] said: ﴿Cause me to die in submission and join me with the righteous.﴾

If you say: "On what is fatir al-samawat (Originator of the heavens) in the accusative?" I say: it is an adjective of rabb (Lord), like your saying "akhu Zayd hasan al-wajh" (the brother of Zayd, handsome of face), or it is in the vocative (an address).

That (ذلِكَ) is a reference to the account of Yusuf mentioned before it, and the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ); its position is as the subject (mubtada'). His saying "from the tidings of the Unseen We reveal it to you" (مِنْ أَنْباءِ الْغَيْبِ نُوحِيهِ إِلَيْكَ) is the predicate (khabar) of inna. It is also permissible that it be a relative noun (ism mawsul) in the sense of "that which," with "from the tidings of the Unseen" as its relative clause (silah), and "We reveal it" as the predicate. The meaning is: this account is something unseen which did not reach you except through revelation, because you were not present with the sons of Ya'qub when they resolved upon their matter, which was casting their brother into the well, as in His saying: ﴿and they agreed to put him in the depth of the well﴾. This is a mockery of Quraysh and of those who denied him, for it was not hidden from any of the deniers that he (ﷺ) had not been among the transmitters of this narrative or its like, nor had he met anyone in it or heard from anyone about it, and it was not part of the knowledge of his people. So when he reported it and recounted this wondrous story, which overwhelmed its bearers and narrators, no doubt could arise that it was not from him and that it came by way of revelation. Then if they denied it, he mocked them, and it was said to them: "You know, O obstinate ones, that he was not a witness to the generations of the past." A similar verse is: ﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed the command to Musa, nor were you among the witnesses﴾, while they were plotting against Yusuf and devising harm for him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verses 103–104:

"And most of mankind" (wa-ma aktharu al-nas): he means the whole category, as in His saying, ﴿But most of mankind do not believe﴾. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he meant the people of Makkah. That is, "they are not believers."

"Even if you were eager and keen for their faith" (wa-law harastA wa-tahallaktA ʿala imanihim): because of their determination in disbelief and their obstinacy.

"And you do not ask them" (wa-ma tasaluhum) "for anything" ('ala ma tuhadithuhum bihi wa-tudhakkiruhum): for what you tell them and remind them of, that they should bestow upon you some benefit or gain, as givers of gifts give to the narrators of stories and reports.

"It is only a reminder" (in huwa illa dhikrun): an admonition from Allah "to all the worlds" (li-l-ʿalamin), in general, and an exhortation to seek salvation through the tongue of one of His messengers.

"And you do not ask them" (wa-ma tasaluhum) "for anything" ('ala ma tuhadithuhum bihi wa-tudhakkiruhum): for what you tell them and remind them of, that they should bestow upon you some benefit or gain, as givers of gifts give to the narrators of stories and reports.

"It is only a reminder" (in huwa illa dhikrun): an admonition from Allah "to all the worlds" (li-l-ʿalamin), in general, and an exhortation to seek salvation through the tongue of one of His messengers.

From the sign: a proof and indication of the Creator, of His attributes, and of His oneness. They pass by it and see it, while they turn away from it and do not take heed from it.

It is read also "wa-l-arḍu" (and the earth) in the nominative, as a subject (mubtada'), with "yamurrūna 'alayhā" (they pass by it) as its predicate (khabar). And al-Suddi read it in the accusative: "wa-l-arḍa" (and the earth), meaning: they tread upon the earth, passing over it.

In the codex of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): "wa-l-arḍu yamshūna 'alayhā" (and the earth, they walk upon it), with "al-arḍu" in the nominative. The intended meaning is what they see of the traces of the destroyed nations and other lessons.

And most of them do not believe in God, even while they acknowledge Him and that He created them and created the heavens and the earth, except that they associate others with Him in worship by worshipping idols. It is also reported from al-Hasan: they are the People of the Book, who have both shirk and belief. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: they are those who liken Allah to His creation.
*Ghashiyah* (an overwhelming): a vengeance that overtakes them. It is said: what overwhelms them of punishment and envelops them. It is said: the thunderbolts.

This is my way: the way here means the call to faith and monotheism (tawhid). "Sabil" and "tariq" (way, path) may be masculine or feminine.

Then he explains "his way" with His words: ﴿I call to God with insight﴾, that is, I call to His religion with clear proof, not blind. "Ana" (I) is an emphatic confirmation of the pronoun hidden in "ad'u" (I call). "Wa man ittaba'ani" (and whoever follows me) is coordinated with it. The meaning is: I call to it, and whoever follows me calls to it.

It is also permissible for "ana" to be the subject (mubtada'), with "ala basirah" (with insight) as its fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and "man ittaba'ani" coordinated with "ana" as a statement that he and whoever follows him are upon proof and evidence, not upon whim (hawa). It is also permissible for "ala basirah" to be a circumstantial clause (hal) from "ad'u," its governing factor being the nominative in "ana" and "man ittaba'ani."

﴿And glory be to God﴾, and I exalt Him above the partners.

[[The author's note on the phrase "wa anzahu minash-shurakaa'" (and I exalt Him above the partners): "perhaps it is 'an' (from)" (ʿ).]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 12, verse 109:

﴿Only men,﴾ not angels, "because they used to say: ﴿If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels.﴾" And Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: he means, "there was no woman among them." It was also said: (this refers) to Sajah the false prophetess.

*And the prophets of Allah have never been males only*
*She has become a prophetess, a female among women...*

*So may the curse of Allah and of all the people be upon Sajah, and upon whoever was led astray by falsehood with her.*

*I mean Musaylima the liar — may his echoes never be watered*
*by rain-cloud wherever it may be.*

(The verses are) by Qays ibn ʿAasim. It is also transmitted as "nutiffu bihā" instead of "nisāʾ bihā." Ṭāfa bihi yaṭūfu means he circled around it; Ṭāfa bihi yaṭīfu means he came upon him and alighted upon him. This is the passive form of the latter, coordinated with "aḍḥat." It is also transmitted in place of the first hemistich: "fa-mā samiʿtu bi-unthā qaṭṭu arsalahā," where the subject is the pronoun of Allah even though no referent has preceded it, because it is evident. It is also transmitted in place of the second: "wa-aṣbaḥat anbiyāʾu n-nāsi dhukrānā."

Sajah: a proper name of a woman, from *sajaḥa* (to be forgiving and to pardon). She was the daughter of al-Mundhir, a noblewoman among her people, the Banu Hanifa. She claimed prophethood, then married Musaylima the liar, and her people followed him. Then Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) fought him, and he was killed at the hand of Wahshi, the slayer of Hamza. She embraced Islam after him, and her Islam was good. It is also transmitted as "bi-l-lu'm" in place of "bi-l-ifk." "Lā saqat" is a supplicatory clause. *Al-aṣdāʾ* is the plural of *ṣadā*, which is the "bird of the day." The Arabs used to claim that the bones of a slain man's head turn into an owl that screeches, "Avenge me, avenge me," until his blood is taken; here it is a metaphor for his entire corpse. *Al-mazn* is singular *mazna*, meaning cloud. That is: O Allah, make his grave scorching for him, so that no rain reaches it.

It is also read: ﴿nūḥī ilayhim﴾ with the nūn (we reveal to them), in the active voice; so the original reading is with the yāʾ, in the passive voice. (ʿ)

﴿from the people of the towns,﴾ because they are more knowledgeable and more forbearing, whereas the people of the desert have ignorance, coarseness and harshness. ﴿And the Abode of the Hereafter﴾, i.e., the abode of the Hour, or the state of the Hereafter, ﴿is better for those who are mindful of Allah,﴾ i.e., for those who fear Allah, so they do not associate partners with Him and do not disobey Him. It is also read: ﴿afa-lā taʿqilūn﴾ with the tāʾ and with the yāʾ.

Al-Zamakhshari, *al-Kashshaf*, on Surah 12, verse 110:

﴿Until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied, Our help came to them, and whom We willed was delivered. And Our punishment is not averted from the guilty people.﴾ *Hatta* is connected to an omitted element implied by the context, as if it were said: ﴿And We did not send before you except men﴾, so that their help was delayed until they despaired of help and thought that they had been denied. *Kudhdhibu* means that their own selves denied them. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is that they despaired of help and thought that their souls had denied them…" etc. Ahmad said: It does not necessarily follow that God had promised them victory in this world. Rather, they were thinking this and hoping for it without report or revelation,]] when I told them that they would be given victory, or their hope was based on their own words, a true hope or a false hope. The meaning is that the period of denial and enmity from the disbelievers, and the waiting for help from God and hoping for it, had stretched out and prolonged upon them, until they sensed despair and imagined that there would be no help for them in this world, and then Our help came to them suddenly, unexpectedly.

It is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him: "And they thought, when they were weakened and overcome, that they had failed in what God had promised them of help." [[His speech returns. He said: "It is transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: 'So they thought, when they were weakened and overcome…' etc." Ahmad said: This is also a good interpretation that reconciles the two readings, because the nations' thinking that their messengers had lied is a denial of them, so it has the same effect as the emphatic reading.]] He said: They were human, and he recited ﴿And they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of God?"﴾ [2:214]. If this is authentically from Ibn Abbas, then by *zann* (thought) he meant what occurs to the mind and passes through the heart as a whisper and self-talk, as is the nature of humans. As for *zann* in the sense of inclining toward one of two possibilities over the other, this is not permissible for any Muslim. So what about the messengers of God, who are the people most knowing of their Lord, and that He is exalted above breaking promises and free of every ugliness?

It was also said: The thought of those to whom they were sent was that the messengers had lied, that is, had failed to fulfil. Or: the thought of those to whom they were sent was that they had been denied by the messengers, that is, the messengers had denied them in their claim that they would be given victory over them, and they had not believed them in it.

It was read *kudhdhibu* with emphasis (*mushaddadan*), meaning: and the messengers thought that their people had denied them in what they had promised them of punishment and of victory over them.

Mujahid read *kudhdhibu* without emphasis, with the active form (*bina' lil-fa'il*), meaning: and the messengers thought that they had lied in what they had told their people of victory. This is either on the interpretation of Ibn Abbas, or because when their people did not see any sign of their promise, they said to them: "You have indeed lied to us," so they became liars in the eyes of their people. Or: the thought of those to whom they were sent was that the messengers had lied.

If this were read emphatically, its meaning would be: the messengers thought that their people had denied them in their promise.

*Fa-nunajji* is read with light and heavy emphasis, from *anjahu* and *najjahu* (both meaning "to deliver"). *Fa-unjiya* is read in the past passive form. Ibn Muhaysin read *fa-najaa*.

By *man nasha'* (whom We will) is meant the believers, because they are the ones deserving that God wills their deliverance. This is explained by His words: ﴿And Our punishment is not averted from the guilty people.﴾

The pronoun in "qasasihim" (their stories) refers to the messengers, and the reading of those who recite "fi qasasihim" with a kasra on the qaf supports this. It was also said that it refers to Joseph and his brothers.

If you say: to what does the pronoun in "ma kana hadithan yuftara" (it was not a fabricated narration) refer, according to the one who reads it with a kasra? I say: to the Qur'an, meaning: the Qur'an was not a narration that is fabricated, but rather it is a confirmation of what is before it (tasdiq alladhi bayna yadayh), i.e., the scriptures revealed before it, and a detailed explanation (tafsil) of every thing that is needed in the religion, because it is the standard (qanun) upon which the Sunnah, the consensus (ijma') and analogy (qiyas) rest after the proofs of reason. The accusative of "ma nusiba" after "lakin" is in coordination with the predicate of "kana." It has also been read as "dhalika" in the nominative, meaning: "but it is the confirmation of what is before it."

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Teach your slaves Surah Yusuf, for whichever Muslim recites it and teaches it to his family and to those whom his right hand possesses, Allah will ease for him the agonies of death, and grant him the strength not to envy any Muslim."

[The chain of narration for this was mentioned previously in the tafsir of Surah Ali Imran, and it is at the end of Ali Imran, and also at the end of the book.]
